title: Given circumstances, Amani Hooker addition was Buffalo Bills best potential move at trade deadline
summary: Nothing happens in a vacuum. Using words like “good” or “bad” inevitably unlocks a more nuanced “good relative to what” or “bad relative to what” conversation. Thus, when the time comes to evaluate the Buffalo Bills’ acquisition of safety Amani Hooker from the Tennessee Titans, the question of whether or not the move is good […]
full_text: Nothing happens in a vacuum. Using words like “good” or “bad” inevitably unlocks a more nuanced “good relative to what” or “bad relative to what” conversation. Thus, when the time comes to evaluate the Buffalo Bills’ acquisition of safety Amani Hooker from the Tennessee Titans, the question of whether or not the move is good is a very different question than whether or not the move is optimal . “Good” is a value in vs. value out proposition, with the acknowledgement that the concept of value is subjective based upon how someone weights Hooker’s skill, short vs. long term considerations, and financial items. “Optimal” is instead a reflection of the level of “good” achieved from this maneuver compared to the level of “good” that could have hypothetically been achieved through a different maneuver entirely. It’s a question that folds in opportunity cost amongst all potential other maneuvers. In this author’s opinion, the Hooker transaction is both good and optimal. Other content pieces can discuss the “good” part of that statement. Hooker’s skill set, the compensation, the need at safety, the fact that he’s under contract through 2028 with reasonable cap hits…I’ll let other articles and podcasts outline why those factors all come together to form a conclusion that the addition of Hooker is a good one. I’d instead like to make the argument here that not only was the Hooker addition good , it was the most good the team could have done with its resources at the trade deadline and therefore optimal. In order to do that, I will need to discuss two separate items: what the Bills could have spent and what they could have received. Everything in life is a value proposition: what you give vs. what you get. In order to prove that the Hooker trade was optimal, I need to create a clear picture of all the potential combinations of “give” and “get” and when none of them create a better (“more good”) outcome when compared to the Hooker trade, I can then argue that the transaction was optimal. The Bills came into the trade deadline with about $4 million in cap space. In any discussion about the salary cap, it’s important to note that how much current cap space a team has is not as important as how much cap space they can create . Teams have releases and restructures on certain contracts available to them (henceforth called “levers”) that can generate current-year cap space while frequently increasing the cap burden in subsequent years (important note: mid-season veteran releases do not typically create any cap space for the releasing team because veteran salaries become fully guaranteed upon the regular season beginning). Inevitably, conversations come up that include statements like “the (Team) made it fit on their salary cap” while ignoring the fact that a team with X amount in cap space after pulling their levers is very different than a team with that same X amount in cap space before pulling their levers. I say this to say: the Bills had pulled almost all of their levers and still had $4M in cap space. The two main remaining levers to create current year cap space were a trade of wide receiver Josh Palmer (rendered almost impossible by his injury) and a restructure to the contract of left tackle Dion Dawkins (due about $15.5M in salary for the 2026 year that could be converted, in whole or in part, to a signing bonus). The Bills showed that $4M in cap space, but with a full restructure of all of Dawkins’ 2026 salary, they could have theoretically gotten about $14M more for a total of $18m in cap. So we have successfully outlined that the Bills could have reasonably gone shopping with $18m in cap space and their current crop of draft picks. But what could they have gotten with those resources? The only trades we know for certain could have been executed upon were the trades that were actually, you know, executed upon. We could scream into the ether that Brian Thomas Jr., wide receiver for the Jacksonville Jaguars, would have been available for a fourth-round pick, but he wasn’t actually traded, so we don’t know. The Jaguars could have been holding out for a second-round pick and more in the vein of the Marvin Harrison Jr. deal that was made by the Houston Texans or even more, we can create hypothetical trade scenarios in our heads all we want, but they wouldn’t be based in anything factual and shouldn’t be used in evaluation of the merits of decisions that were actually made. Here is a full list of trades that were executed in the lead up to the 2026 NFL trade deadline, per msn.com : Nov. 10 : The Atlanta Falcons traded C Ryan Neuzil to the Baltimore Ravens for G Andrew Vorhees and a 2028 sixth-round pick. Nov. 10 : The Indianapolis Colts traded WR Josh Downs and a 2027 seventh-round pick to the Kansas City Chiefs for a 2027 fourth-round pick and a 2027 fifth-round pick. Nov. 10 : The Los Angeles Chargers traded LB Daiyan Henry to the Denver Broncos for a 2027 fourth-round pick and a 2027 fifth-round pick. Nov. 10 : The Las Vegas Raiders traded QB Kirk Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings for a 2027 third-round pick. Nov. 10 : The Tennessee Titans traded S Amani Hooker and a fifth-round pick to the Buffalo Bills for a second-round pick. Nov. 10 : The Indianapolis Colts traded WR Keenan Allen to the San Francisco 49ers for a 2027 sixth-round pick. Nov. 9: The Philadelphia Eagles traded DT Jordan Davis to the Jacksonville Jaguars for a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick. Nov. 9: The New York Jets traded S Andre Cisco to the Detroit Lions for a 2028 sixth-round pick. Nov. 9: The New Orleans Saints traded DT Davon Godchaux to the Jacksonville Jaguars for a 2028 sixth-round pick. Nov. 9 : The Atlanta Falcons traded S Jessie Bates to the Jacksonville Jaguars for a second-round pick and a fifth-round pick. Nov. 4 : The Arizona Cardinals traded QB Jacoby Brissett and a fifth-round pick to the Baltimore Ravens for a fourth-round pick and a seventh-round pick. Oct. 29 : The Tennessee Titans traded DT Jeffery Simmons and a 2028 fifth-round pick to the Chicago Bears for two first-round picks and a 2027 fourth-round pick. Oct. 27 : The Indianapolis Colts traded DT DeForest Buckner to the San Francisco 49ers for a fourth-round pick. Oct. 27 : The Indianapolis Colts traded OG Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks for third- and fifth-round picks. Oct. 11 : The Arizona Cardinals traded WR Marvin Harrison Jr. to the Houston Texans for second- and sixth-round picks. Oct. 7 : The Philadelphia Eagles traded OG Cam Jurgens and a seventh-round pick to the Baltimore Ravens for a 2028 second-round pick and 2027 fifth-round pick. Sept. 30 : The Pittsburgh Steelers traded CB Joey Porter Jr. to the Dallas Cowboys for a 2028 second-round pick and 2027 sixth-round pick. Sept. 28 : The Minnesota Vikings traded QB J.J. McCarthy to the New York Giants for a 2027 fifth-round pick. Of those trades, we can outline the Simmons, Buckner, Nelson, MHJ, Porter Jr., Davis, Bates, Cisco, Godchaux, Allen, Hooker, Henry, and Downs trades as moves that would have, in a vacuum, have added talent to the Bills roster at positions of at least mild interest or need. The Bills could have traded for Jeffrey Simmons and fit his 2026 salary cap figure ($7.94M) into their current situation with a partial Dawkins restructure. It would have cost them two first round picks to do so and they would have had to make notable 2027 decisions (where they are currently projected to be at least $47M over the 2027 cap limit), but they could have done it this year. I’d make an argument that the Marvin Harrison Jr. deal was a notable overpay by the Texans given his on-field production thus far in his career. Nelson is an expiring contract at a non-problematic position for the Bills despite his excellence. Buckner and Downs are also expiring contracts, though I could make an argument that Downs is exactly the type of man-beater wide receiver the Bills have continually searched for since the departure of Stefon Diggs…
author: Bruce Nolan

title: Bills S Amani Hooker may play Week 10 vs. New York Jets
summary: It’s sounding more and more like new Buffalo Bills safety Amani Hooker could suit up to play in Week 10 against the New York Jets, at least if we’re to read the tea leaves from head coach Joe Brady’s latest media session. Brady pointed to Hooker’s status as a “savvy” and “cerebral” eight-year NFL veteran […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 20: Amani Hooker #37 of the Tennessee Titans looks on prior to the game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Nissan Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s sounding more and more like new Buffalo Bills safety Amani Hooker could suit up to play in Week 10 against the New York Jets, at least if we’re to read the tea leaves from head coach Joe Brady’s latest media session. Brady pointed to Hooker’s status as a “savvy” and “cerebral” eight-year NFL veteran who oozes “football intelligence” with a ton of experience to boot. Brady said that “(s)ometimes it’s just about learning the terminology, and it might of meant this in one place, but now it’s this — and I think these guys usually pick it up at a fast rate.” As such, Brady and defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard aren’t going to hurry Hooker, nor ask him to do anything he’s not prepared to tackle within Buffalo’s scheme, noting “we’ll take it day by day and see how much he can process, and how fast he can and what he can handle to be able to go out there on the road and be able to communicate — whatever he can handle, we’ll ask him to do that.” It’s undoubtedly a short turnaround for Hooker to potentially suit up and play for his new team. Fortunately, he was on a bye this past week with his old team, the Tennessee Titans. However, arriving on Wednesday and having to navigate everything that comes with packing up and moving to a new city is no small feat for an NFL player. For his part, Hooker sounds ready to go, and very excited, admitting that he’s “on social media, so I hear all the rumors,” which means he probably had a feeling something was brewing. When asked about the challenge of changing teams midseason, Hooker didn’t hesitate in stepping up to the plate, saying “I pride myself on being a pro and being ready when my name is called no matter what.” His plan? Hooker will soak up all he can with his coaches this week, putting in “a little overtime this week and get up to speed on the style of play we want here, and just deliver.” When asked just how different is Leonhard’s scheme is, Hooker simply said that “at the end of the day, it’s football. Every team runs Cover 4. Every team runs Cover 2, and Cover 3. So, it’s really just about terminology, and what they call different things , and how they play certain looks. That Brady isn’t ruling out Hooker playing in Week 10 speaks to the important role he’s set to play as a starter alongside safety Cole Bishop. One Bills Drive has been searching for a new lock-down safety tandem since Micah Hyde and Jordan Poyer hung up their Bills cleats. President of football operations/general manager Brandon Beane went so far as to compare Hooker to Hyde following the news of successful trade. It took a lot of discussion and a ton of convincing for Beane and his team to land Hooker. Asked about the Iowa connection, where Hyde also played collegiately, Hooker remarked that Hyde “was the standard” and someone to whom he said “I idol my game after him.” Could it be that the Bills may have just found the right fit for the start of something special at safety? In noting the opportunity in front of him, Hooker said that “it’s tremendous and it’s exciting. I mean, to be in this position with a contender. It’s a dream come true. I’ve always wanted to be in this position.” We’ll find out what’s in store for Amani Hooker on Sunday afternoon.
author: Matt Byham

title: Four starting offensive linemen limited as Buffalo Bills prepare for Jets
summary: The Buffalo Bills just finished a very tough stretch of their schedule, and they did it while juggling injuries and playing roster-Jenga to keep the right personnel on the game day roster. Now they enter Week 10 as the league’s top team, the AFC’s number one seed and in control of their post-season destiny.   […]
full_text: Bills offensive line work through blocking drills. The Buffalo Bills just finished a very tough stretch of their schedule, and they did it while juggling injuries and playing roster-Jenga to keep the right personnel on the game day roster. Now they enter Week 10 as the league’s top team, the AFC’s number one seed and in control of their post-season destiny. While the next couple of weeks, on paper, look a little easier than the last five, facing division rivals – regardless of their record – is never a walk in the park. However, Buffalo knows what they are facing. They are as familiar with their opponent as possible. So, if they need to take an extra day or two to let some veterans get some rest, get the new guy up to speed, and let a few people work out the kinks, bumps, and bruises, this would be the time. However, instead, the Bills listed everyone as participating in Wednesday’s first practice of the week. Wednesday injury report pic.twitter.com/DBuzVeU6Mv — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 11, 2026 Limited Participation OL Alec Anderson (ankle) CB Christian Benford (wrist) T Spencer Brown (ankle) T Dion Dawkins (rib) TE Dalton Kincaid (ankle) C Conner McGovern (neck) Four of the Bills’ five starting offensive linemen are on this list. Not the best situation for you if your name is Josh Allen. But it’s good to know Anderson and Dawkins, who both missed Monday night in Minnesota, are on the mend. It’s also good – maybe – that Brown’s back isn’t an issue any longer. But sometimes a pain you know is easier to manage than one that’s new. Buffalo signed guard Nick Broeker to the practice squad this morning. We thought that wasn’t a great sign for Anderson. Now it looks like the move may have had something to do with the fact that the entire O-line is banged up. Full Participation DL Greg Gaines (calf) DB Jordan Hancock (IR) G Ar’maj Reed-Adams (back/elbow) DL T.J. Sanders (shoulder) WR Tyrell Shavers (PUP) The Bills aren’t done performing roster gymnastics just because the trade deadline has passed. Both Hancock and Shavers are gearing up for a return to the 53-man roster. Buffalo has one more week to figure out what to do with Shavers and a few days later they will have to make room for Hancock. This will be something to keep our eyes on over the next week. What to watch It’s important to keep in mind that this was a walk through practice and these designations are what the training and coaching staff anticipates a player’s participation would have been had it been a full practice. The real test will come tomorrow. Pads, routes, coverages, the whole thing – that will definitely tell us more about how the Bills are looking ahead of their trip to MetLife Stadium on Sunday.
author: Rachel Auberger

title: Titans GM details Brandon Beane’s pursuit of Amani Hooker before NFL trade deadline
summary: Titans GM Mike Borgonzi spoke to the mention after his team traded Amani Hooker to the Buffalo Bills on Tuesday before the NFL trade deadline, and now we have a good sense for how early GM Brandon Beane was onto this potential acquisition and how hard he pursued the trade. On X/Twitter, NFL Network’s Mike […]
full_text: Titans GM Mike Borgonzi spoke to the mention after his team traded Amani Hooker to the Buffalo Bills on Tuesday before the NFL trade deadline, and now we have a good sense for how early GM Brandon Beane was onto this potential acquisition and how hard he pursued the trade. On X/Twitter, NFL Network’s Mike Garafolo posted Borgonzi’s press conference on the matter, an enlightening trip behind the curtains: #Titans GM Mike Borgonzi said he’d turned away #Bills GM Brandon Beane on Amani Hooker for a week. Saw him at the Notre Dame-Miami game, said to stay in touch and then the deal came together yesterday. pic.twitter.com/dxQGg0B1KB — Mike Garafolo (@MikeGarafolo) November 11, 2026 The detailed story Borgonzi told there was the ideal springboard for me to get this take on the record, which I think is an important one. Before last season’s trade deadline, Beane’s aggression had been crystal clear and widely adored by Bills fans. The aggression consisted of a collection of well-documented swings with the distinct intention of making the Bills a better team in the present. Then, the rather unusual Jaylen Waddle fiasco occurred at least year’s trade deadline, which led to the Bills surprisingly not making a move. The subsequent collective failure of the replacement receivers in Buffalo’s incredibly injured wideout room in the playoffs stoked the flames of disgruntled Bills fans. Being linked but ultimately not trading for the likes of Maxx Crosby or Myles Garrett conjured what I believe is a misperception of who Beane has been as the Bills GM. One year without a trade-deadline acquisition, and it felt like his reputation began to drift from “Big Baller Beane” to the GM who is always just checking in but never closing deals. Regardless of how you view DJ Moore, Beane and Co. did send a second-round pick to acquire the veteran wideout as the first major transaction of the Joe Brady era, a move with a direct impact on Josh Allen in mind. If anything, Beane has struck a sensible balance between risk and restraint. He’s demonstrated the willingness to be aggressive without treating every potential acquisition as the one he must make regardless of cost. Now, if you’re not necessarily a Beane believer due to the team’s current lack of a Lombardi Trophy in the lobby of team headquarters, that’s OK. And I assume if you’ve gotten this far, this article has read like a team-crafted PR campaign. It’s not meant to be that whatsoever. I’m not suggesting every Beane move has been correct. Far from. I’m challenging what was, before yesterday’s acquisition of Hooker, a growing sentiment he was a GM content with sitting idly by as all of Buffalo’s contending contemporaries made active attempts to improve their respective rosters. During his tenure as Bills GM, Beane has consistently explored avenues to make the club better each year. Heck, I think the very continuous inquiries for which he’s criticized because many haven’t led to signings prove he’s quite relentless. And with the team owning its best record since 1993, the last time it won the AFC, Beane added an impact veteran to the roster before the trade deadline.

title: Bills at Vikings was pretty boring (with penalties anyway)
summary: Look, why don’t you do us both a favor. Just refresh on the page a few times to get me some extra clicks and then be on your way. There’s no reason to actually read the content this week as the Buffalo Bills and Minnesota Vikings put on an absolute CLINIC on how to be […]
full_text: Look, why don’t you do us both a favor. Just refresh on the page a few times to get me some extra clicks and then be on your way. There’s no reason to actually read the content this week as the Buffalo Bills and Minnesota Vikings put on an absolute CLINIC on how to be boring as heck with penalties. Wait! You’re insisting on plowing through? Don’t say I didn’t warn you. Standard and Advanced Metrics Penalty Counts So this isn’t too terribly boring in and of itself, but it’s also not very interesting either. As we always do, we start off with the overall volumes for both teams (aka “counts”). This is the usual information for flags that can be found pretty much everywhere. So yes, the Bills had twice as many flags as the Vikings but I bet you already knew that. Penalty Yards If you’re a penalty nerd like I am, this chart is the first blaring alarm for how boring this game might be. If you take the yardage total and divide it by count, the Vikings average five yards per penalty which is a strong suggestion of boring procedural flags. There’s a couple ways that could be wrong, but we’ll see soon enough. The Bills are just a tick shy of eight yards per flag, maybe something will be intriguing there. Penalty Harm Minnesota Vikings Yeah, that’s boring as heck. Three false starts and one defensive offside. All pre-snap flags for five yards each. None had a larger impact outside of that such as a lost down, impacted yardage, etc. So yes, super boring this week. Their 2.0 total Harm for the game is well under our 10.0 bad day threshold. Buffalo Bills Buffalo got close to the bad day numeri with 9.4 Harm total. That said, there really weren’t any controversies. Josh Allen’s intentional grounding call was clearly the right call. It cost the Bills 13 yards and the one down from the foul being on top of the yardage. Spencer Brown had two false starts called, which was only 40% of the Bills total. Damar Hamlin’s defensive holding call came on first down and negated a two yard loss which would also be correctly tallied as a “sack” if it weren’t for this. Terrel Bernard was called for pass interference which had 19 yards assessed to go with two free downs given to Minnesota for a total of 3.9 Harm (1.9 for yards and 2.0 for how many downs the flag gave up). And that’s it. The more boring for the Buffalo Bills the better honestly. Don’t stir the pot with penalties and it helps your odds of winning the game. It just makes this article worse I suppose.

title: Bills Game Balls: James Cook reaches milestone, defense dominates, and Keleki Latu has his moment
summary: The Buffalo Bills didn’t need Josh Allen to put on a superhero cape Monday night. Instead, they leaned on James Cook, a defense that refused to let the Minnesota Vikings find the end zone, and a young tight end who delivered one of the biggest moments of his career. Buffalo’s 23-6 victory over Minnesota was […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills didn’t need Josh Allen to put on a superhero cape Monday night. Instead, they leaned on James Cook, a defense that refused to let the Minnesota Vikings find the end zone, and a young tight end who delivered one of the biggest moments of his career. Buffalo’s 23-6 victory over Minnesota was a team effort, and head coach Joe Brady’s postgame Game Balls reflected exactly that. Cook received recognition for another hard-fought performance and a career milestone, the entire defense earned praise for shutting down Minnesota, and Keleki Latu celebrated his first NFL touchdown. Game Ball No. 1: James Cook Cook was Buffalo’s workhorse Monday night, carrying the football 31 times for 107 yards and a touchdown. It wasn’t necessarily the flashiest performance of his career, averaging 3.5 yards per carry, but it was exactly what Buffalo needed. The Bills dominated time of possession, holding the football for 42:32, and Cook was a major reason why. His five-yard touchdown run in the fourth quarter capped a 15-play, 84-yard drive that drained 8:32 off the clock and effectively put the game out of reach. Brady also recognized Cook for reaching the 5,000-career-rushing-yard milestone, another significant accomplishment for Buffalo’s running back. The milestone adds to a night when Cook carried the offense, helping the Bills dominate time of possession and secure their second consecutive victory. Cook continues to prove he can be more than an explosive-play threat. When the Bills need to grind out yards, extend possessions, and keep their defense fresh, he’s more than capable of carrying the workload. Game Ball No. 2: The entire defense, presented to Terrel Bernard For the second consecutive game, Buffalo’s defense delivered the kind of performance Bills fans have been waiting to see. Minnesota managed just 178 total yards, nine first downs, and six points. The Vikings went 0-for-8 on third down, failed on both fourth-down attempts, and committed three turnovers. They never reached the end zone. Brady recognized the entire defensive unit but singled out linebacker Terrel Bernard to receive the Game Ball on its behalf. Bernard finished with six combined tackles, an interception, and two passes defended. His third-quarter interception was one of two Buffalo recorded against Carson Wentz, with Dorian Williams collecting the other. Perhaps the most impressive statistic was the workload. Buffalo’s defense played just 48 snaps after logging only 51 against Baltimore the previous week. Game Ball No. 3: Keleki Latu Sometimes a Game Ball is about more than the stat sheet. Latu caught just one pass Monday night, but it was a big one. With 44 seconds remaining in the first half, Josh Allen connected with Latu for a 25-yard touchdown, giving Buffalo a 10-3 lead. It was the first touchdown of Latu’s NFL career, and his teammates made sure he received the recognition he deserved. When accepting his Game Ball, Latu kept his message simple: “Really no place I’d rather be than right here with you guys.” Honorable mentions Greg Rousseau: Another disruptive performance from Groot, who recorded a sack, three quarterback hits, a pass defended, and a fumble recovery. Tyler Bass: Perfect on the night, connecting on all three fieldgoal attempts from 39, 25, and 52 yards and two extra points. Final thoughts For the second consecutive week, Buffalo found a way to win without requiring Josh Allen to do everything. Cook handled the heavy lifting, the defense made life miserable for Minnesota’s offense, and Latu delivered a moment he’ll remember for the rest of his career. There are still things to clean up, but the Bills are beginning to show they can win games in different ways.
author: Sara Larson

title: Bills snap counts: James Cook carries the workload as Buffalo’s defense dominates Minnesota
summary: The Buffalo Bills didn’t need an offensive explosion to take care of business on Monday Night Football. Instead, they controlled the clock, leaned heavily on James Cook, and delivered one of their most complete defensive performances of the season in a 23-6 win over the Minnesota Vikings. Buffalo held the ball for an incredible 42:32, […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills didn’t need an offensive explosion to take care of business on Monday Night Football. Instead, they controlled the clock, leaned heavily on James Cook, and delivered one of their most complete defensive performances of the season in a 23-6 win over the Minnesota Vikings. Buffalo held the ball for an incredible 42:32, leaving Minnesota’s offense on the field for just 17:28. The Bills ran 80 offensive snaps compared to only 48 defensive snaps, a significant workload difference that tells much of the story. Minnesota finished with just 178 total yards, nine first downs, an 0-for-8 performance on third down, and failed on both fourth-down attempts. The Vikings also committed three turnovers. Offense: 80 snaps James Cook played 51 offensive snaps (64%), finishing with 31 carries for 107 yards and a touchdown. That’s a substantial workload, particularly considering Buffalo ran the ball 44 times. Cook averaged just 3.5 yards per carry, but his production wasn’t about explosive plays. It was about keeping the offense moving, wearing down Minnesota’s defense, and helping Buffalo control the clock. Ty Johnson played 17 snaps (21%), while Ray Davis saw 11 (14%). Johnson contributed a 36-yard reception on third-and-eight, Buffalo’s longest offensive play of the night. The distribution is interesting because Cook accounted for 31 of Buffalo’s 44 rushing attempts despite playing just 64% of the offensive snaps. When Cook was on the field, the Bills clearly wanted the ball in his hands. Four tight ends continue to play a significant role Buffalo once again leaned heavily into its tight-end personnel. Dawson Knox: 58 snaps (72%) Jackson Hawes: 46 snaps (57%) Dalton Kincaid: 40 snaps (50%) Keleki Latu: 21 snaps (26%) Knox led the group in playing time, catching four passes for 37 yards. Kincaid contributed three receptions for 28 yards, while Hawes added an eight-yard reception.. The continued use of four tight ends is worth watching. Buffalo clearly values the flexibility these formations provide, particularly with helping the offensive line in protection. However, the Bills still allowed four sacks, raising questions about how effectively their heavier personnel packages are helping protect Allen. Offensive line: Grable handles left tackle duties With the left side of the line inactive, Tylan Grable started at left tackle and played all 80 offensive snaps. Austin Corbett also played every snap, while Spencer Brown, O’Cyrus Torrence, and Connor McGovern each played 77 snaps (96%). The final three snaps went to reserves as Buffalo closed out the victory. The offensive line helped Cook reach 100 rushing yards, but pass protection remains an area of concern. Allen was sacked four times for 29 yards, and Buffalo committed eight penalties for 62 yards, including multiple offensive line infractions. Wide receiver rotation remains spread out Buffalo’s wide receiver snap distribution: Keon Coleman: 49 snaps (61%) DJ Moore: 47 snaps (59%) Khalil Shakir: 42 snaps (52%) Trent Sherfield: 10 snaps (12%) Greg Dortch: 8 snaps (10%) Coleman led the receivers in playing time but finished with just three receptions for 17 yards on six targets. Quietly, Shakir was Buffalo’s leading receiver with four catches for 58 yards, while Moore added three receptions for 25 yards. What’s interesting is that no receiver played even two-thirds of the offensive snaps. Buffalo continued rotating personnel rather than relying on a traditional group of three receivers for most of the game. With four tight ends receiving meaningful playing time, that distribution makes sense. Still, it’s worth questioning whether the Bills are getting enough consistent production from their wide receiver group or going heavy wet with their tight ends. Defense: 48 snaps For a consecutive game, Buffalo’s defense benefited from an offense that controlled possession. After playing just 51 defensive snaps against Baltimore in Week 8, the Bills needed only 48 against Minnesota. The result was another strong defensive showing, with the Vikings managing just 51 rushing yards and 127 net passing yards. Buffalo also recorded three takeaways, including interceptions by Terrel Bernard and Dorian Williams and a fumble recovery by Greg Rousseau. Minnesota never reached the end zone. Cole Bishop leads the secondary in snaps Cole Bishop was the only Bills defender to play every defensive snap, logging all 48 (100%). Damar Hamlin followed with 44 snaps (92%), while Davison Igbinosun played 39 (81%). The cornerback rotation was more varied: Dee Alford: 36 snaps (75%) Maxwell Hairston: 29 snaps (60%) Christian Benford: 28 snaps (58%) Benford was listed as questionable to return during the game but eventually returned to limited action. Hamlin also received a questionable-to-return designation before returning. With Minnesota struggling to sustain drives, Buffalo had opportunities to rotate defensive backs without sacrificing much production. Bernard and Williams make their opportunities count Terrel Bernard played 38 defensive snaps (79%), finishing with six combined tackles, an interception, and two passes defended. Dorian Williams played just 19 snaps (40%), but he made one of the game’s most important defensive plays intercepting Carson Wentz early in the third quarter. The linebacker rotation also included Bradley Chubb, who played 37 snaps (77%). Greg Rousseau played 33 defensive snaps (69%) and once again found ways to affect the game. Ed Oliver played 28 snaps (58%) and recorded three quarterback hits, while Deone Walker played 24 (50%). Michael Hoecht played 16 defensive snaps (33%), with another 18 on special teams. Javon Solomon appeared on only four defensive snaps (8%) but recorded a six-yard sack of backup quarterback Max Brosmer late in the fourth quarter. Buffalo didn’t need a massive sack total to control Minnesota’s passing attack. Consistent pressure, coverage, and timely turnovers were enough. Special teams: Dortch provides an early spark Greg Dortch opened the game with a 58-yard kickoff return, immediately putting Buffalo in Minnesota territory. Keleki Latu and Javon Solomon each played 19 special teams snaps (73%), while Michael Hoecht played 18 (69%). Sam Franklin and Joe Andreessen led Buffalo with 21 special teams snaps apiece (81%). Final thoughts The Bills’ snap counts tell the story of a team that dictated how this game would be played. There are still concerns, particularly with pass protection, penalties, and the limited production from the wide receivers. But after consecutive games in which the defense played 51 and 48 snaps, Buffalo is finally finding a formula that doesn’t require Josh Allen to carry the entire team every week. And that’s a welcome change.
author: Sara Larson

title: Buffalo Bills made room for Amani Hooker trade by  restructuring a veteran’s contract
summary: The Buffalo Bills didn’t have much cap space entering the NFL trade deadline on Tuesday and they swung a deal for veteran safety Amani Hooker who was playing a deal that featured a prorated salary of over $4 million. With roughly $4M in cap space to begin the day, many wondered if the Bills actually […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills didn’t have much cap space entering the NFL trade deadline on Tuesday and they swung a deal for veteran safety Amani Hooker who was playing a deal that featured a prorated salary of over $4 million. With roughly $4M in cap space to begin the day, many wondered if the Bills actually had enough cap space to add Hooker’s contract onto their 2026 books. Now we know how they made it work. In order to facilitate the Amani Hooker trade, the #Bills processed a salary conversion on OT Dion Dawkins' salary. Firm numbers on that not yet available, but Buffalo could have opened up a maximum of $5.6M of cap space with that restructure. — Spotrac (@spotrac) November 10, 2026 The Dawkins restructure was the one lever we knew the team could pull to create cap space. As far as the specifics of the transaction, ESPN’s Field Yates reported the following: Teams restructuring contracts yesterday to facilitate trades and/or create space for the rest of the season: Bills: $5.3M via LT Dion Dawkins Broncos: $3.9M via S Talanoa Hufanga Chiefs: $3.4M via LB Nick Bolton Rams: $3M via RB Kyren Williams and S Kam Curl — Field Yates (@FieldYates) November 11, 2026 Mike Ginnitti, founder of Spotrac, responded to a question on X/Twitter regarding the timing of the Dawkins restructure, as some were under the impression any veteran restructures of acquiring teams needed to take place the day before the trade deadline: No, the conversion deadline yesterday only applied to players who were going to be traded (Jessie Bates, etc…). Teams were able to process conversions today on their own rostered players in order to free up trade space. — Spotrac (@spotrac) November 10, 2026 This Dawkins restructure hints at Buffalo’s faith in the left tackle to be with the team for 2027 — and potentially beyond — as the Bills have pushed money into the future with him. Frankly, I was never in the camp of the Bills moving on from Dawkins when that speculation swirled in the offseason. Franchise left tackles can play quality football into their mid 30s, and Dawkins is 32. He’s had a fine start to the 2026 campaign, showing essentially no signs of slowing down in pass protection or as a road-grader in the run game.

title: Panthers injury report is full of reinforcements
summary: The Carolina Panthers are flailing as they try to stay afloat at the top of the ever pitiful NFC South. The team has dropped three straight games with a skeleton crew of a secondary and a revolving door of players on the offensive line. The first injury report of Week 10 brings good news though. […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - SEPTEMBER 20: A Carolina Panthers football helmet on the turf prior to the start of the NFL game between the Carolina Panthers and the Atlanta Falcons on September 20th, 2026 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Carolina Panthers are flailing as they try to stay afloat at the top of the ever pitiful NFC South. The team has dropped three straight games with a skeleton crew of a secondary and a revolving door of players on the offensive line. The first injury report of Week 10 brings good news though. It looks like a lot of key players are soon to return. Panthers Injury Report Chuba Hubbard – DNP – Rest Bobby Okereke – DNP – Foot Jaelan Phillips – FP – Hamstring Mike Jackson – FP – Groin Will Lee IV – FP – Hamstring Lee Hunter – FP – Calf Damien Lewis – FP – Knee Brady Christensen – FP – Hamstring Xavier Legette – FP – Knee Jonathon Brooks – FP – Groin Trevor Etienne – FP – Ankle Torticelli Simpkins III – FP – Ankle The highlight of this injury report is all of the full participation from guys that have been out for extended periods of time. Mike Jackson, Jonathon Brooks, and Xavier Legette all had their practice windows opened on Wednesday. That doesn’t guarantee that they’ll be active on Sunday, but it does mean they need to be activated within the next three weeks. And the fact that they all practiced in full would suggest they’re all very close to getting back to live game action. Will Lee and Jaelan Phillips are both back at practice as well, which means the Panthers will be close to having an actual starting lineup for the first time in a few weeks. They’re just missing Jaycee Horn and Bobby Okereke. The offense will get starting guard Damien Lewis back, which should hopefully alleviate some of the relentless pressure Bryce Young has been feeling when he drops back to pass. Brady Christensen is on his way back to provide versatile depth, and then Xavier Legette and Jonathon Brooks will provide some extra weapons, albeit in smaller roles. All in all, it’s a very positive injury report for a Panthers team that’s entering a part of their schedule where they’re going to be looking to string a few wins together. Saints Injury Report Erik McCoy – DNP – Biceps Alvin Kamara – DNP – Rest CJ Donaldson – DNP – Shoulder Kelvin Banks – LP – Ankle David Edwards – LP – Knee Travis Etienne – LP – Hamstring Noah Fant – LP – Back Asim Richards – LP – Thumb Martin Emersen – LP – Shin Christen Miller – LP – Knee The Saints are very banged up along their offensive line. Starting center Erik McCoy is out. Both starters to his left and the backup left tackle are all dealing with their own injuries, though it doesn’t seem like any will miss the game this weekend. Running back Travis Etienne is back at practice, but I wouldn’t be surprised if he misses the game even after a limited practice since teams tend to be very cautious with muscle injuries like that.

summary: The Carolina Panthers lost another close game in which their lack of top end talent, thanks primarily to injuries, proved the difference. full_text: NEW ORLEANS - DECEMBER 03: Head coach Sean Payton of the New Orleans Saints tosses a red flag to challenge a call in the second half against San Francisco 49ers December 3, 2006 at the Superdome in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Carolina Panthers lost another close game in which their lack of top end talent, thanks primarily to injuries, proved the difference. It is hard to evaluate much about this team when so many of their starters are missing, but such is our duty as fans: to judge failure as harshly as we celebrate success. Then, of course, there is the elephant-sized zebra in the room. The Panthers had the ball stripped from them on the goal line by the officials and handed to the Broncos over a challenge that Sean Payton threw as the ball was being snapped on the next play. Officials let the play continue because they did not see the flag and then announced there was a flag. Multiple video angles from fans in the stands show Payton throwing the flag up to 0.1 seconds before the snap on second and goal, with the flag landing on the ground well after the play commenced. There are two pieces of language that are relevant here. The first is the NFL rule book: The head coach or head coach’s pregame challenge designee can initiate a challenge by throwing a red flag onto the field of play before the next legal snap or kick. The next is the postgame comment from the referee: Replay can get involved to make sure that the head coach throws his challenge flag prior to the next snap,” Butterworth said. “We were actually able to use angles to show that the flag was out prior to the ball being snapped, and so we permitted the challenge. There seems to be some discrepancy between “the flag was out” and “onto the field of play” to me. What do you think? Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Panthers fans and fans across the country. Did the officials get it right? Are you confident in the Panthers? title: Panthers vs Broncos game review: The other stuff
summary: This was the worst loss against the Denver Broncos since, well, you know. At least this one was different, I suppose. Could you imagine if the game on Sunday was surrounded in controversy due to some highly questionable refereeing that seemed to heavily favor one side and for all intents and purposes ended on a […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - NOVEMBER 08: Darren Waller #88 of the Carolina Panthers is tackled by Alex Singleton #49 of the Denver Broncos during the second quarter at Bank of America Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Grant Halverson/Getty Images) | Getty Images This was the worst loss against the Denver Broncos since, well, you know. At least this one was different, I suppose. Could you imagine if the game on Sunday was surrounded in controversy due to some highly questionable refereeing that seemed to heavily favor one side and for all intents and purposes ended on a sack-fumble? That would have been traumatic. The obvious route to take this game review would be to list out and dwell on the many aspects of the game that boiled my blood. I will even encourage you to do so yourselves in the comments and I’ll join in, as there’s probably something cathartic about listing out the laundry list of frustrations stemming from Sunday. That said, rather than add on to that vitriol here, I’m going to take a different direction for the sake of our collective sanity. Let’s take a moment to look back and acknowledge the encouraging moments from Sunday that would have received some praise and fanfare had there note been all the rest of the other nonsense taking up the conversation. Bryce Young bounceback Young had had back-to-back games with less than encouraging performances. While far from being the central issue or reason for the disappointing performances given the state of the offensive line and the quality of football being played by the defense, the downward tick in performance coupled with rumors of a contract extension led to some negative, even if somewhat warranted, takes being spread on social media. The Panthers OL finally gave Bryce Young time to breathe and he rewarded them with a strong performance against the Broncos defense pic.twitter.com/GCGbIlw1cw — Josh Norris (@JoshNorris) November 9, 2026 Despite Facing a defense that’s near the top the league at creating pressure and producing takeaways, Young found a way to be productive and find ways to move the ball. 276 yards, 3 touchdowns on 71.8% completed passes would get the job done on most NFL Sundays. Tight end renaissance in Carolina After Sunday’s 8 reception, 90 yard performance Darren Waller is up to 299 receiving yards this season. For comparison’s sake, that already surpasses Tommy Trembles 249 yards in 2025 which lead the position in receiving yards. Speaking of Tremble, those 249 yards were his career high to date and he currently stands about 80 yards short of that total in in 2026. Darren Waller gets UP to snag the TD! DENvsCAR on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/FTf5Lqayd2 — NFL (@NFL) November 8, 2026 Young talent making splash plays There were a handful of splash plays intertwined with the baker’s dozen of penalties and other mid-play meltdowns. Tetairoa McMillan continues to improve and produce when needed, including a critical first down as well as a touchdown while lined up against Patrick Surtain. Lee Hunter flashed on multiple plays including an outstanding tackle for loss early in the contest that will surely earn him more than the 13 snaps he played Sunday. Chau Smith-Wade had multiple touchdown-saving pass break-ups while Corey Thornton baited Bo Nix to throw him his first interception of his career. GahLEE #DENvsCAR 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/MQq4Zz8oTQ — Carolina Panthers (@Panthers) November 8, 2026 Run defense improvements The Panthers rush defense has some Dr. Jekyll and Mr Hyde thing going on, but overall rank as the 28th rush defense in the NFL. Holding the Broncos to 82 yards and 3 yards per carry is certainly an improvement for the newish-look defense that Todd Wash is trying to implement. Let’s hope they can make a trend out of keeping the opponents to less than 100 yards rushing a game. Held ‘em to 82 on the ground 📲 NFL+ pic.twitter.com/Dvr8akp56Q — Carolina Panthers (@Panthers) November 9, 2026 One game closer to reinforcements It wouldn’t be an article on the Panthers if there isn’t mention of the injuries currently plaguing the roster. Dave Canales spoke on Monday and mentioned that the practice window for Xavier Legette will be opened this week and that Jaycee Horn, Mike Jackson and Jonathon Brooks are close. Brady Christensen is likely to return in the next couple weeks as well to boast the offensive line one way or another. Fingers firmly crossed for the returns of Damien Lewis, Bobby Okereke, and Jaelan Philips who all remain on the active roster. NFL injury report pic.twitter.com/Hj5KzkU4YI — Stick to the Model (@StickToTheModel) November 6, 2026 There’s a lot to be mad about right now. But there’s also a lot of positive aspects and improvements lying underneath. We’ll meet back here next week after the Panthers take on the New Orleans Saints for the first time this season. Until then, keep pounding.

title: Chicago Bears-Tampa Bay Bucs stockwatch: Caleb down, Devin Bush up
summary: The cliché of the week for Chicago Bears fans is “the bye week is coming at the perfect time.” The team is struggling with injuries. And their weaknesses nearly cost them the game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. We know injuries ravage the secondary, which is also the weakest part of the defense. The running […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 8: Devin Bush #12 of the Chicago Bears hypes up his teammates before the game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Soldier Field on November 8, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images The cliché of the week for Chicago Bears fans is “the bye week is coming at the perfect time.” The team is struggling with injuries. And their weaknesses nearly cost them the game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. We know injuries ravage the secondary, which is also the weakest part of the defense. The running backs are banged up, to say the least. The Bears have also turned the ball over way more than they did in 2025. Plus, they’ve been penalized a lot, too. All that said, though, they’re still 7-2 and currently in first place in the division, despite their two losses being to division opponents. And the schedule gets tougher from here. The Bears need to have both a productive and restful bye week in order to finish out the season, correct the things they can and secure a playoff berth for the second-straight year. Let’s get into a review of the Bucs game. Stock up Jaylon Johnson, CB – We should all celebrate Johnson’s 67-yard pick-six. Johnson, a target for criticism this season, made a fantastic play and helped lift the team when the offense was stuck. It wasn’t unlike the interception he had last year against the Cleveland Browns. It was a nice moment for a player who’s often looked like his best football is behind him. Devin Bush, LB – I was critical of Bush just a couple weeks ago, and correctly, told. I was wrong by you, the readers. And I appreciate that. I cannot deny though, that Bush was awesome against Tampa. He was flying around, making plays everywhere. He led the Bears with nine tackles, two passes defensed and a tackle for loss. Cameron Lewis, DB – Cam Lewis nabbed his first interception since 2024. He also finished with five tackles and a pass breakup. For a player who was seen more as a depth piece and back up, he’s played well. Stock down Caleb Williams, QB – This is not a long-term down. In fact, if it were a real stock market, I’d be buying the dip. But after four interceptions, he has to get knocked a little bit. Two of them were on throwaways that just didn’t make it to the sideline, one was a tipped pass. The other was just a case of trusting his arm a little too much and getting fooled by Tampa’s disguise. The main reason I’m not worried is that it’s a total outlier in his career. It was the first time he’s had more than two interceptions in a game. All of his other regular-season multi-interception games came as a rookie. In fact, they were the second and third games of his career. So for his first 3+ interception game to come in game No. 40, I feel like is an OK thing. D’Andre Swift, RB – The bye week is much needed for Swift. The running game has looked rough against two fo the best run defenses in the league. It’s gotten the job done at times, but it hasn’t looked the best. Swift has looked banged up. Hopefully a week off will get him rested and ready for the stretch run of the season. And getting his stablemate, Kyle Monangai, back will help too. Zavion Thomas, WR – The rookie nearly earned a spot in the stock up category this week. His kick return was brilliant, and called back through no fault of his own. The one pass he didn’t catch wasn’t the easiest catch to make, so I wasn’t going to hold it against him. But his penalty for unnecessary roughness after a play, back Chicago up and Caleb was intercepted on the next play. While I don’t think everything that happened afterward was a direct result, it certainly shifted momentum in the moment. He didn’t get another offensive snap after it. Players just can’t make those kinds of mistakes. Who is up and down in your eyes this week? Next week, I’ll look at who is up and down for the season so far. Let me know who ’ s caught your eye through the first nine games.

title: Reviewing the Bears’ PFN grades from Week 9 vs. Buccaneers
summary: The Bears extended their winning streak to four games on Sunday night, squeezing away with a 27-24 win over the Buccaneers at home. They improved their record to 7-2 in the process, and though their offensive performance wasn’t pretty, their strong defense led them to victory. As they prepare to head into their bye week […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - NOVEMBER 02: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears celebrates a touchdown by teammate D'Andre Swift #4 of the Chicago Bears during the third quarter against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on November 02, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Bears extended their winning streak to four games on Sunday night, squeezing away with a 27-24 win over the Buccaneers at home. They improved their record to 7-2 in the process, and though their offensive performance wasn’t pretty, their strong defense led them to victory. As they prepare to head into their bye week in Week 10, they have a well-timed opportunity to rest up and regroup. Each week, I’ll review how Chicago’s eligible performers graded by Pro Football Network’s Impact Scoring model. Now that the rest of the NFL has caught up, and the numbers have all been crunched, here’s how Week 9 looked. Offense Caleb Williams: 71.9 (18th of 30 QBs) D’Andre Swift: 68.9 (44th of 47 RBs) Rome Odunze: 77.2 (14th of 67 WRs) Luther Burden III: 73.7 (33rd of 67 WRs) Kalif Raymond: 69.7 (49th of 67 WRs) Colston Loveland: 75.9 (11th of 33 TEs) Theo Benedet: 79.0 (15th of 66 OTs) Joe Thuney: 73.9 (36th of 64 OGs) Garrett Bradbury: 68.7 (28th of 32 Cs) Jonah Jackson: 78.5 (19th of 64 OGs) Darnell Wright: 86.3 (2nd of 66 OTs) Analytically, Caleb Williams had his worst game of the season since his Week 2 outing in the rain against the Vikings. His -0.21 EPA per dropback marked the worst average he’s had in a single game all year. His four interceptions certainly played a major role in his reaching a negative average for the first time in 2026. That said, he still finished with an above-average completion percentage over expected, coming in No. 13 with a +1.0 percentage. It’s not much of a surprise that the rest of the Bears’ offense didn’t grade incredibly well on Sunday. The offensive interior struggled in particular, with Garrett Bradbury finishing well below average at center and Joe Thuney taking his lumps at left guard. Darnell Wright continued his stellar 2026, though, as his 89.0 PFN OL Impact grade for the year leads all offensive tackles in the NFL. Defense Austin Booker: 80.3 (17th of 101 EDGEs) Shemar Turner: 75.3 (33rd of 101 EDGEs) Montez Sweat: 75.1 (34th of 101 EDGEs) Daniel Hardy: 60.3 (61st of 101 EDGEs) Jeffery Simmons: 82.8 (12th of 97 DTs) Grady Jarrett: 74.8 (32nd of 97 DTs) Neville Gallimore: 62.8 (59th of 97 DTs) Devin Bush: 85.6 (15th of 83 LBs) T.J. Edwards: 65.2 (81st of 83 LBs) Jaylon Johnson: 94.1 (1st of 101 CBs) Clark Phillips III: 79.5 (21st of 101 CBs) Tyrique Stevenson: 72.7 (63rd of 101 CBs) Kyler Gordon: 67.3 (89th of 101 CBs) Cam Lewis: 88.4 (6th of 82 SAFs) Dillon Thieneman: 78.1 (25th of 82 SAFs) Chicago’s defense played a huge role in its win over the Buccaneers on Sunday, and it was highlighted by interceptions from both Jaylon Johnson and Cam Lewis. Johnson returned his interception back for a touchdown, and he allowed a flawless 0.0 passer rating when targeted in coverage in Week 9. Considering the rocky season he’s had in 2026 thus far, putting together such a strong outing had to mean a lot to him. It certainly meant a lot to the Bears. Elsewhere, the defensive standouts included Jeffery Simmons — who had another sack in his second game with the Bears — Austin Booker, and Devin Bush. Bush cleaned up with nine tackles, thriving in space as Simmons plugged up running lanes in front of him. The emergence of Clark Phillips III is a particularly interesting statistic, as he allowed a targeted passer rating of just 39.6 in coverage on Sunday. Special teams (for the sickos) Cairo Santos: 77.3 (20th of 29 Ks) Tory Taylor: 76.0 (22nd of 29 Ps) Though Cairo Santos deserves credit for coming through in the clutch with his 38-yard field goal to win the Bears the game, the relative lack of difficulty of his kicks doesn’t help his analytical profile much. His other converted field goal came from just 25 yards out, so other NFL kickers grade higher thanks to superior field goals made over expected. On the punting side of things, Tory Taylor averaged just 40.3 net yards per punt, which ranked No. 23 among 29 punters in Week 9.

Caleb Williams’ sack […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 08: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears takes off running against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Soldier Field on November 08, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images At the midway point of the 2026 season, the Chicago Bears’ pass protection is trending more positively of late. They’ve allowed only one sack in each of the last two games, dropping their sack percentage to 6.0%, good for 14th in the NFL. In their previous three games, they allowed 11 sacks. Caleb Williams’ sack percentage is down to 6.70%, just above the league average of 6.67%. He hasn’t had many OMG, how did he escape that sack moments since returning from his hamstring injury, but his pocket awareness and escapability haven’t gone anywhere. He may need them in his next game because the Bears have another tough defense on the schedule. The Bears are on their bye this week, but on November 22, they’ll face one of the NFL’s best pass-rushing tandems when they host the New Orleans Saints and defensive ends Chase Young and Carl Granderson, who have 8 and 7.5 sacks, respectively, in 8 games. Hopefully I have another easy Sackwatch in a couple of weeks. Sack 20: 4th Quarter: 2-3-TB 37 (9:48) C.Williams sacked at TB 39 for -2 yards (sack split by A.Nelson and C.Kancey) Watching live, I thought this would be a historic Sackwatch, and then when I got to the All-22, my initial notion was confirmed. For the first time in his Bears career, I’m giving this sack to All-Pro left guard Joe Thuney. His guy didn’t get the sack, but the pressure from nose tackle Vita Vea (#50) is what sent Caleb scrambling. The Bears are running a play-action, so Williams has his back to the defense while he fakes the handoff, and as soon as he turns around, he has a two-time Pro Bowler barreling down on him. Caleb is athletic enough to evade the 350-pound Vea, but the scramble allowed the defenders to slip their blocks, and defensive tackle Calijah Kancey and outside linebacker Anthony Nelson shook free to pursue and get the sack. Vea got the best of Thuney on this rep, but had he stayed in front just a tick longer, Caleb could have rifled it deep over the middle to Kalif Raymond. title: Hot Take Wednesday: Chicago Bears Defense now legit
summary: (First of all, sorry for the one-day delay, but we wanted to wait until after the trade deadline before we published) The Chicago Bears defense has now had Jeffery Simmons for 120 minutes, and the changes are monumental. The defense has been completely transformed, and it has altered the Bears’ paths not just this season, […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 8: Jeffery Simmons #99 of the Chicago Bears reacts during the fourth quarter against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Soldier Field on November 8, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images (First of all, sorry for the one-day delay, but we wanted to wait until after the trade deadline before we published) The Chicago Bears defense has now had Jeffery Simmons for 120 minutes, and the changes are monumental. The defense has been completely transformed, and it has altered the Bears’ paths not just this season, but for many seasons beyond. The Bears defensive line had 11 sacks in six games before the Jeffery Simmons trade. Since he’s arrived, they’ve had seven in two games. Their blitz rate has gone from around 40% prior to the Simmons acquisition, and now it’s just 15%. More pressure, less blitzing. Jeffery Simmons ‘ impact cannot be overstated. Prior to Simmons, the defense was having a lot of success with smoke and mirrors. The Bears really were winning 11-on-11; they were winning with stunts and blitzes and catching the other team off guard. With Simmons, the Bears can do far more straight-up defending, and are doing it at a far more successful rate. The win over the Bucs showed us something. It showed us, without question, that the Bears defense was a championship-caliber defense. With many of these Bears teams over the last 15 years or so, if an offense played that poorly, there was simply no chance the Bears could win, but with this team, and this defense, the defense showed that this was not going to be a team that was just carried by the offense. The defense can carry plenty of weight too. After the first two drives of the game that resulted in touchdowns, the Bears’ drives went like this: Interception, Interception, Field Goal, Interception, Punt, Punt, Interception, Punt, Punt, Fumble, Field Goal. That’s 11 possessions, 6 points, 5 turnovers, and 4 punts, 3 of which were 3-and-outs. That is quite possibly going to be the worst stretch of offense we ever see out of a Ben Johnson offense. But the defense stood tall. They consistently turned down the Bucs offense. The Bears continued to show their success on third down, allowing just two third-down conversions on 12 attempts. The Bears defense won this game where the offense couldn’t have played worse. We entered this season thinking the Bears were going to have to win every game 38 to 34. With Dennis Allen and Jeffery Simmons, the Bears have added another way to win: with defense. We knew the Bears could win with Caleb Williams playing hero ball. We knew they could win with a methodical choke-the-life-out-of-you running attack. We knew they could beat you with short, efficient passes. We now know they can beat you with defense as well. Championship teams have more than one way to win a football game. Championship teams know how to find a way to victory when they aren’t firing on all cylinders. Despite an ugly win, the Chicago Bears took a giant step on Sunday toward potentially winning the Super Bowl this year. I know plenty of Bears fans were upset that the Bears didn’t add another cornerback at the trade deadline. Based on everything I heard and read, it certainly felt like Ryan Poles tried to find the right guy for the right price, but he was unable to find that guy. Can the Bears survive with their questionable cornerbacks? We will see when they square off against teams like the Detroit Lions and Green Bay Packers, who have receivers that will absolutely challenge them. But if their front four can continue to harass opposing QBs and force them into making bad decisions, it will certainly mask other warts on the team. The Chicago Bears roster isn’t perfect. But neither are the other 31 rosters in the NFL. It’s mid-November, and the Bears sit atop arguably the greatest division in the history of the NFL. Four of the conference’s best five teams sit in the same division. Think about that. The 2026 NFC North is on pace to be the greatest division in the history of the NFL, and halfway through the season, the Bears have the best record of any of them. The Bears are a championship-caliber team. It’s a fun thing to type. The Bears are a championship-caliber team. It’s been 40 years since I confidently said that during the season. The back half of the schedule is going to be a challenge, but this Bears team will be up for that challenge week in and week out. Having this level of confidence about this team is certainly foreign, and it’s going to be a fun thing to get used to. Because, in case you haven’t noticed, the Bears are a championship-caliber team.

Crew: Ronald Torbert (R #62), Barry Anderson (U #20), Jay Bilbo (DJ #84), Tripp Sutter (LJ #37), Ryan Dickson (FJ #25), Keith Washington (SJ #7), Courtney Brown (BJ #48), Kevin Stine (RO #0). Hello Chicago Bears fans! Well, what to say about this one? Chicago survived a turnover-filled night at Soldier Field and left with a 27–24 walk-off win on Cairo Santos’s 38-yard field goal. So how did the officating affect this game? Spoiler alert: quite a bit. Official totals: Bears 9–74 , Buccaneers 8–45 . Seventeen total accepted penalties for 119 yards (18 total flags). Every accepted flag and every meaningful no-call is accounted for in our review. Let’s get into it. UFR method : Every accepted flag and every meaningful no-call is graded on the same four-tier scale: Correct , Arguable , Incorrect , Horrible . Weight runs 1–4 by impact: 1 for housekeeping/pre-snap process, 2 for drive disruption or field-position damage, 3 for scoring/red-zone leverage or automatic first down that changes a drive, 4 for wiped score, turnover, or game-ending leverage. Replay overturns are judged against the “clear and obvious” standard. No-calls receive identical grades and weights as thrown flags. Bright-line process fouls (false starts, clear offside, delay of game when the clock hits zero, kickoff short of landing zone) are Correct when the rule is met. Judgment calls (holding, PI, unnecessary roughness) are evaluated against the rule text, available angles, All-22 when reviewed, and broadcast rules analysis. The Flag of the Game is the single most egregious or impactful snap. The League File covers the week’s most contested NFL controversy. And this week we have a special College Flag Focus included for that unbelievable game between Texas and Missouri. First Quarter Bears open with a long drive. Rome Odunze 9-yard touchdown from Caleb Williams. Santos kick. CHI 7, TB 0. Luther Burden III then takes a 56-yard touchdown pass from Williams. CHI 14, TB 0. Kickoff Short of Landing Zone — Cairo Santos (CHI), 0 yards. Q1 9:38. Santos kicks 42 yards short of the landing zone. Ball placed at the Bucs 40. Bright-line special-teams process. Correct. Wt 1. Cairo is a quality field goal kicker, but he is boom and bust on kickoffs. We may need to consider going another direction if he continues to have these problems. Second Quarter Santos and Chase McLaughlin trade field goals. CHI 17, TB 6 at the half. Delay of Game — Unnamed (TB), 5 yards. Q2 14:07, 4th-and-4 at CHI 4. Clock expires before the snap on fourth-and-goal. No play. McLaughlin later kicks a 27-yard field goal. Bright-line. Correct. Wt 1. Unnecessary Roughness — Zavion Thomas (CHI), 15 yards. Q2 8:37, 1st-and-8 at TB 8. After D’Andre Swift’s 2-yard run to the TB 6, Thomas is flagged for late contact to the helmet on a block. Enforced at the TB 6. Backs the Bears up and contributes to a later interception. Bright-line late hit. Correct. Wt 2. False Start — Tristan Wirfs (TB), 5 yards. Q2 5:35, 3rd-and-5. Pre-snap movement. Bright-line. Correct. Wt 1. False Start — Cade Otton (TB), 5 yards. Q2 2:56, 1st-and-10. Pre-snap movement. Bright-line. Correct. Wt 1. False Start — Cody Mauch (TB), 5 yards. Q2 0:25, 2nd-and-10. Pre-snap movement. Bright-line. Correct. Wt 1. Defensive Holding — J. Johnson (CHI), 5 yards. Q2 0:25, 2nd-and-15. Defensive holding flag on Johnson. Available tape and the user’s All-22 review show the contact does not meet the standard for defensive holding. Incorrect. Wt 2. Third Quarter Bucky Irving scores from 2 yards. CHI 17, TB 13. Offensive Holding — D’Marco Jackson (CHI), 10 yards. Q3 11:37 (Flag of the Game). Zavion Thomas fields the kickoff at the Chicago 8 and returns it 91 yards to the Tampa Bay 1 (pushed out of bounds). Officials flag Jackson for holding. The 10-yard penalty is enforced from the Chicago 30, leaving the Bears at their own 20. Available angles and slow-motion replays show an open-palm block on the chest/shoulder area with no sustained grab of the jersey or restriction that meets the holding standard. Josh Blackwell called it a “terrible call” that “took a touchdown off the board for nothing that was really even there.” Broadcast rules analysis did not support a hold. This is not borderline. Horrible. Wt 4. Erased a near-touchdown or first-and-goal at the 1. We will get into this more with our Flag of the Game highlight. Bears' Josh Blackwell on the holding call on D'Marco Jackson that wiped out Zavion Thomas' 91-yard kick return TD: "Terrible call. I didn't think it was a good call. You just took a touchdown off the board for nothing that was really even there. That's annoying." — Phillip Thompson (@_phil_thompson) November 9, 2026 False Start — Luke Goedeke (TB), 5 yards. Q3 10:31, 1st-and-10. Pre-snap movement. Bright-line. Correct. Wt 1. Offensive Holding — Stephen Carlson (CHI), 9 yards. Q3 7:26, 3rd-and-1. Holding flag on Carlson. Judgment call on technique. Available angles show borderline restriction. Arguable. Wt 2. Offensive Holding — Bauer Sharp (TB), 10 yards. Q3 6:52, 1st-and-10. Holding flag on Sharp. Judgment call. Arguable. Wt 2. False Start — Jack Sanborn (CHI), 5 yards. Q3 0:33, 4th-and-4. Pre-snap movement. Bright-line. Correct. Wt 1. Jaylon Johnson intercepts Baker Mayfield and returns it 67 yards for a touchdown. CHI 24, TB 13. Fourth Quarter McLaughlin field goal. CHI 24, TB 16. Delay of Game — Unnamed (TB), 5 yards. Q4 11:28, 4th-and-4. Clock expires. Bright-line. Correct. Wt 1. Correct. Wt 1. Face Mask — Austin Booker (CHI), 15 yards. Q4 7:19, 3rd-and-8. Booker is flagged for grabbing the facemask while sacking Mayfield. Clear contact. Correct. Wt 2. No-call: Helmet-to-helmet hit on Luther Burden III by Rueben Bain Jr. (fumble + concussion). Late fourth quarter, third-and-long near the Bears’ own 15–17. Williams throws a short screen to Burden. Bain delivers clear helmet-to-helmet contact. Burden’s head is driven into the turf; he is knocked unconscious, fumbles, and is diagnosed with a concussion (confirmed by Ben Johnson postgame). title: Breaking Down the Bears Jeffery Simmons Trade
summary: There are days when I admittedly refuse to believe this trade happened for the Chicago Bears. The size, scope, and historic impact October 29th, 2026, will have throughout the league for the foreseeable future is almost impossible to comprehend. A deal many people assumed general manager Ryan Poles would never be bold enough to attempt. […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - NOVEMBER 02: Jeffery Simmons #99 of the Chicago Bears celebrates a win against the Seattle Seahawks after the game at Lumen Field on November 02, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images There are days when I admittedly refuse to believe this trade happened for the Chicago Bears. The size, scope, and historic impact October 29th, 2026, will have throughout the league for the foreseeable future is almost impossible to comprehend. A deal many people assumed general manager Ryan Poles would never be bold enough to attempt. Except, he’s always been this bold. He simply waited for the right time, right price, and only after all his homework was completed and reviewed with their staff. A trade that assessed every possible angle and weighed risk vs. reward more than anything else. Detailing back to the spring of this year, I maintained the Bears would be poised to strike on a major move to bolster their defensive line. This scenario has been one I’ve tracked for the better part of the past calendar year. Many, many big names were floated around behind the scenes. Including Maxx Crosby, of whom the Bears mentioned publicly as a player they checked in on. It always came down to Ryan Poles’ comfort level with the price tag presented. Ironically, it was the least likely option on paper for me that wound up becoming reality. Not a single defensive tackle traded has ever commanded more than a single first-round pick throughout the modern Super Bowl and draft era. Very few players have ever signed a lengthy record-setting contract with their home team only to be shipped off elsewhere before the trade deadline. That paragraph might be the reason Ryan Poles pulled this trigger then and there. Not a single team in the league was made aware of Jeffery Simmons’ availability until only after the trade was announced. Ryan Poles mentioned in his press conference that he eyeballed Jeffery Simmons for the past few years. He called current Tennessee Titans general manager Mike Borgonzi several times dating back to 2025 and checked in on Simmons’ availability. The answer usually received: “No, Ryan.” Fast forward to late October of 2026. The Bears are rolling and have a legit MVP-caliber quarterback in Caleb Williams, priming the Monsters of the Midway for a potential run at the Super Bowl. Ben Johnson, the Bears’ head coach and dual-major graduate of mathematics and computer science from North Carolina at Chapel Hill, has the vision on how to get Chicago to the promised land. Dennis Allen, their mad scientist of a defensive coordinator, mixed and matched to the best of their abilities. Everything was trending in the right direction. There was just one big problem facing the Bears. They didn’t have a destroyer of worlds for the interior of their defense. A kind of player Ryan Poles referenced the last five Super Bowl champs having on their rosters. 2025 – Seattle Seahawks (Leonard Williams) 2024 – Philadelphia Eagles (Jalen Carter & Jordan Davis) 2022 & 2023 – Kansas City Chiefs (Chris Jones) 2021 – Los Angeles Rams (Aaron Donald) 2020 – Tampa Bay Buccaneers (Vita Vea & Ndamukong Suh) Meanwhile, the Tennessee Titans were facing the exact opposite situation. Endless debates are being entertained after having just one win up to this point in 2026. A season that can be best described as a lost voyage featuring yet another head coach — Robert Saleh — as their captain, paired with a quarterback and helmsman they didn’t handpick themselves. A sailboat with patchwork rigging and a broken rudder but a fine motor in reserve named Jeffery Simmons. The very kind of motor Ryan Poles sought after for his defense. Determined to get his white whale, Ryan Poles called Mike Borgonzi once again on October 28th. This time, per Jay Glazer, he straight up offered two first-round picks before even beginning their conversation in earnest. Usually you’d contact the football front office of your primary target, ask, “What are your demands?” Then circle back once your own staff is briefed. Ryan went straight to business and threw out all traditional negotiation tactics. Similar to a method when abandoning the traditional second interview for Ben Johnson before hiring him as head coach. Mike Borgonzi never thought he’d receive a Myles Garrett-level package for Jeffery Simmons. A true Godfather offer that you cannot refuse on first glance. He knew as much as anyone the precedent Ryan Poles’ offer stood to redefine. True to their own principles, Mike told Ryan he’d call him later after mulling over this massive deal. The next morning he briefed Titans owner Amy Strunk along with their executive leadership and Robert Saleh about his latest offer in hand. Interestingly enough, the Bears weren’t the only franchise attempting to poach Simmons away. Prior to this meeting at the Titans’ ownership level, John Harbaugh of the New York Giants attempted to contact Amy Strunk directly, of which Strunk deferred back to Borgonzi and the terms of the conversation were discussed. It has been suggested John Harbaugh’s offer would not have trumped what the Bears were willing to do. Then there are these potential considerations when discussing the human element – where were the Bears headed this season in comparison to the Giants? Where would Jeffery Simmons, a player beloved from ownership on down, get their best chance to win a Super Bowl? And how would they go about doing right by Big Jeff? Early on Tuesday morning, the Titans finalized their decision. Todd France, Jeffery Simmons’ agent, called his client later that day. It was to inform him of his immediate departure for Halas Hall on a short fused flight to Chicago O’Hare. Jeffery Simmons informed his family, said his “see you later’s” to his daughter, and reported to Bears HQ to finalize their physical that very evening. Two practices and a few days later he would make his regular season debut for the Chicago Bears at Lumen Field in Seattle, WA. Of course, the results have been immediate. The Bears are, finally, generating pressure with just their front four while keeping their defensive backs in coverage. That doesn’t mean Dennis Allen won’t blitz anymore; it just means he can keep those aces up his sleeves more often. Prior to “El Jefe’s” arrival, the Bears were blitzing more than anyone else not named the Minnesota Vikings out of necessity. Through the first seven weeks, the Bears defensive line was unable to register more than two full sacks on their own for any single game. Their pass-rush win rate was roughly 25%, which ranked near the bottom of the league. Following Jeffery Simmons’ arrival the Bears defensive line has exploded – against the Seahawks alone that unit won a whopping 53% of their matchups and Montez Sweat had two of his three sacks taken away due to penalties. Against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, the Bears’ front four registered four sacks between five players. Blasting quarterbacks isn’t the only feat Big Jeff is capable of performing. The run defense has been much improved too – for the first seven weeks, the Bears ranked 26th in defensive EPA (-0.01). Since his arrival in week eight that has improved to 19th (-0.07). There is optimism this group will break the top 15 once they return from their bye. Let’s now talk about the sheer cost of this trade and how it’s not the most expensive ever for a defensive tackle. We will use the Draft Pick Trade Value Chart as designed by Mike McCoy and famously used by Jimmy Johnson as reference. Shortly before the start of the 2026 NFL Draft, the Cincinnati Bengals struck a deal to send their 10th overall pick, which netted Dexter Lawrence in return. On face value alone, the 10th overall is worth 1300 points. And this isn’t a future draft pick – it’s locked in at its current spot. Which then gave the Giants two picks within the top ten of the draft order at 5th (1700) and 10th (1300) to open the first round. Those picks combined are worth 3000…
