title: Will the Broncos make any changes to the starting lineup over the bye week?
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country. The Denver Broncos are 7-2 and hold the AFC West lead for now. That record is impressive all things considered. If you would have told me that would have been their record before the bye, I would have respectfully disagreed given the gauntlet of opponents they have played to date. There […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 4: Ben Powers #74 of the Denver Broncos jogs off of the field during halftime of an NFL football game against the San Francisco 49ers at Levi's Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country. The Denver Broncos are 7-2 and hold the AFC West lead for now. That record is impressive all things considered. If you would have told me that would have been their record before the bye, I would have respectfully disagreed given the gauntlet of opponents they have played to date. There is no doubt the Broncos have a lot of room for improvement. They haven’t been at their best but are certainly trending in the right direction. Over the next week, Denver will have the opportunity to rest, recuperate, and also do some reflection on what they’ve accomplished this season. Moreover, what they need to do moving forward to have the best shot at earning the franchise’s fourth Lombardi Trophy. Yesterday, Head Coach Sean Payton spoke with Colin Cowherd on the status of the team. If you haven’t had a chance to watch the interview, you certainly should at the link above. One of big questions was Cowherd asked for was Payton’s assessment of the offense in the first half of the season. “The cool thing about the bye right now is you really get a chance and zoom, and look really close what’s been going well, what hasn’t, and why hasn’t it been—and let’s not be kidding ourselves,” stated Payton. He went on to exert extreme confidence in Bo Nix. The third-year quarterback hasn’t made the huge jump fans were expecting this year. Nevertheless, Payton was adamant that the team has the right signal caller behind center. Despite some struggles, he is happy with what he has seen from Nix going up against some very tough defenses. Payton went on to talk about what they can do to set up Nix for better success in the second part of the season. Without hesitation, he discussed a position group that has experienced some regression this season at a few positions—the offensive line. “I’m watching the cutups from the game we just played [versus the Carolina Panthers]. We didn’t block them very well. I’m just being honest—that has to improve. We have plenty of depth on the offensive line. During this bye, we’re going to look at all those little things closely,” added Payton. I’m certainly not an offensive line expert by any means. Though I think it’s safe to say the Broncos have only had two consistent starters in their offensive trenches. Those would be left tackle Garett Bolles and right guard Quinn Meinerz. When it comes to center Luke Wattenberg, left guard Ben Powers, and right tackle Mike McGlinchey—all three have struggled and haven’t been at their best this season. I’d be skeptical that the Broncos would consider benching McGlinchey. I also find it hard to believe they would bench Wattenberg for Alex Forsyth. However, I wouldn’t be surprised if Powers was replaced. Last season when he got hurt, Powers was replaced by Alex Palcewzki and he performed admirably. Well enough for Denver to give him a multi-year extension this offseason. Powers had a restructure that lowered his base salary significantly but upped his guarantees. As noted in a feed post yesterday, Powers has struggled this season. In nine games, Powers has been credited with 14 blown blocks per SIS Data Hub . Ten of those have been pass blocks with four of them credit against the run. Though based on the eye test, I’d say they are drastically underestimating his issues paving lanes for the Broncos’ backs in the run game. We’ll just have to wait and see if the Broncos wind up making a change on their offensive line. Based on Payton’s discussion with Cowherd, that seems like a legitimate possibility. Denver certainly has to be better up front in the trenches if they want to be top-level competitors the rest of the way. What do you think, Broncos Country? Should Denver make a change on the offensive line? If so, what position and who do you feel should be inserted into the starting lineup. Sound off in the comments section and let me know. As always, thank you for reading. Here is today’s slate of articles for Horse Tracks .

summary: Yesterday, the Denver Broncos made a splash prior to the NFL trade deadline acquiring Los Angeles Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley for a 2027 fourth-round draft selection and a 2028 fifth-round draft selection. It was a mild surprise for Broncos Country. While fans certainly have wanted to see some changes at inside linebacker the past few […]
full_text: Nov 30, 2025; Landover, Maryland, USA; Denver Broncos safety Talanoa Hufanga (9) looks on during warmups prior to the game against the Washington Commanders at Northwest Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Peter Casey-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Yesterday, the Denver Broncos made a splash prior to the NFL trade deadline acquiring Los Angeles Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley for a 2027 fourth-round draft selection and a 2028 fifth-round draft selection. It was a mild surprise for Broncos Country. While fans certainly have wanted to see some changes at inside linebacker the past few offseasons, fans didn’t necessarily peg it as one of the positions the Broncos were going to be aggressive finding an addition to help them in the second half of the season. This morning, Spotrac reports the Broncos have converted a portion of safety Talanoa Hufanga’s 2026 base salary into a signing bonus. In turn, the Broncos will save nearly $4 million against the cap this season. However, the restructure does change the math on Hufanga’s future cap hits, which includes a staggering $14.8 million in dead money for the 2028 season. The #Broncos converted $4.89M of S Talanoa Hufanga's salary into signing bonus, creating $3.9M of 2026 cap space. Updated Cap Hits (dead) 2026: $9.5M ($17M) 2027: $7.6M ($8.4M) 2028: $14.8M (void) — Spotrac (@spotrac) November 11, 2026 Why the Broncos chose to do this remains a mystery. I’d have to assume at some point in time they give Hufanga an extension. That’s a lot of dead money to have to deal with in 2028 if they can’t come to a future agreement. With acquiring Henley, the Broncos will be taking on around $1.8 million in his salary for the rest of the season. However, this could signal they have something else in the works with another in-house player. Last season, Denver opted to extend Wil Lutz, Malcolm Roach, and Luke Wattenberg around their bye week in November. Perhaps this season, the Broncos could be looking to do the same. Henley is in the final year of his contract. With that in mind, he could potentially be one of those players. However, it wouldn’t be a surprise to see a cornerback like Ja’Quan McMillian potentially earn a well-deserved extension. What do you think, Broncos Country? Do you believe the Broncos will end up rewarding one of their own with a big contract extension over the bye week? Let me know your thoughts in the comments section.

title: No quarterback in NFL history has done what Bo Nix is doing
summary: Another week – another fourth quarter comeback and game-winning drive for Bo Nix. He now has 13 and 16 respectively in 43 games started. That’s one 4QC every 3.3 GS and one game-winning drive every 2.7 GS. If you do the rate stats per game started most of the top 10 are names that most […]
full_text: Another week – another fourth quarter comeback and game-winning drive for Bo Nix. He now has 13 and 16 respectively in 43 games started. That’s one 4QC every 3.3 GS and one game-winning drive every 2.7 GS. Top 50 in career GS/GWD pic.twitter.com/1EpM9JFQmc — Joe Mahoney (@ndjomo76) November 10, 2026 If you do the rate stats per game started most of the top 10 are names that most NFL fans have forgotten, and this is because QBs with long career generally don’t spend much time playing for a team with a combination of offensive and defensive proficiency/deficiency that leads to many opportunities for them. They are either playing in wins where they get the lead and keep it, or games when they are getting blown out most of the time. Close games were rare (at least until this year). Even some of the greats didn’t have this much opportunity at roughly the same points in their careers. Comparing Bo Nix to some other notable QBs at this same point (roughly) in their careers. pic.twitter.com/Nwh2pHX6i0 — Joe Mahoney (@ndjomo76) November 2, 2026 There were 154 one score games in the 2025 regular season. In the 2006 season there were 132. In the 1996 season there were only 117. We are half-way through the 2026 NFL regular season and there have already been 77 one-score games so they are occurring at the exact same rate as last season. The league loves parity (not to be confused with parody) and that is what they are getting with all of these close games. The Broncos appear to not be making any moves at running back so let’s talk about the Bronco run game so far. The Broncos are 21st in rushing success rate at 45.8. That is slightly below average. A successful run gains 40 percent of the needed yards on first down, 60 percent on second down, and converts on third or fourth down. Ranking NFL run games by successful run rate. Success on 1st down gains 40% of yards needed. On 2nd down gain 60% and on 3rd and 4th converts. pic.twitter.com/bAauB7UcC5 — Joe Mahoney (@ndjomo76) November 9, 2026 Looking at yards before contact per attempt is one way to see how well the OL of a given team is blocking. Right now RJ Harvey and Jonah Coleman are doing significantly better than JK Dobbins running behind the same offensive line. Coleman is getting 2.6 and Harvey is getting 2.4 while Dobbins is getting 1.7. The problem with the Bronco run game may be partly Powers and Wattenburg, but Harvey and Coleman have had much better YBC/att than Dobbins behind the same OL. 2.6 and 2.4 to 1.7. That's all on JK who is great this year at turning a 5 yard run into a 2 yard run pic.twitter.com/Av5Az22pBl — Joe Mahoney (@ndjomo76) November 9, 2026 Now, I’m sure some of you will think back to how badly Ben Powers and Mike McGlinchey looked run blocking last game and say “It’s the OL not the RB.” But you would be wrong. Those are a few instances and in general the OL has been doing fairly well at run blocking this season. JK Dobbins has just lost a step relative to last season. Coleman and Harvey have also had much better success rates so far this year on runs than Dobbins. The Bronco defense allowed a conversion on 4th and 18 last game on a play that would have effectively ended the game if the the defense could have stopped the conversion. So far this season the Broncos have been terrible at stopping teams on 3rd (or 4th) and long. They have allowed conversion on 20 of 63 plays. The Bronco defense allowed a conversion on 4th and 18 near the end of the game vs CAR. They now have allowed the most conversions on 3rd or 4th and long this season with 20 of 63 conversions. Ravens have been worst, Bears best. 7 or more is long pic.twitter.com/CCPtSSO5aY — Joe Mahoney (@ndjomo76) November 10, 2026 The Bears have been the best so far and the Ravens have been the worst.

title: No Bull thoughts on the ILB room after the Daiyan Henley trade
summary: I’ve been hammering the Broncos on their reluctance to upgrade the inside linebacker position for years. No serious draft picks spent on it, no trades, and no serious free agent pursuit. One of the most overlooked reasons that our 2015 defense was so dominant was the quality of talent we had at ILB. We had […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 08: Daiyan Henley #0 of the Los Angeles Chargers walks onto the field before an NFL game against the Houston Texans at SoFi Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Ryan Sun/Getty Images) | Getty Images I’ve been hammering the Broncos on their reluctance to upgrade the inside linebacker position for years. No serious draft picks spent on it, no trades, and no serious free agent pursuit. One of the most overlooked reasons that our 2015 defense was so dominant was the quality of talent we had at ILB. We had Danny Trevathan and Brandon Marshall. Both of those guys could cover. Both defended the run. They were playmakers just like everyone else on that defense. The Broncos signing Daiyan Henley is an A+ move, and I darn near would give them the same grade if they had traded a 3rd-round pick for him. Henley is a player that has been loved and respected in the Chargers’ locker room. He’s a captain of the team. He’s also a guy who has worn the green dot for the defense (calling the plays for the defense). This is yet another high-character player added to a locker room built on high character and positive culture. Athletically, he’s the most talented linebacker on the inside we have seen in a very long time. His capability at coverage is excellent. He’s also a more sure tackler than either of our current starters. So the question for this team becomes: what happens with our defense? While I think he’s a real option for the future captain of our defense over Alex Singleton, that day will not be soon. He’s going to have to learn the defense and be in the system a while before the Broncos can even think of that. I expect him to be in the mix in nickel downs coming out of the bye. I think he’s likely going to take Justin Strnad’s spot as the starter before the season is over. No matter what happens with the snap count, having depth at inside linebacker is a big deal. Having a linebacker who can cover running backs in the flat and tight ends could very well be the missing piece for this defense to take a big step forward. Lions | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The NFL trade deadline has come and past, and the Detroit Lions made just a modest move. They sent a 2028 sixth-round pick for depth safety Andre Cisco. While Cisco had been taken out of the starting lineup for the New York Jets—who are sporting a solid duo of Dane Belton and Mikah Fitzpatrick at the position—he comes to Detroit with plenty of playing experience and a knowledge of their system, having played under Aaron Glenn. It appears Cisco will have a role quickly with the team. “We would like to get him going ASAP,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said Wednesday. “We’d like to get him going. He’s obviously going out to Germany with them. Our plan is to get him going in this game and let him help us a little bit. How much, that’s not quite there yet, but we do have a plan for him to help us.” For many fans, that move wasn’t enough to move the needle for the Lions. They were hoping for a bigger splash, and potentially some help at the linebacker and cornerback position. So today’s Question of the Day is: Which move made at the NFL trade deadline do you think the Lions should have made? My answer: First, let me explain why I asked the question this way. Many people are mad that the Lions didn’t go out and get a player like Riq Woolen, Zack Baun, or Donte Jackson. But it’s hard to get mad at a move that no one made, because we don’t know the conditions required to trade for those players. Were they even available to trade for? Did the Lions try aggressively to acquire one, but the team wasn’t offering them at a reasonable price? Did the Lions ignore those player completely because they didn’t view them as scheme fits? It’s impossible to informatively critique the Lions for failing to make a move when we have zero reliable knowledge on what it would’ve taken to acquire those players. Those conversations feel like a waste of time and energy. However, we do know the conditions it took to trade for players who were moved over the last few weeks. We know for certain that they were available for trade, and we know (around) what it would’ve cost Detroit to acquire said player. So, among the moves that were made over the past few weeks, which one appeals to you the most? YOU CAN SEE THE FULL LIST OF TRADES MADE IN-SEASON HERE IN OUR TRACKER Interestingly, since the Joey Porter Jr. trade over a month ago, there have only been a few defensive trades made: Bears trade for DT Jeffery Simmons 49ers trade for DT DeForest Buckner Jaguars trade for DT Davon Godchaux Jaguars trade for S Jessie Bates Bills trade for S Amani Hooker Lions trade for S Andre Cisco Then two trade that were agreed upon fell through: Bengals trading for EDGE Arnold Ebiketie and Broncos trading for LB Daiyan Henley. So, essentially, zero trades were made at positions of need for the Lions. I saw many wishing they had trade for Henley (Broncos were going to spend a fourth and 2028 fifth-round pick for him), and at this point, it’s unclear why the trade did not go through. I will say, I’m intrigued by the other safety moves that were made. I think Jessie Bates is a game-changer, but a second-round pick for a half-season rental is a bit pricey for a Lions team that is getting healthier at the safety position right now. Hooker is a younger option who is signed through 2028, and comes with reasonable price tags of $9.57 million in 2027 and $11.8 million in 2028. If the Lions don’t believe Kerby Joseph will be around beyond this year, this could’ve been a very savvy move for what amounted to a second-round pick with a fifth-round pick in return. However, the trade I keep going back to is the Joey Porter Jr. one. I still think that’s a move I would’ve made (cost the Cowboys a sixth and 2028 second-round pick). While Porter has struggled with injuries with Dallas, his play on the field has been as advertised. I thought he was a great scheme fit, and a potential long-term option for a position Detroit has struggled to find consistency at. I wrote more about why I thought the Lions should’ve traded for Porter Jr. back in October . Which trade deadline move that was actually finalized do you think the Lions should have made? Share your thoughts in the comment section below.

title: Lions, Patriots Week 10 injury report: Jared Goff limited; DJ Wonnum returns to practice
summary: The Detroit Lions (6-2) head to Germany in Week 10 to take on the New England Patriots (5-4), but before they travel overseas, they’ll hold two practices in Allen Park: a walkthrough on Wednesday and a standard practice on Thursday. A walkthrough practice means that all participation levels are estimates from the coaching staff based […]
full_text: Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) high-fives teammates at warmup ahead of the game between Detroit Lions and Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions (6-2) head to Germany in Week 10 to take on the New England Patriots (5-4), but before they travel overseas, they’ll hold two practices in Allen Park: a walkthrough on Wednesday and a standard practice on Thursday. A walkthrough practice means that all participation levels are estimates from the coaching staff based on how the player would have participated in a traditional practice. So, with that in mind, let’s look at Wednesday’s injury report and get you up to date on what we know. Note: Any changes from the most recent injury report will be bolded . Injured list updates RB Isiah Pacheco (MCL/Back, IR) — expected to be out until December OL Giovanni Manu (undisclosed, NFI) — eligible to begin practicing at any time OL Ben Bartch (foot, IR) — eligible to begin practicing at any time LB Devin White (forearm, IR) — eligible to begin practicing at any time LB Jack Campbell (neck, IR) — determined to play football again S Kerby Joseph (knee, PUP) — injury evaluation clock started S Thomas Harper (ankle, IR) — eligible to begin practicing at any time Campbell was officially added to the Lions injured reserve list last Saturday, and while he continues to improve, his overall health and status with the team remain undetermined. That said, Campbell is reportedly determined to play football again and wants the team to “make sure the house is taken care of until [he] can get back.” Estimated n o practice RB Sione Vaki (ankle) — downgraded to no practice C Cade Mays (low ankle sprain) CB D.J. Reed (hip) Vaki popped up on Week 9’s injury report late in the week, and while he was given a questionable designation for the game, he was available and contributed in RB2 and starting special teams roles. The Lions may take things slowly with him this week, but unless he had a set back, he still has a chance to play in Germany. Mays and Reed were both injured in Week 8, missed Week 9, and appear to be longshots to suit up in Week 10, according to Lions coach Dan Campbell. “I don’t see Cade and Reed practicing today,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said on Wednesday. “I don’t see them practicing today. They have got a way outside shot of playing. Way, way, way outside shot.” Juice Scruggs has been starting at center while Mays recovers, and the Lions have rotated corners to split snaps while Reed is sidelined. Last week, Rock Ya-Sin got the start and played the majority of the rotation, but Khalil Dorsey, Ennis Rakestraw, and recently promoted Nick Whiteside saw some situational work as well. Estimated limited practice QB Jared Goff (chest) — New Injury WR Amon-Ra St. Brown (rib) S Brian Branch (hip) — New Injury S Kerby Joseph (knee, PUP) — Days remaining in injury evaluation clock: 6 Goff took a few more shots against the Dolphins than he normally does, so this could be a light day for him to recover, as there have been no indicators that they’re worried about him missing this game. We’ll still have to wait until Thursday to get a better idea, but there’s no need to panic just yet. St. Brown was injured in Week 8 and had limited practice time ahead of Week 9, but he didn’t appear limited in the game. With this week’s game in his mother’s home country, and all the charity work he’s done in Germany over the last two years, you can be sure he’s playing. Branch just cleared the NFL’s concussion protocol only to show up on this week’s injury report with a new ailment. It’s not clear when he suffered this hip injury, as he played the entire game last Sunday, but like Goff, we’ll have to double check his status on Thursday before we can feel totally comfortable. Joseph continues to make positive strides as he acclimates back to football, and the Lions are happy with his progress, but Campbell has already told the media that Joseph won’t play in Germany . The Lions don’t have to decide on his PUP status until next Tuesday. Estimated full practice RB Jacob Saylors (neck/hamstring) — Upgraded after limited practice last week EDGE DJ Wonnum (concussion) — Upgraded after no practice last week Saylors injured his neck in Week 7, couldn’t play the entire game in Week 8, and fully missed Week 9, even though he was a limited participant, he’s now added a hamstring injury to his list of ailments. Getting more work this week is positive, and despite the full practice, the Lions will probably take it slow with him. Wonnum suffered a concussion in Week 8 that kept him from playing in Week 9, but he’s made progress since then and is close to completing the NFL’s concussion protocols, according to Campbell: “Wonnum, he’s cleared his first obstacle; second obstacle here. So, he’s going to be able to practice today. As long as he gets through practice, he should be good to go. So, that’s encouraging.” No longer on the injury report LB Amen Ogbongbemiga (toe) CB Rock Ya-Sin (cramps) The players listed in this section no longer require a spot on the injury report. All three players are injury replacements for starting guards Alijah Vera-Tucker and Mike Onwenu, who are both on injured reserve. title: Christian Mahogany back in at starting LG spot in Week 10
summary: After being pulled from the starting lineup in Week 9 for a “rules violation,” Christian Mahogany is set to return to his starting left guard spot in Week 10, according to Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell. “Mahogany is going to go out there (today), and he’s going to start with the first unit,” Campbell said […]
full_text: Oct 11, 2026; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Detroit Lions offensive lineman Christian Mahogany (73) against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect After being pulled from the starting lineup in Week 9 for a “rules violation,” Christian Mahogany is set to return to his starting left guard spot in Week 10, according to Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell. “Mahogany is going to go out there (today), and he’s going to start with the first unit,” Campbell said at his Wednesday press conference. Mahogany’s career got off to a delayed start after contracting mono and missing the first half of his rookie season. In his second year, he won the starting left guard job but broke his left leg during the season and struggled to find his footing after returning. Now, in year three, Mahogany once again won the starting role at left guard and, with his health issues kept at bay, found his groove and has been excelling—currently ranked the 13th-best guard in the NFL by PFF, including grading inside the top 10 as a pass blocker. Ahead of Week 9, Mahogany broke an undisclosed team rule and was benched in the Lions game against the Dolphins. Miles Frazier stepped into a starting role and struggled right out of the gate, committing holding penalties, allowing pressure, and failing to generate drive in the run game. He settled in well in the second half, but several of the Lions’ first-half drives stalled or ended early because of the offensive line’s play. Immediately after the game, Campbell told the media that Mahogany committed a team rule violation, and while he was benched for that game, it “doesn’t mean it stays that way.” On Monday, Campbell said the two had discussed the matter and that “we’re good” moving forward, adding that it’s now up to Mahogany to show he can put this mistake behind him. In addition to disclosing that Mahogany will return to his starting role, Campbell also shared that “he was good this morning,” suggesting everyone is taking positive steps forward.

title: Song of the game: ‘Shut Up’ by Trick Daddy
summary: If you were a 90s baby coming of age in the early to mid-2000s, you likely know who Trick Daddy is. For a period of time, he was one of, if not the biggest artist to hail from Miami, Florida. Beyond that, he was instrumental in the bond that began to form between sports and […]
full_text: If you were a 90s baby coming of age in the early to mid-2000s, you likely know who Trick Daddy is. For a period of time, he was one of, if not the biggest artist to hail from Miami, Florida. Beyond that, he was instrumental in the bond that began to form between sports and hip-hop during that same period. From stadium anthems like “Let’s Go” and “Take it to Da House” to classics like “I’m a Thug,” these songs have been played at barbecues across the country until the end of time—the Dade County native has a song for nearly any occasion. In honor of the Detroit Lions’ Week 9 win over the Miami Dolphins, I’m bringing you another staple from the Trick Daddy archives: “ Shut Up .” Without all that fancy s***, way too advanced for this Just Polo socks, tanktops and drawers up under my pants and s*** Shut up! Ah hah, okay, whassup? Shut up! Ah hah, okay, whassup? Shut up! It wasn’t the prettiest win for the Lions, but at the end of the day, that doesn’t matter. What matters is that they found a way to grind out their fourth win in a row against a Miami team that seemed set on not making it easy for Detroit. After all, this is the NFL, and no win should be taken for granted. If someone complains that it was too close a call down in South Beach, tell them to “shut up” and play them this song.

title: Film study: Andre Cisco’s fit and Sione Vaki’s expanded role
summary: The NFL trade deadline came and went, leaving most of the Detroit Lions faithful underwhelmed, disappointed, and frustrated with Brad Holmes for not matching the impact-level trades of the Chicago Bears or the Minnesota Vikings. Count me as one of them. I had my wish list of defensive backs I thought Holmes should target. The […]
full_text: Detroit Lions edge rusher Derrick Moore (8) makes a catch against New York Jets safety Andre Cisco (8) during the second half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The NFL trade deadline came and went, leaving most of the Detroit Lions faithful underwhelmed, disappointed, and frustrated with Brad Holmes for not matching the impact-level trades of the Chicago Bears or the Minnesota Vikings. Count me as one of them. I had my wish list of defensive backs I thought Holmes should target. The good news, however, is that the Lions did not come away empty-handed. In fact, the trade for safety Andre Cisco stabilizes the safety room for Kelvin Sheppard’s defense for the cost of just a 2029 sixth-round pick. At that price, Cisco is essentially a free acquisition with 59 career starts, 8 interceptions, and 4 forced fumbles . Shortly after the news of the Lions trade for Cisco, coach Dan Campbell shared his thoughts on the safety: “We’ve liked Cisco from afar, having played against him and then even in free agency when he was with Jacksonville coming out. He’s athletic, he’s versatile, he knows our system, he knows our verbiage (via his time with Aaron Glenn and the Jets), so we feel like this is a guy that can help us here a little bit. We’re excited.” The key takeaway is that Cisco knows the Lions’ system and verbiage, making him a plug-and-play contributor in the Lions’ rotating use of defensive backs. The defense spent the first half of the season working through a flood of missed assignments and trust issues. Cisco’s familiarity with the scheme should reduce the likelihood of those fatal errors from creeping back onto the tape. For this film study, I set out to learn about Cisco and how he fits on this Lions. I also reviewed the film from the Week 9 game against the Miami Dolphins for anything noteworthy. Cisco plays Dan Campbell’s brand of football The first thing that stood out in Cisco’s film is that he plays safety as an aggressor, with violence and resilience. In the Lions’ Week 3 home game against the New York Jets, Cisco played 66 defensive snaps and played through the whistle on each one of them. Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, and Isaac TeSlaa are known for their physicality and effort as blockers, but Cisco was up for the challenge and battled the Lions wide receivers all game. Below, on the Lions’ first run play of the game, Cisco (No. 8) shows on tape his desire to deliver the hit at the point of contact rather than finesse the block. On the second play below, Cisco matches St. Brown’s physicality and sustains his effort in the tight red zone to get in on the tackle. It cannot be emphasized enough how big of an impact this level of physicality and effort will matter down the stretch, especially against Ben Johnson and the Bears’ run game. Cisco is versatile on defense and reliable on special teams Beyond effort and physicality, Cisco has always been known for his versatility. Although used primarily as a high safety, Cisco showed he can blitz when he took down Jared Goff for a 10-yard loss. With Brian Branch, Kerby Joseph (presumably), and likely Chuck Clark set to take on most snaps at safety, Cisco will have to contribute on special teams. For the Jets this season, Cisco has logged 130 special teams snaps . After reviewing a sample of these snaps, the common role he was tasked with on both punt and kickoff coverage units was as a contain/safety/trail player, a sign of his ability to instinctively read, react, and reliably tackle as a last line of defense. For example, below is Cisco on kickoff coverage, lined up as the “L1” outside player on the left side of the formation. Instead of aggressively engaging with the return, Cisco’s role is to read and react with outside-contain leverage. Once the returner makes his vertical cut through an inside alley, Cisco closes down to make the play. At the end of the day, Brad Holmes upgraded the Lions’ safety room with a clear play style and schematic fit, with a wealth of starting experience in Cisco at a negligible cost. By the end of the season, I expect this move to garner strong approval from even the most frustrated Holmes critics. Don’t be surprised if Cisco also earns himself a spot on the Lions 2027 roster. Vaki the offensive chess piece Without bypassing the Miami game entirely, one play Drew Petzing dialed up shows the continued evolution of both the offensive scheme and Sione Vaki’s role. As shown below, Vaki is lined up as a fullback/h-back directly in front of Jahmyr Gibbs and used as a lead blocker on the crack-toss sweep. Expanding Vaki’s role to include a pseudo-fullback option opens up many different options for the Lions offense. For example, the “sidecar” or “offset full house” formation the Lions used so effectively against Brian Flores and the Vikings’ defense could be adapted to use Vaki in one of the previously used tight end roles, opening up a host of different run and pass concepts from the same look. When Ben Johnson ran the Lions offense, one noticeable feature was multiple layers, with formations and plays building off each other and setting up defenses weeks in advance. This is the art of play calling and offensive design. Petzing is starting to show that same talent and ability as an offensive coordinator. If this trend continues, this offense could have another gear we haven’t seen yet.

title: Detroit Lions scouting report: Do the New England Patriots have a Super Bowl hangover?
summary: For the first time since 2015, the Detroit Lions are heading overseas! The Lions have played only two international games in their history—going 1-1 in London, England—but this time they’re headed to Munich, Germany. Entering this matchup, they’ve won four straight games and want to keep that streak alive while claiming their first-ever win in […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - NOVEMBER 08: Drake Maye #10 of the New England Patriots looks on after losing to the Green Bay Packers 45-27 at Gillette Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Billie Weiss/Getty Images) | Getty Images For the first time since 2015, the Detroit Lions are heading overseas! The Lions have played only two international games in their history—going 1-1 in London, England—but this time they’re headed to Munich, Germany. Entering this matchup, they’ve won four straight games and want to keep that streak alive while claiming their first-ever win in Germany. Detroit takes on the New England Patriots, who appear to be in a rough spot right now, losing two of their last three games and barely above .500. Coming off a Super Bowl appearance last season, New England is currently the seven seed in the AFC, and with injuries also piling up, they’ve got a lot to overcome to keep their playoff hopes alive. Let’s take a deep look at the Patriots’ season so far as they head into Week 10. New England Patriots 2026 season thus far (5-4) Week 1: Lost to Seattle Seahawks 13-10 Week 2: Defeated Pittsburgh Steelers 20-3 Week 3: Lost to Jacksonville Jaguars 35-6 Week 4: Defeated Buffalo Bills 29-26 Week 5: Defeated Las Vegas Raiders 45-17 Week 6: Defeated New York Jets 26-19 Week 7: Lost to Chicago Bears 30-24 Week 8: Defeated Miami Dolphins 24-19 Week 9: Lost to Green Bay Packers 45-27 Offensive stats: Quarterback Drake Maye has had a rocky performance after being an MVP finalist last season. He had a rough first month, throwing “meatball subs,” as the kids say nowadays. Maye played well but had an abysmal Week 9, throwing three interceptions. This season, Maye is averaging 253.6 yards per game with 18 touchdowns and 11 interceptions, tied for the league lead in interceptions. The Patriots’ running game has been lackluster this season. Second-year running back TreVeyon Henderson is in a sophomore slump, compounded by injuries, with just 203 yards, a touchdown, and 3.9 yards per carry. Starting running back Rhamondre Stevenson hasn’t been explosive either, averaging 3.9 yards per carry with 399 yards and two touchdowns—and he could be held out of this game with a knee tendon issue. The team has seen a little bit of life in third-string back Corey Kiner, who is averaging 4.9 yards per carry with 244 yards and a touchdown. At receiver, it’s been an interesting ride: the Patriots traded for wide receiver A.J. Brown to be their top receiver after losing Stefon Diggs in free agency, and Brown has battled ankle injuries, playing in only three games with 101 yards on nine catches. The top receiver currently is DeMario Douglas, who leads the team in yards (434) and touchdowns (four). The Patriots also signed Romeo Doubs in free agency to a big contract, and he is currently on IR, though he will return this season—he’s got 261 yards and three touchdowns in 2026. One reason for the running game struggles is injuries on the offensive line. The Patriots are without both starting guards, Mike Onwenu and Alijah Vera-Tucker, and now left guard Ben Brown will most likely miss this week’s game, according to head coach Mike Vrabel. PFF ranks them 19th in run blocking (62.7), which plays a big part in why the running backs can’t find success on the ground. With them not having success on the ground, that puts more pressure on Maye to air it out, and suddenly he’s turnover-happy, trying to make plays for the offense. Defensive stats: On defense, the front seven has done a solid job overall. EDGE Elijah Ponder leads the team with 7.5 sacks and is tied for fourth-most in the NFL. Defensive tackle Christian Barmore has 4.5 sacks while rookie EDGE Gabe Jacas has 3.0. The secondary has been about average, as newly extended cornerback Christian Gonzalez has six pass deflections and a 51.4 PFF coverage grade. Former Lions cornerback Carlton Davis III has been doing well, with a 72 coverage grade. Nickelback Marcus Jones has played well, tied with Gonzalez for the team-leading six pass deflections, and earned a 59.5 coverage grade. New England is allowing a 67.5 percent completion percentage, the third-highest in the NFL, and is just nine yards behind the Lions for most passing yards allowed this season (2,256), according to Next Gen Stats. They’ve allowed some big plays in the air, including 32 20+ yard passing plays (second-most) and seven 40+ passing-yard plays (tied for fourth-most). Despite the pass rush getting home, it isn’t getting there fast enough for the secondary to hold up its end of the bargain. With teams struggling to run against New England, they’ve had to air it out and risk that pressure, and the secondary has had its share of woes. Injury notes Key players ruled out : WR Romeo Doubs (IR), G Mike Onwenu (IR), G Alijah Vera-Tucker (IR), LB Harold Landry III (PUP) Key players to monitor : WR A.J. Brown (ankle/knee), RB TreVeyon Henderson (illness), LT Will Campbell (knee), RB Rhamondre Stevenson (knee), CB Carlton Davis III (knee), LG Ben Brown (knee) Injuries have started to pile up for the Patriots over the past few weeks. It started after Week 1 when A.J. Brown suffered an ankle injury and went to IR. He has returned from IR but has played only two games, as the injury is still bothering him. He has missed the last two games and, according to Tom Pelissero , should return sooner rather than later, perhaps after the Week 11 bye. In his absence, Doubs and Mack Hollins stepped up but also suffered injuries: Hollins just returned from IR in Week 9, while Doubs is set to return from IR after the team’s bye week. The interior offensive line has seen both starting guards, Onwenu and Vera-Tucker, land on IR, with Vera-Tucker likely returning this season, though Onwenu’s status remains up in the air. New England is still waiting to activate linebacker Harold Landry III off PUP as well. Week 9 was a bad week for New England injuries, starting with Henderson having a medical emergency that forced him to miss the game; his status is unknown. On the field, the Patriots saw four starters go down, all with knee injuries. Left tackle Will Campbell, Stevenson, Davis III, and Brown all left the game and didn’t return with their injuries. Campbell told the media after the game that he’s fine, while Vrabel didn’t provide an update on Stevenson or Davis III on Monday. Biggest strength: Front seven New England’s defense has been helping this team a lot, especially in stopping the run and getting to the quarterback. Starting with the pass rush, New England has 25 sacks overall, tied for ninth most in the league. Ponder has been playing lights out and has given this defense a big spark in their pass-rushing abilities. PFF grades them with an 82.8 pass rush grade, second-highest in the NFL. Elijah Ponder closing out the first half with a SACK 😤 @LVvsNE on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/SFquxShY2n — NFL (@NFL) October 11, 2026 This front seven can do more than get to the quarterback; they can also slow down the running game. They’ve allowed an average of 3.9 yards per carry, tied for ninth-fewest. More impressively, though, they’ve allowed only one run over 20 yards, for 34. This team makes it really hard to run the football and dares you to drop back to throw it. When you’re forced to air it out, that pass rush comes into play and pressures your quarterback. It’s a seesaw battle opposing offenses have to deal with. Do you go aggressive and try to run on them, or lean on your passing game to hopefully light it up? If the passing game succeeds, it opens the door for the run game to have a better chance of breaking one through; if you can’t do either, it’s going to be a long day for your offense. Biggest weakness: Offensive injuries While the data and numbers show the Patriots offense is average to slightly above average, injuries are piling up on that side of the ball. Moore is currently on the injured reserve, but the team has a 21-day opportunity to activate him to the 53-man roster. Along with Moore, running back Chris Brooks (also on the injured reserve) practiced […]
full_text: (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers opened up their practice window for receiver/returner Skyy Moore, who was a limited participant (ankle) on Wednesday. Moore is currently on the injured reserve, but the team has a 21-day opportunity to activate him to the 53-man roster. Along with Moore, running back Chris Brooks (also on the injured reserve) practiced with the Packers today (limited, ankle). Edge defender Micah Parsons was listed as an estimated limited participant on Wednesday, despite head coach Matt LaFleur stating that Parsons would not be participating in today’s action due to an illness. The only non-participants on the injury report today were safety Javon Bullard (ankle/knee), linebacker Zaire Franklin (shin), center Sean Rhyan (ankle), edge defender Lukas Van Ness (back) and tight end Josh Whyle (concussion). Hockenson (wrist/chest), defensive lineman Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins (ankle), receiver Jauan Jennings (calf), quarterback Kyler Murray (hamstring) and outside linebacker Kyle Van Noy (calf). full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur already said this week that the injuries to linebackers Ty’Ron Hopper and Isaiah McDuffie are not expected to be serious, a great sign — considering that the Packers just had two healthy off-ball linebackers left after those injuries last week. On Wednesday, though, LaFleur continued the optimism about the team’s injury situations. According to LaFleur, he’s hopeful that linebacker Zaire Franklin and receiver Skyy Moore will be able to practice with the team this week, too. He also said it’s possible that center Sean Rhyan is back for their game against the Minnesota Vikings. Moore is currently on the injured reserve, while Franklin and Rhyan are on the active roster but have missed multiple games now. On the subject of Micah Parsons, LaFleur said that Parsons will do some team drills this week — unlike last week, when he just went through individual drills — but it won’t be today, as Parsons is dealing with an illness. Look for him to return later in the week. Several reports have claimed that running back Josh Jacobs could miss two to three weeks of action as he recovers from surgery on his right ring finger. Apparently, the team will decide whether or not to place Jacobs on the injured reserve on Saturday. At the moment, the Packers’ 53-man active roster and 17-man practice squad are full, despite the team needing room for the additions of Parsons, Moore and running back Chris Brooks in the near future. Look for Green Bay to make some roster moves in the coming weeks.

title: The Packers are preparing for a Kirk Cousins start
summary: At his pre-practice press conference on Wednesday, Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur was asked whether Kirk Cousins, the quarterback who was previously LaFleur’s responsibility in Washington, would start for the Minnesota Vikings this weekend. Cousins, a former Vikings starter, was traded back to the team on Tuesday from the Las Vegas Raiders for […]
full_text: (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) | Getty Images At his pre-practice press conference on Wednesday, Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur was asked whether Kirk Cousins, the quarterback who was previously LaFleur’s responsibility in Washington, would start for the Minnesota Vikings this weekend. Cousins, a former Vikings starter, was traded back to the team on Tuesday from the Las Vegas Raiders for a third-round pick. Here was LaFleur’s response: Yeah, he’ll be out there. He’ll be starting. I’m fairly confident of that. Obviously, he’s got familiarity with their system. Even if he didn’t, he’s a really intelligent guy, and I think he’s been playing at a high level. I was surprised they didn’t get more for him, quite honestly. I was shocked when I saw what they traded him for. It was mind-blowing to me. Going into the season, the Vikings’ QB1 was Kyler Murray, who is currently out with a grade 2 hamstring strain. Minnesota sent off their former first-round pick J.J. McCarthy to the New York Giants earlier this year, pushing Carson Wentz up the lineup. Wentz had an all-time bad game on Monday Night Football against the Buffalo Bills, where the Vikings came away with just three points. Wentz was 8 of 25 passing for 81 yards and 2 interceptions for a passer rating of 8.9 on the game. Meanwhile, Cousins posted a 97.1 passer rating for the Raiders in the first half of the season, going 202 of 315 for 2,340 yards, 20 touchdowns and 8 interceptions. With that being said, Cousins is coming off his worst game of the season, as he threw three interceptions against the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday.

title: Green Bay Packers News: Packers stand pat at trade deadline
summary: The Packers, more or less as expected, didn’t do anything at this year’s edition of the NFL trade deadline. Reportedly, it wasn’t for lack of trying. The Packers apparently had an offer on the table for Indianapolis Colts defensive lineman Grover Stewart, but the Colts dragged their feet and the Packers moved on, content to […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-OCTOBER 25: Green Bay Packers offensive tackle Travis Glover (79) and Green Bay Packers guard John Williams (73) converse with teammates between plays during an NFL football game between the New York Jets and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, September 27, 2026 (Photo by Amy Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images The Packers, more or less as expected, didn’t do anything at this year’s edition of the NFL trade deadline. Reportedly, it wasn’t for lack of trying. The Packers apparently had an offer on the table for Indianapolis Colts defensive lineman Grover Stewart, but the Colts dragged their feet and the Packers moved on, content to stand pat with what they have (which includes a couple of options still yet to return from injured reserve). Time will tell whether they made the right moves. Or, rather, didn’t make the wrong moves. Or maybe made the right move by not making any moves at all. But I still sense an undercurrent of frustration among some fans and writers. To be sure, there’s a point to some of the criticism. The Packers do have needs. They could stand to get better at running back and on the offensive line. They’re not exactly awash in defensive line options. But having needs doesn’t mean you can just go fill them at the drop of your hat. What if nobody wants to trade you an offensive lineman? What if the cost to get a running back is prohibitive? What if the Colts decide to just hang on to a guy who’s going to be a free agent in the spring anyway? I’ve never done it, but I’m told it takes two to tango. That’s true in the trade market as well, and arguably you might need at least three: a GM in Green Bay willing to deal, a prospect worth acquiring, and an opposing GM willing to play ball. The Packers have at least one of those and may have had two, but couldn’t find a dance partner. Them’s the breaks sometimes. Perhaps more to the point, I don’t know if any trade the Packers could have made would have solved what ails them. Put Jonathan Taylor behind this offensive line and you probably get better performance than the Packers have had from the position so far, but also a worse version of what you’d probably expect from Taylor. Outside of Quenton Nelson, I don’t know if a single offensive lineman fixes much. The best move might have been a defensive lineman, but, again, you can’t trade for what nobody wants to give you. 5 things Packers must do to win Super Bowl after quiet trade deadline | Packers Wire No trades, but there’s still work to be done. title: Malik Willis going on IR can cost the Packers a round in the 2027 draft
summary: The NFL’s compensatory pick formula is a little complicated, but to boil it down: Players are awarded points for their average salary over the life of the contract that they signed in free agency and receive playing-time bonuses based on the percentage of snaps they play during the regular season. If you lose players worth […]
full_text: (Photo by Carmen Mandato/Getty Images) | Getty Images The NFL’s compensatory pick formula is a little complicated, but to boil it down: Players are awarded points for their average salary over the life of the contract that they signed in free agency and receive playing-time bonuses based on the percentage of snaps they play during the regular season. If you lose players worth more points than the ones you sign, you get a draft pick from the NFL (which essentially mints an extra round of the draft, awarding 32 picks from the third to seventh rounds). That’s why the news of Malik Willis, a former Green Bay Packers quarterback, going on injured reserve impacts Green Bay in 2027. Already, Over The Cap has adjusted Willis’ compensatory draft pick projection to be a fourth-round pick, rather than the third-round pick he was initially expected to earn for the Packers. Willis was already a borderline third-round case (there are only two players currently set to earn third-round compensatory picks: edge defenders Jaelen Phillips and Trey Hendrickson), but losing at least four games of action is essentially a nail in the coffin for that selection. So instead of having what was projected to be the 98th pick in the draft for the loss of Willis, the Packers are now projected to receive the 133rd pick, according to Over The Cap. Former Packers leaving Green Bay haven’t had much luck this year. Offensive tackle Rasheed Walker, who was expected to net the Packers at least a fifth-round pick in free agency, overplayed his hand and signed late — leaving him with just a one-year deal. At the moment, the Packers are not expected to be awarded a pick for the loss of Walker. On top of that, receiver Romeo Doubs, who had a chance to earn Green Bay a fourth-round pick, is also on the injured reserve, which likely means that the Packers will only get a fifth-round pick for losing him. Overall, here’s the breakdown of the current outlook for the Packers’ compensatory picks in 2027: 4th round (Malik Willis) 5th round (Quay Walker) 5th round (Romeo Doubs) 6th round (Kingsley Enagbare) Teams are capped at four compensatory draft picks, or Walker (seventh round) would have been in play — had the team not canceled out that selection with the addition of cornerback Benjamin St-Juste in free agency. As a reminder, the Packers own their original draft picks outside of the first (Micah Parsons trade) and sixth (Darian Kinnard trade) rounds. They will also get the Cowboys’ fourth-round pick (Rashan Gary trade) and the Eagles’ sixth-round pick (Dontayvion Wicks trade) in 2027, bringing their overall total to 11 picks.

title: Here we go again: Can Houston’s 3–5 start spark another playoff run?
summary: At this exact point in time last season, the Houston Texans were 3-5 coming off a gutsy loss to the 6-2 Denver Broncos. Both seasons have been filled with optimism and frustration, criticism and accolades, clumsy losses and big wins. Texans fans are well aware of what happened last year; they went on a nine […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 08: Tank Dell #1 of the Houston Texans is unable to catch a pass against Genesis Smith #22 of the Los Angeles Chargers during the second half at SoFi Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Ryan Sirius Sun/Getty Images) | Getty Images At this exact point in time last season, the Houston Texans were 3-5 coming off a gutsy loss to the 6-2 Denver Broncos. Both seasons have been filled with optimism and frustration, criticism and accolades, clumsy losses and big wins. Texans fans are well aware of what happened last year; they went on a nine game winning streak to close out the season and secure the fifth seed in the AFC Playoffs. The question is, can they do it again? This article will compare the Texans current situation in the AFC South, AFC, and remaining schedule through Week Nine of the NFL season against last year’s team. 2025 AFC South Standings through Week Nine Indianapolis Colts: 7-2 Jacksonville Jaguars: 5-3 Houston Texans: 3-5 Tennessee Titans: 1-8 2026 AFC South Standings through Week Nine Jacksonville Jaguars: 6-2 Houston Texans: 3-5 Indianapolis Colts: 2-7 Tennessee Titans: 1-8 In theory, Houston is in a much better place in the AFC South than last year. While the Colts were predicted to come back to earth, no one would predict they wouldn’t miss the playoffs entirely. Given both the Jags and Colts were playing such good football, winning the division was out of the question. The Jags play the Titans two out of the next three games and also have Dallas (4-5), Washington (2-5-1), and Indianapolis (2-7) on their schedule. That’s five easy victories to get them to 11 wins. Catching Jacksonville may once again not be feasible. They’re currently the most efficient offense and most dominant defense in the league statistically. With Houston three games back from the Jags, it makes more sense to evaluate their place in the AFC. 2025 AFC Playoff Picture after Week 9 Indianapolis Colts (7–2, 6–1 AFC) New England Patriots (7–2, 4–2 AFC) Denver Broncos (7–2, 4–2 AFC) Pittsburgh Steelers (5–3, 4–1 AFC) Buffalo Bills (6–2, 4–1 AFC) Los Angeles Chargers (6–3, 5–1 AFC) Jacksonville Jaguars (5–3, 3–1 AFC) Kansas City Chiefs (5–4, 2–3 AFC) Houston Texans (3–5, 2–2 AFC) Baltimore Ravens (3–5, 2–3 AFC) Cincinnati Bengals (3–6, 3–2 AFC) Las Vegas Raiders (2–6, 2–4 AFC) Cleveland Browns (2–6, 1–4 AFC) Miami Dolphins (2–7, 1–6 AFC) New York Jets (1–7, 1–4 AFC) Tennessee Titans (1–8, 0–7 AFC) 2026 AFC Playoff Picture after Week 9 Buffalo Bills (7-1, 4-1 AFC) Denver Broncos (7-2, 3-1 AFC Jacksonville Jaguars (6-2, 5-2 AFC) Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2, 3-2 AFC) Kansas City Chiefs (6-2, 6-1 AFC) Cincinnati Bengals (6-2, 4-2 AFC) New England Patriots (5-4, 5-1 AFC) Cleveland Browns (5-4, 3-3 AFC) Las Vegas Raiders (4-5, 3-3 AFC) Baltimore Ravens (4-5, 2-4 AFC) Houston Texans (3-5, 3-3 AFC) New York Jets (2-7, 2-4 AFC) Indianapolis Colts (2-7, 1-5 AFC) Miami Dolphins (1-7, 1-4 AFC) Tennessee Titans (1-7, 1-5 AFC) Los Angeles Chargers (0-8, 0-5 AFC) Visually, the Texans occupy a more precarious position within the conference than they did at this juncture last year.Statistically, however, they remain right on track. The AFC boasts a combined 65 wins through this point in 2026—identical to its total at this exact stage in 2025. Among the current top seven playoff seeds, the numbers mirror each other precisely as well: 43 combined wins for the conference’s current postseason field. Houston faces four remaining games against opponents with superior records. At this time last year, that figure stood at five. That represents one fewer hurdle where the Texans can directly alter the postseason race by knocking off an established contender. While the exact trajectory of the remainder of the season remains unwritten, expecting a repeat rescue via total collapses from the Indianapolis Colts and Kansas City Chiefs is a statistical long shot. Still, the path forward relies entirely on self-execution rather than outside charity. Given the current playoff race mirrors last year’s the magic number to make the playoffs is 11. That means Houston has to go 8-1 to earn a Wild Card spot. With games against the Packers, Jags, and gritty Browns, there’s little room for error. The Texans schedule has eased up a bit with the Ravens, Commanders, and Eagles all struggling thus far. 2025 Houston Texans Remaining Schedule after Week 9 vs Jacksonville Jaguars (5-3) @ Tennessee Titans (1-8) vs Buffalo Bills (6-2) @ Indianapolis Colts (7-2) @ Kansas City Chiefs (5-4) vs Arizona Cardinals vs Las Vegas Raiders (2-6) @ Los Angeles Chargers (6-3) vs Indianapolis Colts (7-2) 2026 Houston Texans Remaining Schedule after Week 9 @ Cleveland Browns (5-4) vs Indianapolis Colts (2-6) vs Baltimore Ravens (4-5) @ Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2) @ Washington Commanders (2-5-1) vs Jacksonville Jaguars (6-2) @ Philadelphia Eagles (2-7) @ Green Bay Packers (6-3) vs Tennessee Titans (1-8) Houston benefitted from playing almost an exclusive slate of AFC opponents down the stretch. Their wining streak helped bring them into the Wild Card race by defeating their rivals for those final few spots. The Texans playoff hopes aren’t in their hands. Just like last year, they need several teams to collapse to make way for their run. A Lamar Jackson-less Ravens team, a Steelers team who hasn’t faced much competition, and a young but unproven Browns team all are prospective teams to fall a part down the stretch. Even then, Houston would still be only eighth in the AFC. To make it to the playoffs for the fourth straight season, they’ll need to get hot at the right time. They’re warming up as we speak.

title: As competitor, QB Daniel Jones wasn’t happy to see Colts as recent major trade sellers
summary: Indianapolis Colts starting quarterback Daniel Jones publicly voiced his disappointment that his struggling team was a recent major seller ahead of this past Tuesday’s league-wide trade deadline, while acknowledging, at least in his eyes, that it outside the players’ control (via the Athletic’s James Boyd): In fairness, as a competitor, it would be a tough […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - NOVEMBER 08: Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts reacts against the Dallas Cowboys after the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Hickey/Getty Images) | Getty Images Indianapolis Colts starting quarterback Daniel Jones publicly voiced his disappointment that his struggling team was a recent major seller ahead of this past Tuesday’s league-wide trade deadline, while acknowledging, at least in his eyes, that it outside the players’ control ( via the Athletic’s James Boyd ): Daniel Jones, asked about the #Colts making trades for the future while he’s trying to win in the present: “You’re not happy to see a lot of those decisions, but like I said, that’s outside of our control. And our job is to play. Be prepared and play well. …” pic.twitter.com/0BH46dDY8x — James Boyd (@RomeovilleKid) November 11, 2026 In fairness, as a competitor, it would be a tough pill to swallow as a starting quarterback, knowing that your already below average wide receiver room to whom you regularly throw the football to is now without two of its best wideouts: Keenan Allen and Josh Downs—who were traded to San Francisco and Kansas City respectively. It looks like still rehabbing Colts top wideout Alec Pierce is not coming back to the football field anytime soon, and you also lost your perennial All-Pro left guard Quenton Nelson, who consistently helped keep you upright in pass protection, as he was traded to Seattle to help jumpstart the ongoing rebuild for Indianapolis. That being said, it’s not as though Jones and his teammates, including those who recently were traded, didn’t share in culpability to what led to the team’s recent fire sale. The team currently sits at 2-7, and among their defeats, lost to a winless Tennessee Titans team at home. Their brutal loss led to their longtime general manager Chris Ballard being fired thereafter, and that was the first domino to fall regarding the recent sell-off. Two weeks later, the Colts would go on to be blown out in Jacksonville, 42-7, and it was clear their season was definitively over—if it wasn’t already, after that dreadful rock bottom showing. The Colts have now lost 5 straight games in 2026. Dating back to 2025, they’ve lost 14 of their last 14 regular season games. In particular, after landing a 2-year, potential $100 million contract extension, Jones, who’s coming off a torn Achilles, has struggled this season and provided the Colts well below average starting quarterback play in 2026. He’s completed 182 of 302 pass attempts (60.3%) for 1,722 total passing yards, 6 passing touchdowns, and 10 interceptions during 9 starts so far in the 2026 campaign. It’s not all Jones’ fault offensively though. Even before the recent wide receiver trades, this was one of the league’s worst wide receiver rooms collectively without Pierce back. It now resembles closer to a 2nd-team preseason squad. His pass protection also hasn’t been great, even when Nelson was here, as a number of once reliable o-linemen have since struggled in pass protection. That being said, a starting quarterback is the league’s most valuable position, and almost always, if you don’t have a ‘dude’ there, who can consistently elevate his teammates, carry the offense for stretches, and make pivotal, even difficult winning plays late in games, the whole team will struggle—or at least reach its inevitable end.

title: Colts rightfully noncommittal on whether WR Alec Pierce will still return this 2026 season
summary: Indianapolis Colts head coach Shane Steichen was rightfully non-committal on whether rehabbing lead wideout Alec Pierce will still return this season—and rightfully so (via The Athletic’s James Boyd): The Colts returning lead wideout from last season has been out since Week 2 on the road against the Kansas City Chiefs, when he reinjured his left […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - DECEMBER 28: Alec Pierce #14 of the Indianapolis Colts runs out of the tunnel prior to an NFL football game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Lucas Oil Stadium on December 28, 2025 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Indianapolis Colts head coach Shane Steichen was rightfully non-committal on whether rehabbing lead wideout Alec Pierce will still return this season—and rightfully so ( via The Athletic’s James Boyd ): #Colts HC Shane Steichen, asked if WR Alec Pierce (heel/IR) has a chance to return this season: “We’ll see. Like I said last week, he’s still in that rehab process, and I’m not going to put a timetable on return.” — James Boyd (@RomeovilleKid) November 11, 2026 The Colts returning lead wideout from last season has been out since Week 2 on the road against the Kansas City Chiefs, when he reinjured his left heel and was subsequently placed on injured reserve. Pierce had previously missed all of this past training camp and preseason after undergoing a once thought minor cleanup surgery on that same heel in late March. However, after an expedited return to the football field, he reinjured it just a few weeks later on Sunday Night Football primetime. He hasn’t played for the Colts since. On the 2026 season, Pierce has 5 receptions for 72 total receiving yards during 2 starts. Of course, with the Colts currently sitting at a disappointing 2-7, and having undergone a recent fire sale of key veterans and even some young players alike, it doesn’t make much sense to rush Pierce back to the football field again anytime soon—even though Indianapolis was initially targeting (and realistically hopeful) for a potential midseason return. It’s not like they certainly couldn’t use Pierce given their remaining patchwork wide receiver room of Laquon Treadwell, Ashton Dulin, Nick Westbrook-Ikhine, Anthony Gould, and rookie Deion Burks, but with this clearly being another lost season in Indianapolis, there’s no reason to risk him suffering another setback. Giving that we’re in Week 10, it seems as though the Colts have pushed back that potential midseason return, and if Pierce even does return much later in the season, it will likely mean that he’s fully, and I mean fully cleared physically. He shouldn’t be rushed or have his return to the football field expedited by any means whatsoever. My calculated safe guess though is that we won’t see him until the start of the 2027 campaign for the Colts.

Commentary will be brief but feel free to let me know in the comments that stats aren’t everything. (click charts for larger view) 64 offensive yards in the first half? It’s a bold strategy, Cotton. HOW WELL? mouseover definitions: arsr , edp , sg% , oz% , pr% , tip , ttt , adot , ay/c , yac , yacoe , yd/c , ac% , cpoe , aypa , drp , scr% , ta% , sck% , aa% , ny/d , ny/p , 1st% , td% , to% , qbsr , epa/p , adj/p Indianapolis got strong production from its running game while utilizing a balanced approach on early downs. (7th ARSR; 17th EDP ) Jones faced relatively little pressure even though he held the ball longer than most quarterbacks, which let plays develop and should have given him plenty of time to find an open man downfield. ( 20th PR%; 10th TIP; 8th TTT ) Or at least that should have been the case. Instead, his completions generated relatively little yardage through the air. Better-than-average production after the catch helped compensate, but his overall yards per completion remained below average. ( 26th AY/C; 10th YAC; 12th YCOE; 21st YD/C ) Jones completion rate fell well short of expectations. Combined with the limited yardage on his completions, that left his yards per attempt near the bottom of the league . . . AGAIN! ( 21st AC%; 29th CPOE; 24th AYPA ) Receivers dropped two passes, which certainly didn’t help, while Jones abandoned six plays: two scrambles, two throwaways and two sacks. Even so, his abandoned-attempt rate was below league average, preventing his already poor yardage efficiency from falling even further. (7th DRP; 13th SCR%; 17th TA%; 19th SCK%; 20th AA%; 23rd NY/D; 23rd NY/P) The Colts struggled to generate first downs through the passing game and managed just one touchdown, with the interception locking in the loss. (27th 1ST%; 18th TD%; 17th TO%) Overall, Jones struggled to consistently generate positive plays. The 55-yard touchdown pass provided one enormous bright spot, but it wasn’t nearly enough to overcome the numerous negative plays. He finished with an ugly -0.17 EPA per play, once again ranking near the bottom of the league in overall efficiency. ( 22nd QBSR; 26th EPA/P ) mouseover definitions: ay< , dp% , ay/c , yac , yd/c , ac% , aypa , drp% , aypa , ta% , ypa , sck% , ny/a , scr% , ny/d , car% , ny/p , 1st% , any/p , td% , any/p , to% , any/p , epa/p , opd , adj/p Jones’ efficiency curve starts near the bottom of the league, reflecting very little production through the air on completed passes. Strong yards after the catch provided a modest boost, but little else he did moved the needle. Jones’ performance was dominated by negative plays, particularly in the first half, when a 10-yard sack cost the Colts 2.1 EPA. His 55-yard touchdown pass to Ashton Dulin (+4.6 EPA) provided a huge boost, and a 40-yard pass interference penalty added another 2.3 EPA. Unfortunately, those big gains were overwhelmed by numerous smaller negative plays and a game ending interception (-2.5 EPA). Overall, Jones generated positive EPA on just 40% of his plays finishing with a miserable -0.17 EPA per play. Jones’ longer-term trends continue to paint a pretty bleak picture. His success rate improved slightly, but his first-down rate fell for the fourth consecutive week to just 23.1%, continuing a catastrophic downward trend. On the production side, net yards per play improved for the second straight week to 5.4, while EPA per play rebounded from last week’s disaster but remained firmly negative. Despite those modest improvements, the rolling averages continue to trend downward, with all four metrics sitting well below league average. HOW FAR? Jones had a few productive stretches of short completions, but struggled to sustain any meaningful passing production. The touchdown pass and the pass interference plays are the clear outliers on the day. Jones failed to complete a single pass beyond 14 air yards, and his final four throws resulted in three incompletions and a pick. After two weeks of unusually short passes, Jones returned to a more typical target depth, increasing his average from to 8.2 yards. However, his completed passes averaged just 4.5 yards downfield, an improvement over last week’s god-awful 3.1 yards, but still in the bottom third of the league. TO WHO? Ashton Dulin led the Colts with 55 receiving yards, all coming after the catch on his lone reception, which went for a touchdown. Tyler Warren added 44 yards, while Keenan Allen led the team with 25 completed air yards but managed just one yard after the catch. Keenan Allen and Josh Downs continue to lead the Colts in receiving production, with Downs holding a slight edge in total yards. . . but not for long. Tyler Warren is a distant third. Ashton Dulin was the lone bright spot off of one — count them —one catch. Everyone else fell below league average, with Keenan Allen (-0.47 EPA per target) and Jonathan Taylor (-0.37) producing particularly poor value despite combining for 13 targets. Even Tyler Warren and Josh Downs, who fared somewhat better, generated essentially zero EPA per target. Other than Pierce, there are no receivers with significant value above average on the season. HOW ACCURATE? Jones completed 21 of 31 adjusted attempts (drops/throw-aways removed), finishing with a 68% adjusted completion rate and -6% CPOE, a noticeable decline from last week’s +2% CPOE. For the season, his completion rate remains below league average at nearly every passing depth, with particularly poor results on throws beyond 20 yards. The one bright spot continues to be screen passes and checkdowns behind the line, where he’s completing 87% . . . hooray! HOW FAST? Jones averaged 2.87 seconds to throw this week, a significant increase from last week’s 2.44 seconds, while taking one fewer sack. For the season, his time to throw remains slightly quicker than expected for the depth of his targets, sitting just below the league trend line. TO WHERE? Jones only real success was on passes behind the line of scrimmage, which really tells the whole story. Red is bad. Any questions?

title: Colts ownership just showed “Find a Way” was not to be taken lightly
summary: The challenge came down from the top. Was it a challenge or an ultimatum? Either way, the marching orders for 2026 were set in training camp by the owner of the Indianapolis Colts, Carlie Irsay-Gordon. The mantra was simple: “Find a Way.” The underpinnings were subtle but understood, win or else. After the trade deadline, […]
full_text: The challenge came down from the top. Was it a challenge or an ultimatum? Either way, the marching orders for 2026 were set in training camp by the owner of the Indianapolis Colts, Carlie Irsay-Gordon. The mantra was simple: “Find a Way.” The underpinnings were subtle but understood, win or else. After the trade deadline, the Colts are finding themselves on the “else” side of things. DeForest Buckner, Quenton Nelson, Keenan Allen, and Josh Downs all wear new uniforms now. Grover Stewart and Jonathan Taylor were on the chopping block too. Let’s not forget about Chris Ballard either. David Bowie sang about “changes,” and the Colts organization has gone through plenty. The worst or possibly best part of it all is that those changes don’t appear to be done. Irsay-Gordon inherited a mess with a team that hasn’t produced in a decade and a GM who was around for all of it. Her message sent a shot across the bow, seemingly, in the softest way possible. Find a Way was all she said. What she meant can be seen from top to bottom in this organization. Shane Steichen and Daniel Jones’ days appear to be numbered too. The production isn’t there, and they haven’t found a way, to say the least. New owners, coaches, or even CEOs of companies like to have their own people, those that fit their vision. The good ones don’t come in and start slashing without cause, though. If someone shows their worth and circumstances are right, chances are they stay. Irsay-Gordon did that. Everyone got another chance. She could have cleaned house when she took over. She would have been more than justified to do that after last year’s collapse too, but she didn’t. Everyone got plenty of grace, but the NFL isn’t built on grace. It is built on winning. It is built on finding a way to win no matter what. Pieces of this once-proud franchise are scattered on the ground. The facade is broken and all is exposed. When put under the microscope and intense pressure to perform, the Colts couldn’t. If they can’t do it, Carlie Irsay-Gordon will find someone who can because that’s what it’s about. Win, just win. Find a way to fight through it, make the play, and come out on top. Right now, the Colts are at the bottom. It’s going to take a lot, but this organization must find a way to rise, once again, to the top.

title: Stampede Blue Reacts Survey (Week 10): Are Colts fans confident after major roster changes?
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, where Colts fans and NFL fans nationwide share their opinions throughout the season. The Indianapolis Colts have officially entered a new chapter following one of the most eventful trade deadlines in franchise history. After parting ways with Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner two weeks ago, Indianapolis continued its roster overhaul […]
full_text: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, where Colts fans and NFL fans nationwide share their opinions throughout the season. The Indianapolis Colts have officially entered a new chapter following one of the most eventful trade deadlines in franchise history. After parting ways with Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner two weeks ago, Indianapolis continued its roster overhaul Tuesday by sending veteran wide receiver Keenan Allen to the San Francisco 49ers and Josh Downs to the Kansas City Chiefs. The departures of four established players have allowed the Colts to accumulate additional draft capital, although they have also created significant holes across a roster that was already struggling to compete. With Chris Ballard no longer in charge and a new general manager expected to take over during the offseason, the organization appears increasingly focused on building toward the future rather than salvaging the remainder of 2026. Interestingly, Jonathan Taylor was one of the few major names who ultimately remained in Indianapolis despite considerable interest from around the league. The Colts reportedly received multiple offers involving second-round selections but maintained a much higher asking price for their star running back, deciding to retain him rather than accept compensation they considered insufficient. Keeping Taylor provides some stability for an offense that has already lost several important contributors, although questions remain about whether his remaining prime seasons will align with the franchise’s next competitive window. The decision also leaves the next general manager with an important choice regarding the long-term direction of the offense. Meanwhile, the situation on the field hasn’t improved much. Indianapolis suffered its fifth consecutive defeat Sunday, falling 27-23 to the Dallas Cowboys and dropping to 2-7 on the season. Last week’s Reacts survey showed that just 19 percent of Colts fans believed the franchise was headed in the right direction, down from 31 percent the previous week and 47 percent two weeks earlier. While the continued losing has understandably frustrated fans, the organization’s willingness to make significant changes could provide some optimism that a more sustainable future is being built. With several additional draft selections now available but plenty of uncertainty surrounding the roster, coaching staff and quarterback position, the question remains whether fans believe the Colts are finally taking the necessary steps toward returning to contention.
