title: NFL Betting Advice: Giants-Commanders picks and props
summary: Welcome to the New York Giants betting angle, Week 10 edition! Each week, I’m giving you my three favorite wagers for that week’s New York Giants game. My one rule: I won’t ever give you wagers that go beyond -120. No gimmes! The 5-2-1 Giants host the 2-5-1 Commanders on Thursday Night Football, and it’s Big Blue’s […]
full_text: Rematch! | Getty Images Welcome to the New York Giants betting angle, Week 10 edition! Each week, I’m giving you my three favorite wagers for that week’s New York Giants game. My one rule: I won’t ever give you wagers that go beyond -120. No gimmes! The 5-2-1 Giants host the 2-5-1 Commanders on Thursday Night Football, and it’s Big Blue’s first rematch of the season. Fans will remember that the first contest between these teams resulted in the NFL’s only tie this season, with each team blowing an easy chance to win at the end of overtime. I’m guessing we’ll get another close game this time around. Jameis Winston was the Giant’s quarterback in that Week 5 contest, but now he’s backing up J.J. McCarthy, who gets his third start for New York on Thursday. The Giants are coming off their first win in Philadelphia in 13 years, and they continue to lead a weakened NFC East. It wasn’t pretty, but a win is a win. Not only did the Giants break their long losing streak at the Linc, but they also broke a strange streak of scoring 27 points in three straight games, starting with that Week 5 tie with Washington. They scored 19 against the Eagles, and their only touchdown drive was led by Winston, after McCarthy was briefly knocked out of the game. McCarthy is good to go on Thursday and Big Blue should also have Cam Skattebo back. The Commanders fell at home to the Rams last week, 20-13. Jayden Daniels continues to play mistake-free football, but Washington struggled to move the ball and score. For the second straight week, the Giants have an opportunity to effectively put away a division rival for the 2026 season. My picks were 1-2 in Week 9 and I’m 13-11 on the season. I did go 3-0 when these teams met the first time, so I’ll try to replicate that this week. Let’s get to this week’s picks. All lines and odds are from Fanduel , as of Wednesday, November 11. The line for the game is Giants -1.5, with a total of 41.5. Giants -1.5 (-120) . Looking at the teams’ records, and the fact that this game is being played at MetLife Stadium, this line feels surprisingly low. Is it a trap line? Maybe. But throw in that the Giants are coached by John Harbaugh while Dan Quinn is on the other side and I’m jumping on the value. Outside of the quarterback position, it’s hard to find a spot where Washington is clearly better. Both teams have dealt with a lot of injuries, but Washington is not only without its top receiver and running back, but now both of its starting defensive tackles (DaRon Payne and Javon Kinlaw) are out. This won’t be an easy game for New York by any stretch, but I think they’re the better team and will come away with the win. The Giants’ moneyline (-135) offers similar value. Jayden Daniels OVER 34.5 rushing yards (-114). This was my favorite prop is Week 5, and it hit big-time, with Daniels rushing for 103 yards and two touchdowns. New York will need to do a much better job of trying to contain him this time around, and I’m sure Dennard Wilson has a plan. Maybe Arvell Reese will spy him some? I still think Daniels should easily get to this total. New York’s secondary is playing great football, and Daniels won’t hesitate to take off when there’s nothing there. Malik Nabers longest reception OVER 23.5 yards (-106). I’d really like to take Nabers over 5.5 receptions, but at -134 its not eligible. I’ll take this prop. The Commanders have a porous secondary, and they rank 30 th in the league in passing yards allowed per game (240). McCarthy struggled to get Nabers the ball last week but that shouldn’t be the case on Thursday. Puka Nacua absolutely demolished Washington last week (14 catches for 150 yards and a touchdown, on 19 targets), even though everyone in the building knew he was the first read on most dropbacks. Nabers just needs one big play for this to hit, and I don’t think that’s a problem. He’s had a catch of at least 22 yards in five straight contests. Those are the picks for Week 10. Good luck with your wagers! And if you play fantasy football, be sure to check out my Week 10 fantasy preview, with start/sit advice and more, coming soon.

The Giants have a number of players dealing with some type of ailment heading into Week 10, but that is typical of NFL teams at this time of year. That list includes: Edge Abdul Carter, knee/back; CB Colton Hood, finger; WR Charlie Jones, thumb; WR Darnell Mooney, chest; OT Jermaine Euemunor, calf; TE Theo Johnson, neck; WR Malik Nabers, knee; OT Andrew Thomas, groin. All of them will play, with none of them carrying an injury designation. For the Commanders, starting center Lucas Patrick (concussion) and tight end Colson Yankoff (knee) will not play.

title: Giants-Commanders matchup: Giants’ offense needs to be better than it was vs. Philly
summary: The New York Giants have a quick turnaround and little time to get ready to face the Washington Commanders on Thursday Night Football. The Giants are currently 5-2-1 and leading the NFC East, while the Commanders come into the game with a 2-5-1 and in third place in the division. We should expect another tough […]
full_text: New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers runs with the ball against the Washington Commanders. | Getty Images The New York Giants have a quick turnaround and little time to get ready to face the Washington Commanders on Thursday Night Football. The Giants are currently 5-2-1 and leading the NFC East, while the Commanders come into the game with a 2-5-1 and in third place in the division. We should expect another tough game, and not just because the Giants can’t seem to do anything easy. The last time these two teams met, Jameis Winston was the Giants’ quarterback and the game ended in a tie. The Giants’ offense was in control of that game until an untimely fumble by Cam Skattebo. This time, the Giants have J.J. McCarthy as their starting quarterback, adding a much-needed element of athleticism and big-play ability to the Giants’ offense. The Giants are coming off of a tough (and sloppy) win over the Philadelphia Eagles, while the Commanders had a tough loss to the Los Angeles Rams. Both teams will be out to prove that the tie was a fluke, but can the Giants get their offense back on track after a rough showing against the Eagles’ defense? Stats that matter J.J. McCarthy’s health Giants’ head coach John Harbaugh announced on Monday that McCarthy suffered a hip pointer in the Giants’ win over the Eagles on Sunday. He also said that he expects McCarthy to play through the injury, though it’s a painful one. From the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center: A hip pointer is a bruised hip. More specifically, it’s a bruise near the top curve of your hip bone. You get a hip pointer from falling onto your hip or having a direct hit to your hip. Though a hip pointer can be painful, with rest you can make a complete recovery. A hip pointer usually does not need interventions like surgery. However, an athlete who gets a hip pointer needs to take a break while it heals. And, depending on how severe the hip pointer is, physical therapy might be beneficial. Hip pointers are deep bruises, and the big question with regards to McCarthy isn’t so much a risk of another injury or making it worse so much as how much the bruise will impact his play. It’s possible that swelling from the injury could impact his gait or mobility, which could in turn impact his mechanics, accuracy, and ability to deliver the ball. Likewise, we don’t know whether McCarthy will be as effective a runner (or scrambler) with the injury. We should expect that the training staff is doing everything reasonable to manage the swelling and pain, but it’s a factor the Giants will need to consider. We could see the Giants try to lean further into their running game with Cam Skattebo back (also confirmed by John Harbaugh), as well as the quick passing game to try and limit the stress on McCarthy’s body. About the offensive line The health of the Giants’ starting quarterback is the most important piece of the puzzle, there’s no argument about that. However, we simply can’t ignore how poorly the Giants’ offensive line played against the Eagles. The offensive line, and the interior offensive line in particular, was simply bad for long stretches where the Giants’ blocking was neigh-nonexistent. The Giants surrendered 6 sacks on the afternoon and both McCarthy and Winston often had to throw under pressure. The run blocking was, if anything, even worse. While left guard Jon Runyan Jr. was the biggest offender, there wasn’t any one player who was the sole reason for the unit’s poor performance. In fact, it’s more useful to view an offensive line as a unit than as five players to be assessed individually. Likewise, there were a myriad of issues that cropped up on tape, but they were shared by all five linemen and not just one player’s problems. At times linemen would let their hands drop low, giving up inside leverage, allowing Eagles’ defenders to control them. Other times, their punches would be late or wide with their hands landing outside defenders’ framework and denying the blocker the opportunity to win inside leverage. There were other occasions where the Giants’ blockers would drop their heads and lunge into contact, or conversely play too upright. In either case, they were either beaten quickly or put on skates and driven into the backfield. We do also need to acknowledge that the Eagles boast one of the best defensive fronts in the NFL. It’s possible that the Giants were pressing in the face of a talented opponent, but rather than raising their game they were allowing their technique to slip. That’s unacceptable coming out of a bye week. That said, there might be a couple silver linings for Week 10. First and foremost, the Commanders’ defensive front isn’t nearly as formidable as the Eagles, and they’ve been struggling with injury. Daron Payne and Jevon Kinlaw are both on the injured reserve, and Johnny Newton will be playing in his second game back from pec surgery. The Giants might be more likely to play within themselves against a front they’ve matched up against before. Second, the short week might work in the Giants’ favor as well. One of the most important parts of succeeding on Thursday Night is to do the basics well. There simply isn’t time to focus on wrinkles or complex strategy and simply executing the foundation of your scheme can be the difference. That focus on execution and technique is what the Giants’ line needs most. It’s possible we could see the Giants’ offensive line rebound in Week 10 simply because there isn’t time to overthink things. And in that, the good news is that while there were far too many bad blocks and breakdowns, there were also some very good blocks against the Eagles. The Giants’ line can play at a high level, they just need to consistently execute their fundamentals. Easier said than done, but still doable. Dealing with speed at the second level The Giants had a tough time against the Commanders’ defensive front in the first match-up between these two teams. However, that front will look a bit different this time around, with defensive tackles Kinlaw and Payne out, and Newton back in. Newton only played 20 snaps against the Los Angeles Rams, but did get three tackles in that limited action and is coming off of a five-sack season. He can’t be ignored, but the bigger threat is likely at the second level for the Commanders. Their Vikings-inspired defense frequently lines up in five-man fronts to gap out opponents’ run games, allowing linebackers Frankie Luvu and Sonny Styles to flow to the ball, drop into coverage, or blitz. It’s effective when it works, however there are a couple potential areas that the Giants can exploit. First and foremost, if (and that’s a loadbearing if ) the Giants’ blockers will need play with more consistently good technique. If they’re able to do so, there are opportunities to use alignment and misdirection to turn Styles’ and Luvu’s speed against them. Cam Skattebo will never be able to outrun either, but their speed can be used to pull them out of position, forcing bad angles and the kinds of tackle attempts that Skattebo routinely pinballs off of. Greg Roman loves using man-gap blocking in his run schemes, but also using pulling blockers to change the math on the play-side. He also uses secondary blockers like FB Patrick Ricard, TE Isaiah Likely, TE Chris Manhertz, and even WR Malachi Fields to add to the box count on the Giants’ side of the equation. That all is well known, which also creates the opportunity to use pullers as misdirection pieces, using a move blocker to pull a linebacker out of position and get them to flow away from the play. The Los Angeles Rams did something a bit different that could be instructive for the Giants. Rather than spreading the Commanders out, they used condensed sets and tight alignments to match up against Washington’s five-man fronts and create additional gaps. That forced Washington to concentrate their defenders tightly, and the Rams were able to use the traffic to slow the linebackers and allow…

title: Giants’ rookie linebacker named NFC Defensive Player Of The Week
summary: New York Giants rookie linebacker Arvell Reese has been named the NFC Defensive Player Of The Week. Reese had an absolutely monstrous game against the Philadelphia Eagles, notching 3.0 sacks, 12 total tackles (10 solo), 3 tackles for a loss, 3 QB hits, and a forced fumble. He’s the rookie since 1994 (when individual tackles […]
full_text: New York Giants linebacker Arvell Reese against the Philadelphia Eagles | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images New York Giants rookie linebacker Arvell Reese has been named the NFC Defensive Player Of The Week. Reese had an absolutely monstrous game against the Philadelphia Eagles, notching 3.0 sacks, 12 total tackles (10 solo), 3 tackles for a loss, 3 QB hits, and a forced fumble. He’s the rookie since 1994 (when individual tackles were first tracked) to have at least 3.0 sacks and 10 tackles in a game, and just the fourth player to put up these kinds of numbers While Reese’s performance may not have impressed Pro Football Focus , the rookie linebacker is quickly becoming one of the NFL’s premier apex predators. And he’s a weapon that defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson isn’t shy about unleashing. Wilson’s scheme has quickly evolved to center around Reese and Abdul Carter, devising innovative ways to use them to attack the opposing offense. “He’s so coachable,” Giants’ Head Coach John Harbaugh said. “We’re bringing him from a lot of different places, and a lot of times he’s picking, or he’s setting the pick, or he’s spying. He does everything. He never gets into that world like, ‘I want to do this or that.’ Or ‘I want to rush the passer.’ Or ‘I want to cover man to man.’ He doesn’t worry about it. He just says, ‘You tell me what to do. What does the defense call for? What’s my job?’ He’s going to be doing it 100 miles an hour every time, and it’s just very, very cool and refreshing to see that, especially in such a young guy.” While there were questions about the strength of the Giants roster coming into the season, they’ve been racking up awards. Safety Jevon Holland was voted the NFC Defensive Player Of The Month for September, and WR Malik Nabers was the NFC Offensive Player Of The Month for October. CB Deonte Banks was the NFC Defensive Player Of The Week for Week 4 following his game-winning interception against the Cardinals. Reese himself was previously voted the Pepsi Defensive Rookie Of The Week after he took over the game in the Giants’ win over the Arizona Cardinals. Reese has also been nominated for that same award again this week.

title: Are the Washington Commanders still suffering a Week 5 hangover?
summary: The New York Giants face the Washington Commanders on Thursday, the second and final meeting of the season between the two NFC East teams. We turn to Andrew York of Hogs Haven to answer our ‘5 questions’. Ed: How have the Commanders moved on from the dysfunctional way that the Week 5 game against the […]
full_text: Dan Quinn | Getty Images The New York Giants face the Washington Commanders on Thursday, the second and final meeting of the season between the two NFC East teams. We turn to Andrew York of Hogs Haven to answer our ‘5 questions’. Ed: How have the Commanders moved on from the dysfunctional way that the Week 5 game against the Giants ended? Is there still a hangover from that? Andrew: It’s funny, because the Giants fumbled away a chance at the win in overtime when they could have made a field goal to win, yet all the media scrutiny seemed to be on the Commanders… However, I’d agree that the decision making around the very last play drew lots of justified criticism on both the Commanders coaching and Jayden Daniels for not having better situational awareness. It was followed up with a similar end-of-game play against the 49ers the very next week that drew criticism of both the coaches and Jayden Daniels. I think that double whammy got people looking at everything a bit more closely, but it’s really just been a litany of questionable decisions (mostly with the coaching and offensive playcalling) over multiple games that has Commanders fans unhappy with their play on the field. Most of the scrutiny has been on OC David Blough, who skipped a few grade levels going from Assistant QB Coach to OC when maybe he needed more time to learn his craft. I honestly put that more on Dan Quinn for promoting him too quickly though, I wouldn’t expect anyone to do well with that big of a promotion. Ed: Jameis Winston was the Giants’ quarterback in Week 5. Now, it will be J.J. McCarthy. Does that change anything for the Commanders? Andrew: From a gameplanning standpoint, sure, mainly in that McCarthy is a mobile QB and the defense will have to account for his scrambles. McCarthy also seems to have done a better job throwing deep this year. However, those are just things they’ll have to account for in the gameplan. I don’t think it provides more of a challenge over QBs like Brock Purdy that they’ve already faced. His mobility might be the biggest challenge, as the Commanders allowed Jalen Hurts to scramble for 46 yards earlier this year, getting several critical first downs. Ed: Can Dan Quinn possibly keep his job if this turns into a four- or five-win season for the Commanders? Andrew: I don’t think so. The biggest problem for the Commanders seems to be coaching, with the most yards erased by penalty in the NFL, slow playcalls and players taking too much time to get into position, and regular mistakes in situational awareness and game management that lose games. The defense has looked better coached the last few games with the addition of Steve Wilks as a defensive consultant , but it speaks very poorly of Dan Quinn (a supposedly defensive head coach) that he had to bring in an external defensive consultant to improve the defense mid-season. Ed: I can’t ask you my “which Giants player would you take for the Commanders” question since we did that a couple of weeks ago. Let me ask this: Which Giants star player do you fear more — Arvell Reese or Malik Nabers? Andrew: I suppose Arvell Reese simply for the fact that he can directly injure Jayden Daniels on a play, whereas that’s not very likely for Nabers. Keeping Jayden healthy and getting him more experience should be one of the top priorities for a team that is on the outside looking in for any sort of relevance in the postseason. Ed: NFL teams change constantly. How have the Commanders changed since Week 5, and have those changes made them better or worse? Andrew: There are two big ways they’ve changed, one negative and one positive. In terms of the negative, they’re more injured. Terry McLaurin suffered a patellar tendon tear and may never be the same player again. DTs Javon Kinlaw and Daron Payne have both gone on IR and are likely done for the year. RB Jacory Croskey-Merritt has gone on IR and won’t be back for a few weeks. That’s $74M in salary cap on injured reserve . On the positive side, the defense looks better coached. This largely coincides with the hiring of Steve Wills as a defensive consultant several weeks ago, as mentioned earlier. For some reason, the Commanders didn’t fire or hire any defensive position coaches in the offseason, despite hiring a new defensive coordinator. That means DC Daronte Jones didn’t get to bring staff with him that knew his scheme and instead had to work with the terrible defensive position coaches that coached a historically bad defense last year . Wilks has seemed to help with teaching the defense (and particularly the secondary) their responsibilities, which has resulted in fewer players looking confused and out of place after giving up big plays. The defense looked better coached the last few games, here’s hoping it continues.
author: Ed Valentine

title: NY Giants RB Cam Skattebo: ‘I know what I’m capable of’
summary: New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo thrives on emotion. You can bet he will be filled with it Thursday night against the Washington Commanders. Skattebo was held out of Sunday’s division game against the Philadelphia Eagles because of his hamstring injury. That was at Lincoln Financial Field, the place where he dislocated his ankle […]
full_text: Cam Skattebo | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo thrives on emotion. You can bet he will be filled with it Thursday night against the Washington Commanders. Skattebo was held out of Sunday’s division game against the Philadelphia Eagles because of his hamstring injury. That was at Lincoln Financial Field, the place where he dislocated his ankle a season ago. Thursday’s game will be in the national spotlight, and we know Skattebo loves that. Oh, and this will be the Giants’ first game since their heavily-publicized pursuit of Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor failed at the NFL trade deadline. So, yeah, Skattebo will have plenty of emotional fuel to pour on the fire on Thursday. Skattebo seemed unbothered by the Taylor pursuit when media spoke to him on Tuesday shortly before the trade deadline expired. “I know who I am and I know what I’m capable of when I get on the football field,” Skattebo told Steve Serby of the New York Post . “Whether they were thinking about it or not, it doesn’t bother me. I know I’m here, I’m healthy, and I’m ready to play football, that’s it.” Skattebo leads the Giants with 418 rushing yards on 98 carries, 4.3 yards per attempt. Skattebo’s last game, Week 7 against the Houston Texans was the first 100-yard game of his career. It also included his longest run, a 42-yarder. The second-year running back understood the pursuit of Taylor. Prior to his Week 7 breakout, Skattebo had five straight games of 60 or fewer rushing yards. As a team, the Giants are 24th in the NFL at 3.9 yards per carry. By Expected Points Added (EPA) per rush, the Giants are 22nd in the league at -0.10. They are a rush-first team that, despite being in first place in the NFC East, has not consistently run the ball the way they need to. “I would be skeptical too if my running back was going for 60 yards a game and not really exploding out,” Skattebo said. “But I’m still getting comfortable, man. This is like my 13th game [11 starts] in the league. I’m not even through a full football season yet. You obviously can see I’m getting more comfortable as I play the game. Houston [124 yards on 17 carries] kinda proved that. “When I come out and I’m ready to play football on any given night, I can be one of the most dangerous backs in the league. Simple as that.”

title: Giants-Commanders matchup: New York defense needs to stay on the attack
summary: The 5-2-1 New York Giants host the 2-5-1 Washington Commanders on Thursday Night Football. The teams tied 27-27 in Week 5. New York is favored by just 1.5 points, and the Over/Under is set at 42.5 points. Both the Giants and Commanders allowed victory to slip through thier fingers in Washington. Cam Skattebo’s fumble led […]
full_text: The 5-2-1 New York Giants host the 2-5-1 Washington Commanders on Thursday Night Football. The teams tied 27-27 in Week 5. New York is favored by just 1.5 points, and the Over/Under is set at 42.5 points. Both the Giants and Commanders allowed victory to slip through thier fingers in Washington. Cam Skattebo’s fumble led to a subsequent six-snap game the following week, and Washington’s botched final ten seconds of overtime will be notorious in Commanders’ lore for years to come. Still, the Giants are now starting a different quarterback in J.J. McCarthy, and sitting comfortably at the top of the NFC East. This is an important home game on a short week for John Harbaugh and the Giants, who are looking to go on their first three-game winning streak of the season. Washington’s offense Washington ranks 20th in total offense, 22nd in passing offense, and 11th in rushing offense, largely due to Jaydeon Daniels’ 252 yards on the ground, which leads the team. The Commanders average 21.5 points per game, which is 21st in the league. Despite the underwhelming numbers, the Commanders aren’t a pushover team; they defeated Seattle in Week 3 and made their Week 6 loss in San Francisco kind of interesting in the second half. Still, the Commanders lack an identity on offense. Washington lost star receiver Terry McLaurin three weeks ago, and the Washington rushing attack has struggled all year. Jacory Crosky-Merrit had an early 33-yard touchdown run against the Giants in Week 5, but he’s still on I.R., and the rushing attack hasn’t exactly taken off with Richaad White and Austin Ekeler. Rookie wide receiver Antonio Williams has 26 catches for 284 yards on the season, but he hasn’t exactly stepped up yet post-McLaurin injury; he has talent, and a big game could be coming for him soon. Williams has led the Commanders in snap share since the McLaurin injury. Stefon Diggs plays 60-65% of the snaps, and he leads the Commanders in receiving yards. He has 30 catches on 49 targets for 303 yards with a team-high five touchdown receptions. Treylon Burks has been playing through injury, and Luke McCaffrey is a good special teams player who doesn’t receive snaps on offense every week. Van Jefferson played 58% of the snaps against the Rams in Week 9, catching five of seven targets for 58 yards with a touchdown. Jefferson seemed comfortable, and Washington looked for him in key situations; it’s something to pay attention to on Thursday night. Tight end Chig Okonkwo was used early and often against New York, and I expect more usage in Week 10. Ben Sinnott and John Bates are the two-and-three tight ends. Washington’s offensive line consists of ( from left to right ) Brandon Coleman, Chris Paul, Lucas Patrick, Sam Cosmi, and Josh Conerly Jr. Giants’ game plan ATTACK! Dennard Wilson dialed up pressure against Jayden Daniels and forced four three-and-outs in the game. Wilson blitzed on 62% of the Giants’ dropbacks; 40.5% quick pressure rate, which is a 99th percentile performance. They blitzed on 23 dropbacks and got a quick pressure on 12 of those. Dru Phillips had 5 quick pressures on 7 pass-rush snaps as a blitzer. New York used Cover-0 in critical moments toward the end of the game. Washington offensive coordinator David Blough is going to have better contingencies than he did in Week 5. New York out-coached a young coordinator, and the Giants should continue to show pressure, but be willing to change it if Blough’s adjustments start to yield success. The Giants surrendered a 33-yard touchdown to start the game against Washington, but the team has been much better with their run fits over the past two games. Disciplined football up front and better-angle discernment by the safeties in the alley can help mitigate an already struggling rushing offense; Jason Pinnock and Ar’Darius Washington have been solid so far, displaying those traits. Blough’s offense used simplified concepts against Wilson’s heavy man defense. A lot of simple half-field curl/flat to slant/flat reads with stacks/BUNCH in third-and-short to create rubs/picks upon the release. New York must be dialed in spatially in man coverage and very communicative if they’re passing routes off to one another; pick/wheel and post/wheel were used several times in Week 5. When Blough uses condensed formations, New York should — and will — load the line of scrimmage and bring defensive backs on five-man pressure blitzes. Expect Fire-Zone blitzes and a lot of interior isolation for Arvell Reese and Micah McFadden against the interior offensive line. Reese vs. a running back in protection on third-and-longs will be a mismatch to exploit — as it was in Week 5. The Giants must be cognizant of Jayden Daniels’ legs. His ability to extend plays and evade defenders is difficult to handle, but Wilson incorporated these rush-spies that forced offensive linemen to commit to blocking but were tepid enough to watch Joe Milton as he tried to pick up yards with his legs. Arvell Reese’s second sack was one of these rush-spies . New York needs to continue to send six rushers at the snap, with two bailing into underneath coverage half a second after the sack. Wilson has used defensive linemen and linebackers in the rush this season; some of those underneath players and zones can help contain the quarterback. High-side rushes can’t just abandon rush responsibilities with no spy if it is man coverage. Final thoughts The Giants defense is playing like a top-10 unit, and the potential of these high picks is being actualized. Containing Daniels is difficult, but doable, and I expect the Giants to make Washington’s offense uncomfortable. Giants win, 20-13.

title: Scouting Jets defensive lineman Isaiahh Loudermilk
summary: The Jets recently signed former Steelers defensive lineman Isaiahh Loudermilk to their practice squad. Today, we break him down in detail. The 29-year old Loudermilk is listed at 6’7” and 293 pounds and was a fifth round pick out of Wisconsin in 2021. He has started seven games in his NFL career, with 63 tackles, […]
full_text: EAGAN, MINNESOTA - JUNE 10: Isaiahh Loudermilk #69 of the Minnesota Vikings participates in a drill during minicamp at Twin Cities Orthopedics Performance Center on June 10, 2026 in Eagan, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jets recently signed former Steelers defensive lineman Isaiahh Loudermilk to their practice squad. Today, we break him down in detail. The 29-year old Loudermilk is listed at 6’7” and 293 pounds and was a fifth round pick out of Wisconsin in 2021. He has started seven games in his NFL career, with 63 tackles, six passes defensed and one sack. Background Loudermilk was a three-star high school recruit despite only having played 8-man football in a small town. He ended up going to Wisconsin, where he redshirted his first season in 2016, but then became a useful player over the next few years. In 2017, Loudermilk had six tackles in 11 games in a reserve role, adding 1.5 sacks and a pass defensed. He started the first six games of his career in 2018 and ended up with 15 tackles, 2.5 tackles for loss, three passes defensed and a sack in nine games. In 2019, he started all 14 games and had his most productive season with 24 tackles, five tackles for loss, three sacks, five pass breakups and two forced fumbles. However, Loudermilk got all Big-10 recognition for the only time in his final season as he was named as a third-teamer by the media and an honorable mention by the coaches. In just six games during the pandemic-shortened 2020 season, he had 13 tackles and two sacks. After not being invited to the scouting combine, Loudermilk played in the East-West Shrine Bowl and was eventually drafted by the Steelers in the fifth round of the 2021 draft. As a rookie, he started two games and ended up with 23 tackles, a sack and two pass breakups in 15 appearances. In 2022, Loudermilk started three times but had just seven tackles and a tackle for loss in 11 games overall. He played in 16 games in both 2023 and 2024 but did not start a game during that time. He ended up with 33 tackles, three passes defensed and a quarterback hit over the two seasons. 2025 saw Loudermilk start the first two games, although he didn’t generate any statistics. An injury in the second game sidelined him for the rest of the season. He was almost ready to return for the postseason but wasn’t cleared in time. Loudermilk signed for the Vikings in the offseason but failed to make their roster and was eventually added to the Jets’ practice squad last month. Let’s move onto some more in-depth analysis of what Loudermilk brings to the table, based on in-depth research and film study. Measurables/Athleticism The Jets’ official website lists Loudermilk as 240 pounds but that is obviously a mistake. He was 274 at his pro day, which clearly meant he would need to bulk up for an interior role at the NFL level. He managed 21 bench press reps at his pro day. He lacks length and would not be athletic enough to play on the edge at the NFL level, having run a 5.08 in the 40-yard dash, with underwhelming explosiveness numbers for his size at his pro day. His agility numbers weren’t bad though. Usage Both in college and at the NFL level, Loudermilk has been an interior lineman, most often employed as a defensive end in a three-man front. Motor Loudermilk is a player who was praised for his “never-quit motor” dating back to his college days. He will chase quarterbacks who are flushed from the pocket and shows hustle in pursuit. Although he has started a handful of games at the NFL level, the most snaps he has played in a single game is 45, in the final game of his rookie year. Pass rush Loudermilk had 7.5 sacks during his college career but his pressure rate has been extremely low at the NFL level. Nevertheless, he can be effective on stunts and shows some instances of pure power. He did get credited with one sack during his rookie year and also had two in preseason that year. Run defense Loudermilk’s run defense grades on analytical sites such as Pro Football Focus have been primarily poor. There are times when he can be dominated in the trenches. He doesn’t penetrate into the backfield to make a lot of plays, with just one tackle for loss at the NFL level. He had 11.5 tackles for loss in college, but of course that includes his 7.5 sacks. However, he moves laterally well and bottles up runs. He has shown some ability to handle two-gap assignments, taking on blocks, making a read and then filling a lane or shedding the block to get in on the stop. Technique Loudermilk is tall, so pad level is a constant concern for him, especially when he lacks the ideal length to recover from an early leverage disadvantage. He brings heavy hands, but his hand placement can be inconsistent. However, when he gets this right, it gives him a good ability to control his man. He doesn’t have an arsenal of pass rush moves by any means but showcases a quick arm-over move to get past a blocker on this stunt, so there may be untapped potential in that area. The pressure he created on this play arguably prevented a certain touchdown. Special teams Loudermilk’s primary role on special teams has been rushing kicks and punts. He blocked a field goal in college and has also blocked two at the NFL level. He’s also blocked on the placekicking unit in the NFL, and he has even played on the kick coverage unit for the Steelers, recording one tackle in 2024. Tackling Loudermilk has never been a particularly productive tackler and will miss tackles from time to time. He had two forced fumbles during his college career. Coverage Loudermilk has never dropped into coverage at any level although he has chased down receivers on dump-off passes to make a tackle a few times. He does contribute in the passing game with his length and ability to bat down passes at the line. He has done this six times during his NFL career and once had five in one year in college. Instincts/Intelligence Loudermilk doesn’t have natural instincts as a pass rusher and can be caught out by down blocks and misdirection at times. He is good at reading the quarterback and getting his hands up in the passing lane to contest throws though. He graduated with a degree ahead of his final season at Wisconsin. Attitude/Demeanor Loudermilk is a coachable player with a positive attitude and made it to the NFL with a combination of grit and hard work. On-field discipline hasn’t been an issue for him, as the only penalty he has had at the NFL level was when the Steelers were flagged for 12 men on the field. He only had one defensive penalty in his college career too. Injuries Injuries have been a factor throughout Loudermilk’s career, although these have mostly been minor issues. Ankle and knee issues affected him early on in his college career as he missed three games in 2017 and four in 2018. He then missed the bowl game at the end of the 2020 season. At the NFL level he missed one game due to a groin issue in his rookie year, but his most serious injury was the one that sidelined him for most of last season. This was a high ankle sprain that required surgery. Scheme Fit Loudermilk previously played for the Steelers in a 3-4 base that has similarities to the system the Jets have been using. His defensive line coach was current Jets defensive line coach Karl Dunbar, so clearly he’s been identified as a potential fit by this staff. He has had some experience with two-gapping assignments which are something the Jets don’t use that much right now, but if they transition towards doing this more, that experience will come in handy. He has been a teammate of current Jets Minkah Fitzpatrick and Chukwuma Okorafor while with the Steelers and Joe Tippmann at Wisconsin. Conclusions The Jets brought Loudermilk in because they were struggling for depth on the interior, and he gives them an option with decent NFL experience, although the depth issues may resolve themselves soon if Harrison Phillips can play through his ankle issue and David…

title: Eagles-Giants Film Review: The defense gave us something worth discussing
summary: This was better. Not perfect, and there are still moments in the secondary that make me want to pause the film and stare at the ceiling and wonder what is going on, but it was better. The Eagles stopped the run and generated some pass rush. Allowing 19 points and 243 yards should be enough […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - NOVEMBER 08: Zack Baun #53 of the Philadelphia Eagles sacks J.J. McCarthy #18 of the New York Giants during the second quarter at Lincoln Financial Field on November 08, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images This was better. Not perfect, and there are still moments in the secondary that make me want to pause the film and stare at the ceiling and wonder what is going on, but it was better. The Eagles stopped the run and generated some pass rush. Allowing 19 points and 243 yards should be enough to keep you competitive. Apparently, that is asking too much of this offense . The Giants averaged 3.8 yards per play, and Devin Singletary finished with 31 yards on 21 carries. The Eagles recorded six sacks. This group will still fight under Vic Fangio. I think that matters, even in a season that has become this frustrating. The defense couldn’t do much more. The defense cannot save this offense every week. With the NFL trade deadline now behind us, I am increasingly interested in who should be part of the next version of this team. Some players are worth getting excited about, and some positions need serious attention. Let’s get into it. Defense This was Zack Baun’s best game for a few weeks. He was everywhere against the run and good in coverage, too. His recent struggles have made it easy to forget just how good he can be when he sees things clearly and gets to attack. On this rep, he reads the run immediately, gets into the backfield, and finishes. There is no hesitation. It’s a lot easier to play linebacker when your defensive linemen aren’t slanting away from the run and letting a guard get to the second level immediately. Baun finished with seven combined tackles, three tackles for loss, and two sacks. Those numbers match the film, but I also thought the defensive line did a better job of allowing him to play like this. The linebackers have spent too much time dealing with blockers in recent weeks. Here, Baun can trust what he sees and go. This was much more like it. Eagles' Defense All22 thread vs. Giants. 1) This was the best Zack Baun game for a few weeks. He was everywhere against the run and good in coverage, too. He's struggled like everyone at times over the past couple of weeks, but it's easy to forget just how good he is. Here he… pic.twitter.com/zkm5Wmp7Vd — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 Unfortunately, we also got an early reminder that the secondary still has issues. The Giants repeatedly attacked the quarters side of Cover 6 from 3×1. Cover 6 combines quarters coverage on one side with Cover 2 on the other. Against this distribution, the Giants send the outside receiver vertically to take the outside corner deep and run a sail route into the intermediate space underneath. The Eagles do not distribute those routes cleanly. Tariq Woolen carries the vertical, Andrew Mukuba cannot get across to the sail, and there is not enough help underneath. The result is a receiver sitting in a huge amount of space on third down. This is pretty poor for a Fangio’ defense. I am not going to pretend I know the exact check because there are a lot of variables. Depending on how the Eagles coach this, the answer could involve Mukuba getting across sooner or Woolen coming off the vertical with help over the top. But somebody has to account for the intermediate route. The receiver cannot simply disappear from the defense’s rules. We have seen far too much uncertainty like this all season. 2) Back to back 3rd and long, the Giants wrecked the Eagles' coverage rules. The Eagles struggled to distribute routes against 3×1 in Cover 6. On consecutive third downs, the Giants flooded the quarters side, clearing the outside corner vertically and leaving the intermediate… pic.twitter.com/UWpcZCEKJJ — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 Well, one final mention for Jordan Davis. Goodbye, big man. The run defense will miss you. A healthy Davis is still one of the best run defenders you will watch, and this rep shows why. Few players his size can make a play like this. The combination of his size and movement ability is unusual, and it has real value. I was not Davis’ biggest fan early in his career, but he turned it around and has played well for a couple of years now. He deserves credit for that, and he deserves our thanks. It feels strange watching the Eagles trade away a young player they drafted because the team is not competitive. That is a fairly miserable place to be. I think they were right to accept the deal. The value was too good to pass up for a player who doesn’t consistently affect the quarterback as a pass rusher. Yes, he had a sack in this game. That does not change the broader evaluation of his pass-rush contribution. You can appreciate how good he became against the run and understand the decision to move him. Both things are true. Personally, I will miss him as a character on this team. Good luck, JD! 3) Well, I had to give him one final mention. Goodbye, Jordan Davis; this run defense will miss you. The Eagles got a great deal and were right to accept it, but a healthy Jordan Davis is still one of the best run defenders you will watch. It still feels weird to watch us trade… pic.twitter.com/PxOH0IMoXF — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 And here is the same coverage problem on the following third down. This time it is third-and-12, and the Giants attack the quarters side again. The outside receiver clears the corner vertically, the second receiver stops short and occupies the underneath defender, and the inside receiver runs the sail beyond the sticks. It is a simple way to put different levels of the coverage under stress, and the Eagles make it look far too easy. I am much more inclined to put this one on Mukuba. Based on the receiver splits and how the other defenders react, I struggle to see how the Eagles can draw this up without asking him to get across to that route. He is so late that the quarterback does not have a difficult decision. The underneath defender has committed to the short route, and the outside cornerback has to take the deep route. There may be details in the coaching rules that we cannot see, but the repeated outcome is the problem. Two third downs, the same basic idea, and another open receiver. Mukuba is becoming a real concern for me. Safety needs to be a serious priority next offseason because the Eagles cannot keep having these issues in their coverage structure. 4) Here's the following 3rd down. The Giants attack the quarters side of the Eagles’ Cover 6 on 3rd-and-12 once again. The outside clears the outside CB, the 2 stops short and occupies the underneath defender, and the inside receiver runs the sail. Once again, Mukuba can’t get… pic.twitter.com/tr1kyfimwY — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 There was some pass-rush juice this week! One reason was that the Eagles stopped the run on early downs and earned opportunities to attack the quarterback. That matters. It is much easier to get into your rush plan when the offense can’t keep threatening you with an efficient run game. This stunt involving Jonathan Greenard and Baun works well here, and Baun finishes the play against J.J. McCarthy. The Giants end up with a third-down sack rather than another easy completion. This defense did not play soft. It created negative plays and forced the Giants to settle for field goals. An opponent puts a tight end across from Quinyon Mitchell and gets…

title: Eagles-Giants Film Review: Tired of trying to find reasons to be interested in an offense that keeps failing in the same ways
summary: What else is there to say about this offense? I keep sitting down to write these reviews hoping that the film will give me something different to discuss. Instead, the Eagles ended up with 220 yards of offense, 13 first downs, and an average of 3.3 yards per play. They had the ball for nine […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - NOVEMBER 08: Joe Milton #14 of the Philadelphia Eagles reacts during the second quarter against the New York Giants at Lincoln Financial Field on November 08, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images What else is there to say about this offense? I keep sitting down to write these reviews hoping that the film will give me something different to discuss. Instead, the Eagles ended up with 220 yards of offense, 13 first downs, and an average of 3.3 yards per play. They had the ball for nine and a half fewer minutes than the Giants. Another week, another miserable offensive performance. Hooray! Joe Milton gave us a few things to enjoy. His mobility prevented an already awful performance from looking even worse, and there were a couple of throws that showed why his arm talent is intriguing. But changing the quarterback hasn’t changed how I feel watching this offense. It is still boring, disjointed, and far too difficult. At this point, I want this staff to move on so I can start looking forward to a new season. It’s November! I’d like to feel excited about the Eagles’ offense again. Anyway, there are still individual players to evaluate and specific problems to explain. Let’s get into it. Offense Welcome to the Eagles’ offense, Joe Milton! No surprise, but play action under center doesn’t work as the pressure arrives before he has a reasonable opportunity to do anything. We have seen versions of this all season. Putting a different quarterback behind it doesn’t make the protection work. The Eagles use a four-man slide to the left, leaving Markel Bell isolated on the right. That gives the edge defender a two-way go against a rookie tackle who has struggled. Meanwhile, the tight end helps on Jordan Mailata’s side. I understand that protection calls have rules, but surely those rules should help you account for your personnel? If I am going to spend a tight end on a chip, I would rather have him help the rookie right tackle than my franchise left tackle. Bell still has to execute his assignment, but the staff could make that assignment more manageable. Eagles' Offense thread vs. the Giants. 1) Welcome to the Philadelphia Eagles' 2026 offense, Joe Milton! Under-center play action: by the time you turn around, you are under pressure and have no chance! Wonderful. The Eagles run a 4-man slide to the left, leaving Markel Bell in… pic.twitter.com/kkq2VA7ltz — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 Milton’s scrambling was one of the few reasons this game remained watchable. On this play, there isn’t a great option unless you expect him to fire the quick out into a tiny window from the opposite hash. He creates something with his legs, which is a useful skill when the passing concept gives him so little. I struggle to imagine what the offense would have looked like without those quarterback scrambles. The rushing numbers show how much he was covering up. Remove all quarterback runs, including scrambles, and the Eagles’ running backs finished with 16 carries for 28 yards. 1.75 yards per carry. The 92-yard team rushing total makes the run game look considerably more functional than it was because the quarterback could move. 2) I struggle to think what this game would have looked like without Milton having some big QB scrambles. It was bad enough with him making some plays with his legs. There's nothing open here unless you are asking Milton to rip it into a tiny window on the quick out from the… pic.twitter.com/EgW465QZnu — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 I rarely criticize a quarterback simply because a screenshot shows somebody open. Route concepts have progressions, and a receiver looking open doesn’t automatically mean the quarterback should have been looking at him. Even so, it is pretty remarkable that Milton doesn’t spot Makai Lemon completely uncovered in the slot here. There is nobody there! That is an opportunity you would want your quarterback to recognize. The Eagles ultimately benefit from defensive pass interference on the throw to Darius Cooper, so the result is successful. The process still frustrates me. Once again, an answer to pressure is to give an outside receiver a one-on-one opportunity and ask him to win. I can live with that more easily when the receiver is prime A.J. Brown. Especially with a new quarterback, I would like the offense to provide a more accessible answer than repeatedly asking for a difficult individual win on a deep shot. 3) I will pretty much never criticize a QB on here for missing a receiver, because many are often far too quick to criticize QBs without understanding how route concepts work, etc. Even here, I'm not going to fully blame Joe Milton (especially as the result ends up being… pic.twitter.com/PkvcMzRkTZ — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 Hey, an actual creative run call! The touchdown uses Willie Lampkin as a fullback, with Tyler Steen pulling on power. Fred Johnson is also out there. So the Eagles use 7 offensive linemen! Lampkin does a good job leading the way; Steen does a great job pulling. This was a nice example of using the players available to create a different picture for the defense. More of this would have been welcome. What frustrates me is how rarely that creativity travels beyond the goal line. Why can’t Lampkin get some opportunities at fullback elsewhere? They don’t need every run to look like this. But when the usual approach produces almost nothing, trying more of what worked seems reasonable. What exactly have they got to lose? Who doesn’t want to see more Lampkin right now? 4) Hey, some creativity in the run game! The run game was dreadful, but this was at least a nice call. Lampkin does a good job as the fullback, and Tyler Steen does really well as a puller. We don't see the Eagles run power very often, so this was nice to see. title: Eagles aren’t rebuilding. They’re retooling, with the immense draft capital as the backbone.
summary: The NFL trade deadline came and went for the Philadelphia Eagles, with the lone move in the days leading up to the deadline being the departure of Jordan Davis. Surprising? Not really, it’s hard to sell players off in the NFL — even for a team with a 2-7 record. It’s even harder to negotiate […]
full_text: Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images | Getty Images The NFL trade deadline came and went for the Philadelphia Eagles, with the lone move in the days leading up to the deadline being the departure of Jordan Davis. Surprising? Not really, it’s hard to sell players off in the NFL — even for a team with a 2-7 record. It’s even harder to negotiate with a general manager like Howie Roseman, a savant at holding onto his players until he can deal them at the right price. See Davis and Cam Jurgens, the other in-season deal the Eagles made prior to the deadline that some seem to (already) forget about. The Eagles got a 2027 first-round pick, 2027 fifth-round pick, 2028 second-round pick, and 2029 second-round pick for Jurgens and Davis — two players drafted in 2022 that clearly weren’t going to be part of the next era of Eagles football. Philadelphia also gave up a 2027 seventh-round pick in the Jurgens deal, and almost recouped a higher pick if the Arnold Ebiketie deal didn’t fall through. Add in the 2028 first-round pick and 2027 fifth-round pick in the A.J. Brown deal five months ago and the Eagles are set for the future. The Eagles have a massive haul of draft picks coming their way over the next three years in the first three rounds — 13 in total. Two first-round picks in 2027 (own and Jaguars), two first-round picks in 2028 (own and Patriots), first-round pick in 2029 (own) Second-round pick in 2027 (own), two second-round picks in 2028 (own and Ravens), two second-round picks in 2029 (own and Jaguars) Third-round pick in 2027 (projected compensatory), third-round pick in 2028 (own), third-round pick in 2029 (own) That’s a lot of draft capital to work for a team that still has a roster with talented players. Roseman saw the core pieces of the next era of Eagles football, enough where he stocked the cupboard with draft picks for a retool. Roseman has done this in the past with veteran players with big contracts. He dealt away Kiko Alonso and Byron Maxwell in 2016, Carson Wentz in 2021, along with Brown, Jurgens, and Davis in 2026. The Eagles general manager has done this before, and Super Bowl appearances have come shortly after. This isn’t a rebuild for the Eagles. Not even close. Roseman won’t be using all those picks Just because the Eagles have 10 draft picks in the first two rounds over the next three seasons (13 in the first three rounds in that span), doesn’t mean Roseman will use them all. Draft picks are assets to Roseman. He will use that draft capital to be aggressive for either a premium player or to move up in the first round. He certainly has the ammunition to make a bold move. Look at where the Eagles currently stand in the 2027 draft. Their own pick is currently slated to be in the top-5 (per Tankathon) while the Jaguars’ pick is currently 25th. That 25th pick certainly has value to move up in the top-5 and get one of the special players in this draft. The Eagles could walk away from the first round of the 2027 draft with Colin Simmons, Jeremiah Smith, or Jordan Seaton. Add one of those players to the star-studded core the Eagles already have and they’ll be in excellent shape for 2027. Oh, and they’ll still have two first-round picks in 2028 with two second-round picks in 2028 and 2029. Roseman has a history of being aggressive with draft capital. Look at the 2022 draft when the Eagles had three first-round picks. The Eagles had their own first-round pick, the first-round pick from the Carson Wentz trade (Colts) and the first-round pick from the swapping of first-round picks from the 2021 draft with the Dolphins. In total, the Eagles had three picks in the teens (No. 15, No. 16 and No. 19). Roseman swapped picks with the Saints, trading No. 16 and No. 19 to the Saints. The highlight of what the Eagles received in the deal was the Saints’ first-round pick (No. 18), a 2023 first-round pick, and a 2024 second-round pick. The Eagles used that draft capital to get A.J. Brown (No. 18 pick), Jalen Carter (2023 first-round pick), and Cooper DeJean (2024 second-round pick) through other maneuvers from Roseman centered around those picks. Having a lot of premium draft picks can set the Eagles up for teh future, while also winning games in the present. The Eagles still have a core of good players The 2-7 record is what it is, and a lot of the Eagles’ stars have not played up to their potential. With that being said, why can’t the core of star players have bounce-back seasons in 2027? The Eagles still have a core in place of Jalen Hurts, Jalen Carter, Quinyon Mitchell, DeVonta Smith, Jordan Mailata, Saquon Barkley, Cooper DeJean, Jonathan Greenard, and Zack Baun. They also have good players in Nolan Smith, Moro Ojomo, Jalyx Hunt, and Dontayvion Wicks to build around. Add in another premier player in the 2027 draft (or two) and develop young players like Jihaad Campbell and Makai Lemon — things can turn around quickly. Who knows? Maybe Markel Bell, Eli Stowers, and Andrew Mukuba improve too. Hunt isn’t going to have a year like this one in 2027, and neither will Greenard if he’s healthy. The same goes for DeJean. Also important to remember the Eagles offense is currently on their QB5 (Joe Milton), RB7 (Elijah Mitchell), a very limited Barkley, their WR3 (Lemon), WR4 (Darius Cooper), and WR5 (Hollywood Brown) heading into the bye week. That cast won’t be the offense in 2027. Even with likely coaching changes across the board, the Eagles still have a core in place to win in 2027 and 2028. There’s uncertainty at a few positions (mainly Hurts’ health and the offensive line), but the talent is there for a quick turnaround. History is on Roseman’s side Since Roseman retook the Executive Vice President of Football Operations role from Chip Kelly in 2015, the Eagles have made quick turnarounds from seasons that signaled a lengthy rebuild. Rebuilds never happen with the Eagles, just retooling of the roster. The Eagles finished 7-9 in 2015. Roseman took over at the end of that season, hired Doug Pederson in 2016 and went 7-9 with a makeshift roster. Thanks to a strong offseason, the Eagles went 13-3 and won their first Super Bowl title just two seasons after that 7-9 campaign in 2015. The Eagles went 4-11-1 in 2020, and Roseman traded franchise quarterback Carson Wentz and gave the reigns to Jalen Hurts. He also fired Doug Pederson and hired Nick Sirianni in that same offseason. Philadelphia went 9-8 and make the playoffs in 2021, then went 14-3 to win the NFC Championship in 2022 and made Super Bowl LVII. Philadelphia won the Super Bowl two years later. Even before Roseman, the Eagles have had quick turnarounds. Here’s how the Eagles responded from every losing season this century. 1999: 5-11 (11-5 in 2000, made playoffs) 2005: 6-10 (10-6 in 2006, won NFC East) 2012: 4-11-1 (10-6 in 2013, won NFC East) 2015: 7-9 (7-9 in 2016, missed playoffs) 2016: 7-9 (13-3 in 2017, won Super Bowl) 2020: 4-11-1 (9-8 in 2021, made playoffs) The Eagles have the structure in place to make a quick turnaround again. This is why they didn’t sell off more players at the deadline. The front office and power structure are in place to turn the franchise around quickly. Even with a few subpar drafts by Roseman that lacked instant impact players, it’s hard to ignore the impact of the 2021-2024 draft classes and how vital they were to the greatest era of football in Eagles history. Roseman has earned the benefit of the doubt. He’s done this before on multiple occasions. Why can’t he do it again? Especially with more draft capital and a talented core already in place.

title: Eagles News: Howie Roseman among biggest winners from the NFL trade deadline
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! Howie Roseman did not have a very good offseason. That much is hardly the only reason the 2026 Eagles are pretty bad. But it’s certainly part of the equation. That being said, he still very much deserves benefit of the doubt […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 26: General Manager Howie Roseman of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on prior to the game against the Dallas Cowboys at Lincoln Financial Field on October 26, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! Howie Roseman did not have a very good offseason. That much is hardly the only reason the 2026 Eagles are pretty bad. But it’s certainly part of the equation. That being said, he still very much deserves benefit of the doubt moving forward. And moves like the Jordan Davis trade are exactly why. He can press the right buttons to get this team turned around. He will do his job to put the Eagles in championship contention. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … The Winners and Losers of the NFL Trade Deadline – The Ringer Winner: Howie Roseman. Over the years, every time the Eagles have made a move—no matter how insignificant—the “HOWIE SZN!!!” posts on social media most likely appeared in your timeline. Sometimes it’s been warranted. Other times it hasn’t. The Jordan Davis trade falls into the former category. Davis has been a nice player for the Eagles, but he has played only 52 percent of the snaps this season. That’s because he is on the sideline for almost every passing situation. To get a first- and a second-round pick for a run-stopping defensive tackle is a minor miracle in 2026. The Eagles have been horrible this year, but they are now positioned to reload with five(!) first-round picks and five(!!) second-round picks in the next three drafts. Roseman’s greatest strength might be realizing when his roster is a mess and figuring out how to escape it. That was the theme for the Eagles at this trade deadline. —Sheil Kapadia Warning to NFL general managers: Howie Roseman is about to fleece you – NBCSP A broken-down receiver, a washed-up guard and an underachieving defensive tackle walk into a bar. And Howie Roseman walks out with two 1st-round picks and three 2nd-round picks. If I were an NFL general manager, I wouldn’t even answer the phone when Howie calls. Because you’re going to get fleeced. And if there’s one thing to feel good about during this miserable season to nowhere, it’s the way Howie has stockpiled premium draft picks with a series of what sure seem like lopsided trades. It all started in June when Roseman shipped disgruntled and divisive A.J. Brown to the Patriots for a 1st-round pick in 2027 and a 5th-round pick in 2027. The Broad Street Bandit – PHLY Eagles Yesterday afternoon, my phone buzzed. A text from Howie Roseman. “I’ll fix this, promise you.” It came shortly after the news broke that Howie had traded Jordan Davis to Jacksonville for a first-round pick in 2027 and a second in 2029. I looked at the return and started laughing. The Broad Street Bandit had struck again. The greatest pickpocket in the National Football League. Somewhere in Jacksonville, James Gladstone, the Jags’ 35-year-old GM, is frantically checking his pants, wondering where his wallet went. Welcome to the world’s most expensive fantasy football contest, young man. In Reservoir Dogs, there was Mr. Pink and Mr. Blonde. And now the NFL has Mr. Fleece. Howie Roseman. NFL trade deadline winners, losers: Vikings find QB, Jags go all-in, Jonathan Taylor stranded – The Athletic Philadelphia Eagles. General manager Howie Roseman began his wheeling and dealing last month by trading center Cam Jurgens to the Baltimore Ravens for a 2027 fifth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick. This week, Roseman couldn’t pass up the haul he received from the Jaguars for Davis. The Eagles now have 10 picks in the 2027 NFL Draft, highlighted by two first-rounders, a second, a third, a fourth, three fifths, a sixth and a seventh. Their 2028 haul features two firsts and seconds, as well as Philadelphia’s standard picks in rounds three through seven. In 2029, they have eight selections: a first-rounder, two seconds and one selection in each of the remaining rounds. Eagles-Bengals trade canceled – BGN The problem, however, is that Ebiketie was signed by the Eagles as a compensatory free agent, which means the Bengals would ultimately be giving up their comp pick from trading Trey Hendrickson during the offseason. So while on paper they were only trading a sixth-rounder, they really were giving up a third-round pick as well — notably, it’s interesting the Bengals hadn’t considered this factor before agreeing to terms… The NFL’s 6 biggest disappointments so far – SB Nation No. 6: Philadelphia Eagles. The Eagles just suck. No way to sugarcoat it. While it’s true that Jalen Hurts’ injury really threw a wrench in things, the Eagles were mediocre before that happened. This was a team supposed to cruise to an easy NFC East championship, maybe have to contend with the Cowboys — and that was really it. Instead, they stepped on rakes for so long it busted their face, leaving them utterly incapable of playing effectively this season. Rotten from the top down, the only question remaining is whether or not Philadelphia has the guts to make some of the difficult choices needed in the offseason to get this team back on the right track. Almost a Trade – Iggles Blitz I really wanted them to move Riq Woolen so this is really frustrating. Moving Davis and adding the first and second round picks means this was a successful trade deadline for the Birds. It would have been nice to make another deal or two, but that would have been for late rounds picks. Those resources can help. They just aren’t nearly as impactful as first and second round picks. Howie made the most of a tough situation (the 2026 season). The Philadelphia Eagles’ 2026 trade haul is likely to age well over time – ESPN This is not exactly screaming quick fix. And with the futures of both offensive coordinator Sean Mannion and defensive coordinator Vic Fangio up in the air — not to mention the fate of coach Nick Sirianni — there’s a good chance some players on the current roster won’t be scheme fits for what comes next. (To that end, the decision to part with Davis now for such a strong return may look prescient should the Eagles shift to a defensive system that doesn’t value a run-stuffing nose tackle as highly.) With just two wins, the Eagles are in the throes of a season that feels similar to 2012 and 2020 when the bottom fell out and change and repair were needed. The outlook has been poor enough this season that the front office felt comfortable trading away of pair of starters in-season in Jurgens and Davis, the latter of which was a team captain. These are not waters the Eagles have found themselves swimming in much over the past couple of decades. But in the mess lay opportunity, and Roseman has found a way to capitalize on it. Twitter bashes Bengals for fumbling Arnold Ebiketie trade over compensatory draft pick – Cincy Jungle It would probably have been better if Cincinnati hadn’t made any move than attempting one and then having to pull the offer. 2026 NFL Trade Deadline: Grades for every team – PFF Philadelphia Eagles: A-. It’s always tough to get a read on what Howie Roseman will do, and it would have been surprising if the league’s most forward-thinking general manager didn’t sell off at least one marquee player. Retrieving a first- and second-round pick for Davis, who owns the 24th-ranked overall PFF grade at his position, was outstanding. Yet Roseman also probably should have dealt pending free agents like Riq Woolen, Dallas Goedert and Arnold Ebiketie, if not considered trading major names like Zack Baun and Cooper DeJean. Beyond that, why would anyone believe him? Last Friday, Sirianni admitted that he misled reporters regarding the…

summary: Former Pittsburgh Steelers running back and coach Dick Hoak has passed away at the age of 86, the team announced on Wednesday. “We are deeply saddened by the passing of Dick Hoak, a legendary member of the Pittsburgh Steelers family,” Steelers President Art Rooney II said in a statement. “Dick was part of the foundation […]
full_text: (Photo by Getty Images) | NFL via Getty Images Former Pittsburgh Steelers running back and coach Dick Hoak has passed away at the age of 86, the team announced on Wednesday. “We are deeply saddened by the passing of Dick Hoak, a legendary member of the Pittsburgh Steelers family,” Steelers President Art Rooney II said in a statement. “Dick was part of the foundation of the organization and played an instrumental role in shaping the Steelers both as a player and coach during his 45 years with the team…” Hoak was a native of Jeannette, PA, a town in West Moreland County about 30 miles southeast of Pittsburgh. He was drafted by the Steelers in the seventh round of the 1961 NFL Draft out of Penn State, where he would go on to rush for 25 touchdowns over a 10-year career, all spent with the Steelers. Hoak was hired by Chuck Noll to be the Steelers’ running backs coach in 1972, where he would go on to be part of all four Super Bowl teams of the 1970s. He would hold the position of running backs coach all the way through the 2006 season, helping the Steelers win a fifth Super Bowl in the 2005-06 season. Let us know what you think in the comments . Harmon was placed on IR after suffering a foot injury in the team’s Week 4 loss to the Cleveland Browns. While his loss was a big one, the Steelers got tremendous production from their defensive line depth after Harmon went down. Since Week 4, the Steelers have the best defensive rush success rate in the NFL, over four percentage points better than that of the second-place Detroit Lions. Pittsburgh also has the fourth-ranked defense in total EPA since Week 4. Harmon’s return comes ahead of a big stretch for the Steelers, who will face the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 10 before a trip to Philadelphia to face the Eagles and consecutive home games against the Denver Broncos and Houston Texans. title: Cam Heyward says Mike Tomlin is still coaching him up from a distance
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers selected Cameron Heyward with the 31st overall pick in the 2011 NFL Draft. His 16 seasons with the franchise make him the team’s longest-tenured player. However, when Mike Tomlin stepped down from his position as head coach of the franchise in January, even the Steelers’ most experienced veteran would be in uncharted […]
full_text: (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers selected Cameron Heyward with the 31st overall pick in the 2011 NFL Draft. His 16 seasons with the franchise make him the team’s longest-tenured player. However, when Mike Tomlin stepped down from his position as head coach of the franchise in January, even the Steelers’ most experienced veteran would be in uncharted waters with a new head coach in 2026. Fast forward to November of the 2026 season, and the Steelers are in first place in the AFC North with a 6-2 record under Mike McCarthy. However, Tomlin’s fingerprints are very much all over this team in more ways than one. On his “Not Just Football” podcast , the Steelers veteran defensive lineman opened up about Tomlin’s impact on the players this season through a group chat. “He’s been texting me all season long,” Heyward admitted on his Not Just Football podcast. “Week in and week out, about different defensive linemen. Who we about to play. It’s me and T.J. together. There’s a crazy group chat going on right now.” Tomlin acknowledged that the group chat is an example of how much he cares for the success of Heyward and Watt as they continue their careers without him leading the charge. “Our relationships are real,” Tomlin said. “It doesn’t have anything to do with the jobs we hold. I love these dudes, man. I care about these dudes, and I wanna see them be successful. And so, sometimes wanting to see them be successful and saying some things that aren’t necessarily nice, but I’m hoping they get it from somewhere else.” Heyward later revealed that Tomlin texted the group chat after their Week 8 win over the Cleveland Browns to thank them for doing their job and picking up the win. Even though he isn’t coaching anymore, Tomlin still has hate in his heart for the Steelers division rival. Tomlin always had the reputation of being a “players coach” and someone that players around the league would want the opportunity to play for. Getting to hear stories from Heyward about how Tomlin continues to push him and talk to him speaks to how special their relationship was and still is. Let us know what you think in the comments . full_text: (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images We are halfway through our Pittsburgh Steelers midseason awards, with MVP and Offensive Player of the Year both going to Jaylen Warren. Well, this will be an award the star running back can’t win, because today we are handing out our mid-season Defensive Player of the Year. Let’s dive in. Ryan Parish – EDGE T.J. Watt: This was a tough one. Patrick Graham has this unit playing well and it’s stronger as a collective rather than one player outshining the rest. Cases could be made for Cam Heyward, Keeanu Benton, Jalen Ramsey, Patrick Queen or even Payton Wilson. But Watt and his 7.5 sacks are the splashiest, and his return to form this season has been a joy to watch. Ryland Bickley – EDGE T.J. Watt: It’s tempting to get creative here: Jamel Dean essentially won the Steelers the Buccaneers game and has been essential in keeping the secondary alive without Joey Porter Jr. Keeanu Benton and Cam Heyward have led a dominating defensive line. But at the time of writing, Watt is tied for the NFL lead in sacks at midseason and continues to draw plenty of attention to open up opportunities for the rest of the front seven. Joey Bray – EDGE T.J. Watt: Much like Ryan and Ryland, I want to branch out here, but Watt is the easy choice here. The Steelers unit is well on their way to being a top 10 scoring defense for the first time since 2023. Watt is the leader of it all, ties for the league lead in sacks through eight weeks. Austin Bechtold – EDGE T.J. Watt: Watt already has more sacks through eight games as he did in 14 last year. He recorded his first career pick-six against the Falcons and has benefitted from a reduced snap count. Patrick Graham is keeping Watt fresh with his usage and while you’d want Watt out there for as many snaps as possible, it’s working well. Watt looks like himself again. Mike Nicastro – EDGE T.J. Watt: There are several worthy candidates on Pittsburgh’s defense, including Jalen Ramsey, Keeanu Benton and Cameron Heyward. However, my vote goes to the player who continues to set the standard for the Steelers’ defense: T.J. Watt. Watt has been a consistent disruptive force and has made his presence felt under defensive coordinator Patrick Graham. When he’s on the field, opposing offenses have to account for him on virtually every passing down. Jason Aponte – EDGE T.J. Watt: Who else? Alex Highsmith has been excellent this season, but 7.5 sacks for Watt, with some game-breaking plays, push him to the top of the list. With 25 pressures, 14 hurries, three QB hits, and 19 pressures in true pass sets, to go with five sacks, 12 hurries, and two QB hits, Watt remains a force for the defensive line. Jarrett Bailey – EDGE T.J. Watt: Yeah, we’re all going chalk here. Watt has turned back the clock, as he was tied for the league lead in sacks going into the Steelers’ bye week. He’s already topped his 2025 season total in sacks, and he is back to being the disruptive player that made him a Defensive Player of the Year Award winner. It’s been great to see No. 90 look like himself again. Consensus mid-season Defensive Player of the Year: EDGE T.J. Watt Let us know what you think in the comments . title: Seahawks-Raiders Wednesday injury report: Leonard Williams still out, Rashid Shaheed returns
summary: The Seattle Seahawks emerged victorious in an injury bowl against the Arizona Cardinals last week, and it appears they may have to do it again on Sunday against the Las Vegas Raiders. Seattle released the first of the three weekly injury reports, which is headlined by the health of backup quarterback Drew Lock, who is […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks emerged victorious in an injury bowl against the Arizona Cardinals last week, and it appears they may have to do it again on Sunday against the Las Vegas Raiders. Seattle released the first of the three weekly injury reports, which is headlined by the health of backup quarterback Drew Lock, who is battling a lingering elbow injury and a new oblique injury. Lock was limited in practice on Wednesday, with head coach Mike Macdonald indicating that the veteran is “making good progress” and may start against the Raiders. The ominous messaging leaves the entirety of Seattle on Jalen Milroe watch yet again as the second-year player is the only other healthy quarterback on the Seahawks’ 53-man roster and would come in if Lock couldn’t play. Whoever is under center will once again be working with a patchwork offensive line as stars Quenton Nelson and Charles Cross did not practice. Nelson is battling a knee injury that might hold him out for his second straight game while Cross has been out with an ankle injury since Week 7. Backup guard Anthony Bradford continues to be hampered by a knee injury and was limited on Wednesday. The Seahawks offense appears to have a weapon returning as wide receiver and kicker returner Rashid Shaheed was a full participant in practice. Shaheed has had a quiet 2026, but remains a key piece to unlocking the Seahawks’ offense as the organization is hopeful he emerges as a second option beside Jaxon Smith-Njigba. On the defensive side, Leonard Williams remains out with a stinger that he suffered against the Kansas City Chiefs, and edge rusher Derick Hall was limited with a new back injury. Both would be a massive loss for the Seahawks front that will hope to ruin Raiders’ rookie Fernando Mendoza’s debut. It wasn’t all negative for the Seahawks’ defense, though, as signs are trending positive for edge rusher Uchenna Nwosu, who was limited with the ankle injury that’s held him out of the team’s last two games. Meanwhile, the Raiders report was considerably smaller, so it appears they’ll be near full-go against their former AFC West rival. For the Seahawks, they will have two more days of practice before setting game designations, so here’s to hoping that the report shrinks throughout the week.
