title: ESPN says ‘several teams’ inquired about Seahawks’ Jarran Reed at trade deadline
summary: Although Seattle Seahawks general manager John Schneider opted to stay put at the Nov. 10 trade deadline, that’s not to say he didn’t have options — including potentially moving on from one of their veteran defensive leaders. “Several teams” were interested in Seahawks defensive tackle Jarran Reed leading up to the deadline but the team […]
full_text: Although Seattle Seahawks general manager John Schneider opted to stay put at the Nov. 10 trade deadline , that’s not to say he didn’t have options — including potentially moving on from one of their veteran defensive leaders. “Several teams” were interested in Seahawks defensive tackle Jarran Reed leading up to the deadline but the team wasn’t motivated to move him, ESPN insider Jeremy Fowler reported on Wednesday . No potential suitors were named. The veteran tackle was previously named a trade candidate on Oct. 31 , meaning Reed likely had a substantial market in the weeks prior to to the deadline and wasn’t just a name thrown around at the last minute. However, considering the Seahawks sit at 5-4 and their defense is allowing the fewest yards as well as the fifth=fewest points per game, it would’ve made little sense trade away a player of his caliber. He remains under contract through 2028, so it’s currently unclear why they would’ve considered moving on especially given his leadership and more importantly — production, where he remains a crucial part of Seattle’s defensive front. Through nine games this season, the longtime interior lineman has recorded 20 total tackles — including three for a loss, four quarterback hits and a sack while remaining an instrumental piece in stopping the run. Drafted 49th overall by Seattle in the 2016 NFL Draft, Reed has spent nine of his 11 seasons with the Seahawks and most recently signed a three-year deal worth up to $25 million with the team in March of 2025 .

title: Post NFL trade deadline, the rest of the NFC fails to bury Seahawks
summary: As the NFL trade deadline approached, I was nervous for the Seattle Seahawks. Not necessarily nervous because of the Sam Darnold injury, or the Drew Lock injury, or the fact that if feels like half the team is hurt while Seattle tries to find itself at 5-4. I was most nervous about what the NFC […]
full_text: As the NFL trade deadline approached, I was nervous for the Seattle Seahawks. Not necessarily nervous because of the Sam Darnold injury, or the Drew Lock injury, or the fact that if feels like half the team is hurt while Seattle tries to find itself at 5-4. I was most nervous about what the NFC was going to do before Tuesday’s trade deadline. The Seahawks kicked off a wild trade deadline by acquiring future hall-of-famer Quenton Nelson , and then watched the San Francisco 49ers and Chicago Bears answer back with major trades of their own. An ass whooping by the Bears, followed by numerous injuries, and the Seahawks felt their most vulnerable in two years, while conference rivals were rolling. With the closing window and pressure facing NFC West rivals San Francisco and Los Angeles as well as the entire NFC North, I assumed all of these teams would make moves at the deadline. Instead of putting the throat on the Seahawks, I think the conference contenders failed to put the champs away. The Rams got their superstar back in Myles Garrett, but then subsequently lost their main offensive weapon in Puka Nacua to a knee injury that landed him on IR. Losing a guy like Nacua really takes a bite out of an offense that feels unrecognizable from what we saw last year in LA. With the Rams still to face the Seahawks twice, as well as the Packers and at the 49ers. It’s hard to imagine this nightmare season ending with a playoff spot. The 49ers continue to lead the pack in the NFC, while they yet again overcome injuries. While they added DeForest Buckner, and Keenan Allen before the deadline, I don’t think they landed a potential haymaker in the way that Chicago did with Jeffery Simmons. In the North, the Lions went silent at the deadline, and although they’re 6-2, they continue to win ugly and yet again are dealing with major injuries to some of their best players. After a dream start to the season, reality hit Minnesota. Despite a championship caliber defense, the Vikings embarrassed themselves on Monday night in the worst offensive performance I have ever seen. Their answer is to go back to the Kirk Cousins Experience , hoping he can save their season. Despite the 6-0 start, they’ve lost two games in a row and now will be facing the red hot Packers and 49ers in the next two weeks. 6-4 feels very real. Speaking of red hot, the Bears and Packers right now have arguably the highest ceilings in the conference. The Packers put on a spectacle in Foxborough, picking off Drake Maye three times and then hanging nearly 50 points on the New England defense. After such a dominating performance, I thought that Green Bay would go for it and make a move for Jonathan Taylor, especially with Josh Jacobs out with a hand injury. I truly thought that he could’ve been their final piece, as I just don’t see a team making a Super Bowl run with the worst rushing attack in the league. This deadline feels like a big miss for a desperate coach in Matt LaFleur, who needs a playoff run to stay employed. And lastly the Bears. If I had to make a Super Bowl bet right now, I’d pick the Bears to come out of the NFC. The Seahawks did themselves no favor in their embarrassing MNF loss, but the Beats owned the line of scrimmage and controlled that game. After the victory, I thought that Chicago would go for the kill shot, and bring Kahlil Mack home. It was the type of move that you see Super Bowl champions make, essentially double-tapping on creating a monstrous defensive line. The Bears are flawed, but their best is better than possibly the rest of the entire league. Adding Mack could’ve made them near unbeatable, now they’re just really scary. Rightfully so, the Seahawks stayed pat. There wasn’t a move out there that made sense, or would realistically give them a 2-3 win bump. The best way the Seahawks could make a move was to survive the trade deadline, and get their shit figured out in the building. They survived the deadline, in my opinion. The offense has Vegas and a bye week to figure out if they can be playoff caliber or more, as Brian Fleury tries to avoid becoming Ryan Grubb 2.0. As for their current standings, the Seahawks sit tied with the Rams as the last teams out, looking in the playoff picture. The NFC North dominates the standings as all three wildcard spots are filled by the North. While the Seahawks currently have a 50% chance to make the playoffs, the North will likely help Seattle’s odds dramatically here on out. The Packers and Lions have three more divisional games on their schedules, while the Lions and Bears still have four. The North is going to be weakened, and I look at the Vikings and Lions as the most clear regression candidates. Seattle controls the playoff fate of the Rams, as they will play twice in their final three games. The NFC West is likely gone, but if Seattle can find a way to finish off the Rams, and get to 11 wins, I truly believe that one of two NFC North teams will regress or fail to hold up against the wrath of such an unforgiving division. The expectations before the season were not about finding a way to scratch and claw to get into the dance, but here we are. The NFC’s best could’ve made some more moves to bury the Seahawks, but they now have left the door open. If Seattle can right the ship and make the playoffs as potentially the No. 5 or 6 seed, they could be looking at going on the road to somewhere like Tampa Bay or New York, where I’d wager they’d be heavy favorites in those contests. Win, and you’re likely heading to Levi’s Stadium (good place), or whoever survived to win the NFC North. It may not be the path we all envisioned, but I think all Seahawk fans right now would sign up for a divisional playoff game again, with the hopes of reaching a second straight NFC Championship. Door still feels (slightly) open, Mike Macdonald and the boys just need to run through it.

title: Seahawks swap practice squad defensive tackles, sign Cole Brevard

full_text: The Seattle Seahawks’ deadline day move was on the margins. The Seahawks signed defense tackle Cole Brevard to their practice squad, they announced on Tuesday . In a corresponding move, fellow defensive tackle Gary Smith III was released to make room for Brevard’s addition. After going undrafted in the 2026 NFL Draft, Brevard signed with the Kansas City Chiefs as a UDFA and spent training camp and preseason with the team. After he was waived during the cuts from 90 to 53, he was briefly signed to the Chiefs’ practice squad but was released ahead of the start of the regular season. A six-foot-three, 346-pound nose tackle, Brevard began his college career at Penn State but appeared in just one game as a freshman. He spent the next three seasons at Purdue, where he played 37 games and totaled 38 tackles, 5.5 tackles for loss, and 2.5 sacks. He closed out his collegiate career at Texas, posting 18 tackles and one TFL. title: Seahawks Week 10 national power rankings: Seattle continues to drop despite win over Cardinals
summary: Entering Week 9, the Seattle Seahawks dropped out of the top ten on many power rankings after losing to the Chicago Bears. Will their Week 9 victory over the Arizona Cardinals help raise them back up the rankings? Let’s take a look at five national media sites (NFL.com, CBS Sports, Bleacher Report (BR), Pro Football […]
full_text: Entering Week 9, the Seattle Seahawks dropped out of the top ten on many power rankings after losing to the Chicago Bears . Will their Week 9 victory over the Arizona Cardinals help raise them back up the rankings? Let’s take a look at five national media sites (NFL.com, CBS Sports, Bleacher Report (BR), Pro Football Talk (PFT), and ESPN) to see where they rank Seattle. These rankings this week may frustrate some Seahawks fans. Despite the victory over the Cardinals, many national media sites did not move Seattle up. In fact, some even moved the team down their rankings. That being said, let’s start with the one site who did give the Seahawks a positive bump. B/R, who ranked Seattle 13 last week, moved the team up one spot to 12 . In their ranking, B/R expressed some doubts around Seattle’s offense, particularly at the quarterback position that has seen a plethora of injuries in 2026. Because of this, B/R states that “it’s hard to feel confident about the Seahawks’ short-term outlook.” Two national media sites did not move Seattle from their rankings from last week. CBS, who was the lowest on Seattle last week, keeps the team ranked 14th best in the league this week . In this ranking, CBS also brings up the injuries at quarterback, however provides a sliver of hope, stating that “[t]he Raiders might be the perfect tonic to get the offense going.” PFT also kept the Seahawks at the same ranking as last week, that being ninth best in the NFL . PFT also interestingly states that “Drew Lock fits this team better than Sam Darnold does.” The last two national media sites to discuss this week both moved the Seahawks down in their rankings despite the victory. NFL.com is the most punitive, moving the team down two spots, from 7 to 9 . In their reasoning, NFL.com notes that the quarterback situation “might become more concerning in the days ahead” due to the recent injuries to Drew Lock and Sam Darnold. However, NFL.com also brings up a non-quarterback talking point as well, shining light on the new running back duo that Seattle has now in Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price. ESPN also moved the Seahawks down, albeit only one spot, from eighth to ninth best in the league . In their rankings this week, ESPN noted each teams’ most important game of the second half. For Seattle that was the San Francisco 49ers in week 12. The hope is that the team can get healthy by that week with six starters currently out due to injury. Overall the national landscape remains skeptical over the Seahawks. Not only has the offense been struggling throughout the season, but the team is now flushed with injuries. Currently out of the playoff picture if the season ended today, it makes sense to see Seattle ranked right in the 9-14 range. Entering Week 9, the average power rankings between the five polled sites was 10.2. Entering week 10, that average has continued to fall to 10.6. This next week against the Las Vegas Raiders appears to me a must win for the Seahawks as they enter the bye week and hopefully get healthy for the final stretch of the season.

title: 5 final observations for the 49ers following Raiders win and trade deadline
summary: The San Francisco 49ers are coming off an eventful few days following their 38-17 win over the Las Vegas Raiders and the trade deadline, where the team added Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Keenan Allen after trading for DeForest Buckner last week. Now, the 49ers are set for the second half of the season with two […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 08: Jordan Watkins #17 of the San Francisco 49ers catches a touchdown pass over Hezekiah Masses #35 of the Las Vegas Raiders in the third quarter at Levi's Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers are coming off an eventful few days following their 38-17 win over the Las Vegas Raiders and the trade deadline, where the team added Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Keenan Allen after trading for DeForest Buckner last week. Now, the 49ers are set for the second half of the season with two new veterans in the fold, as they await several injury updates for this weekend’s game against the Dallas Cowboys. San Francisco was still banged up offensively against the Raiders, playing without Deebo Samuel and Mike Evans, but they still put up 38 points. Meanwhile, the defense continued to shine, creating five turnovers that sealed the deal for the Raiders. Here are five observations from after the trade deadline following the Raiders win. Trust in a young WR We’ve heard Kyle Shanahan talk about ‘trust’ when referencing Jordan Watkins, and we really saw that come out this past weekend, as the second-year wideout had his best game with four catches for 86 yards and a touchdown. Watkins has paced the 49ers wide receivers in snaps with Mike Evans out, leading the team in the Washington, Atlanta, and Las Vegas games. That wasn’t the case before that, though, as Watkins had been behind Brandin Cooks and Jacob Cowing in addition to San Francisco’s top receivers in the weeks prior. But now, post trade deadline, it feels like he could be in the top group for the 49ers until Mike Evans returns, joining Keenan Allen and Deebo Samuel. With this group of receivers, Watkins and Demarcus Robinson can play the vertical role, which means they’re live for big plays every week. We saw one of those come down last weekend with Watkins’s 37-yard touchdown grab. On the season, he’s now averaging 22.6 yards per catch. That trust is finally starting to pay off. Unique deployment for young LB The 49ers have made it a goal to get Jaden Dugger on the field in a variety of roles this year. Dugger played 12 defensive snaps against Las Vegas, with only three coming in the box. 5 came on the line of scrimmage, while four were in the slot. He’s been a tackling machine, but also got a pick-six this past weekend. There were initial questions on usage for Dugger coming into the NFL as a Day 3 rookie, but he’s been a fit everywhere. Against Atlanta, Dugger played 31 snaps, with a ton coming on the line of scrimmage. With Dre Greenlaw out against Washington, he was much more of a full-time linebacker. Back in Week 5, he played 47 defensive snaps, with 16 being in the slot or on the line. The snap count might dwindle with Upton Stout getting fully healthy and less need in the nickel, but Dugger has been a pleasant surprise so far this year in his usage. No rest for Buck DeForest Buckner was welcomed to the Bay Area and instantly played the most snaps of any defensive tackle against Las Vegas. He was on the field for 34 of the 50 defensive snaps, recording two pressures while Osa Odighizuwa had three. Buckner was one of the most-played linemen in the NFL in Indianapolis, ranking in the top five in snap count. The 49ers will look to rotate him more than Indianapolis did, but it’s clear he’s going to have a big role, and the need was only further exacerbated by Gracen Halton’s injury. Receiver room future The 49ers seemed pretty adamant on adding a wide receiver, and even in his current state, Keenan Allen seems to fit what the team wants with his separation and blocking skills. But with him in the fold, the future of the 49ers wide receiver room this season got more interesting. San Francisco seems to be getting Deebo Samuel back this weekend. They also should get Mike Evans in the coming weeks, while De’Zhaun Stribling is expected back in the regular season. Then, there’s Demarcus Robinson and the emerging Jordan Watkins alongside punt returner Jacob Cowing. The first question comes with the starting group. When Evans, and really Stribling is back, will the 49ers rely on Allen still? And then, who is the odd man out of the group? San Francisco will have Allen, Evans, Samuel, Stribling, Robinson, Watkins, and Cowing as their receivers then. They likely don’t dress seven guys. Cowing has not been good as a receiver, but has maintained the punt return job. Does that go elsewhere and he’s the odd man out? Or will the 49ers make a different move? Run game success A lot of the 49ers focus on offense has been about the passing game, with Brock Purdy enjoying a career year and Mike Evans shining in his first season in the Bay. But the 49ers run game has sneakily been elite this year from an efficiency perspective. The 49ers are seventh in yards per game (135.3) and seventh in yards per attempt (4.6). They’re also third in EPA per rush and first in rushing success rate, so they’ve really turned things around in the run game. San Francisco has adapted to the two-headed monster with Christian McCaffrey and Kaelon Black, whose efficiency has risen in recent weeks. The offensive line has done a good job overall, and the Niners are quite balanced offensively. That’s a big sign for the coming weeks as the passing game still works through injuries, with the 49ers having their hardest stretch of the schedule coming up.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: Is Trent Williams enjoying a career year at age 38?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers are rolling at 7-1, coming off a big 38-17 win over the Las Vegas Raiders last weekend, as they set up for the second half of the year. San Francisco’s offense has been the story, with Brock Purdy being a top MVP candidate, while the 49ers rank third in points per […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 19: Trent Williams #71 of the San Francisco 49ers enters the field during player introductions before the game against the Washington Commanders at Levi's Stadium on October 19, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Lachlan Cunningham/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers are rolling at 7-1, coming off a big 38-17 win over the Las Vegas Raiders last weekend, as they set up for the second half of the year. San Francisco’s offense has been the story, with Brock Purdy being a top MVP candidate, while the 49ers rank third in points per game. Mike Evans has been a godsend for the passing attack, but San Francisco has also been running the ball much more efficiently this year. Christian McCaffrey and Kaelon Black are both averaging 4.5 yards per carry, while the team ranks seventh in the NFL with 135.3 rushing yards per game. The 49ers have also been the seventh-most efficient team, averaging 4.6 yards per carry on the ground. From an EPA perspective, the 49ers are third in EPA per rush and first in rushing success rate. They’ve completely flipped things around from the 2025 season, where the run game was a bit of a struggle, even with a healthy Christian McCaffrey. A big part of the success has been 38-year-old star left tackle Trent Williams. The 49ers are averaging 5.9 yards running behind the left tackle and 4.8 yards to the left end behind Williams. Then, there’s the pass protection, which has been a big strength for the 49ers this year. Remember, the 49ers didn’t allow a sack over the first four weeks of the season. They’ve allowed just eight on the whole year. Williams has allowed just eight pressures and one sack this season, while being fully healthy at 38 years old. The superstar left tackle has enjoyed a number of extremely good seasons in the NFL, with the 2021 campaign being the most notable. Since joining the 49ers in 2020, he’s been a three-time First Team All-Pro, while also earning five Pro Bowl nods and one Second Team All-Pro honor. And yet, this could be his best season yet, despite him being 38 years old. Williams was ESPN’s Protector of the Year a quarter way through the season in Bill Barnwell’s awards. And he feels like the clear frontrunner for the award at the midway point. What has Kyle Shanahan seen from his left tackle this season? “He’s playing damn good,” Shanahan said on Wednesday. “I mean, stat-wise, probably statistically and things like that, I’d say yes, [it’s the best year of his career]. He’s playing at a real high level. It’s hard to compare Pro Bowl years to other Pro Bowl years, but he’s playing at a very high level.” Last week, offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak was asked about Williams’s excellence at 38 years old, and he broke down how rare of a player the star left tackle was. “Yeah, I don’t know how to explain it,” Kubiak said of Williams’s level of play at his age. “It’s why he’s the best. Trent’s got his way of preparing. A way of getting his body ready and his mind ready to play football games every week that’s unlike anyone I’ve been around. The way that he goes out there on Wednesdays and he practices, and he goes through his routine. He gets himself ready to play, and he knows what it takes to get himself ready. “He’s continuing to play at a very, very high level. To me, he’s still the best offensive lineman in the league, and to me, that’s a credit to his process and the way he approaches the game mentally and his love of the game. He’s a great teammate. Just all around, everything he does to get ready to play football games and to be the best for his team, is exceptional. To me, it’s what makes him so rare.” Williams is likely reaching retirement at some point over the next few years. But you’d never be able to guess that from his level of play this season.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: Explaining the 49ers’ trade for Keenan Allen
summary: The San Francisco 49ers traded a sixth-round pick for veteran receiver Keenan Allen before the NFL trade deadline concluded on Tuesday. Breathe, 49ers fans. While everyone would love a young, explosive wide receiver, the truth is there wasn’t any to be acquired. The 49ers offense is better off with this move, and I’m here to […]
full_text: (Photo by David Rosenblum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers traded a sixth-round pick for veteran receiver Keenan Allen before the NFL trade deadline concluded on Tuesday. Breathe, 49ers fans. While everyone would love a young, explosive wide receiver, the truth is there wasn’t any to be acquired. The 49ers offense is better off with this move, and I’m here to make the case. Let’s address Allen’s age. I find this to be a fascinating discussion. Mike Evans is 33. Allen is 34 and separated by a few months. So, is Allen too old and Evans isn’t? The fact is, they are both “old” in football years, but that doesn’t take away from their ability. Neither has been a speed option. Not when they were 21, and not now. There was a large subset of fans who clamored for a Jauan Jennings reunion, and the 49ers did everything in their power to reunite with him. While I was against the move, Allen will play the same role with a twist. At age 34, and every single day he has woken up, Allen is better than Jennings and could be the perfect fit with Brock Purdy on third down and for tough catches. Allen’s time in Indianapolis only strengthens his case as a good player. With 40 catches and Daniel Jones as his quarterback, the veteran receiver is the opposite of “washed.” Here’s the other factor to consider: Allen was productive without a bona fide “X” receiver, who was supposed to be Alec Pierce. The number of catches in Indianapolis is worth three times that in the 49ers offense. Another overlooked factor is how well the 49ers have run the ball in 2026. Christian McCaffrey, while not the same player from years past, has been solid, and the emergence of Kaelon Black has led to the second-highest EPA/rush at 0.05. Yes, I’m aware that Purdy’s rushes help that number out, but the point remains. This team is still rooted in running the football, and timely catches to continue drives and move the chains are precisely where Allen fits in. Lastly, Allen is a master of sitting in the correct spots against zone coverages, something that is Seattle’s specialty. What about Minnesota? He’s faced them this season as well and can provide valuable insight. In an ideal world, Evans returns to take over the “X” spot and rotates with Demarcus Robinson. Allen can play “Z” or in the slot with Deebo Samuel and Jordan Watkins. One takeaway I have from the Allen move is that the 49ers could be confident in De’Zhaun Stribling’s recovery and ability to contribute upon his return. A receiver room of Evans, Allen, Samuel, Stribling, Robinson, and Watkins is a group I will be fine going to war with every Sunday and in the playoffs. As you can tell, I’m a big fan of the move. Allen can shake free in a phone booth and earn Purdy’s trust instantly. If Purdy loved Jennings, he will be head over heels for Allen. Welcome to the squad, Keenan. Let’s chase this chip.
author: Jason Aponte

title: Where the 49ers will miss Gracen Halton and how they can replace his production
summary: The San Francisco 49ers didn’t replace rookie defensive tackle Gracen Halton. That tells you everything. Gracen Halton broke his ankle with four minutes left in a 21-point game in Week 9. Two days later, the trade deadline came and went, and John Lynch didn’t bring in a single defensive tackle. Now, that doesn’t mean they […]
full_text: (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) The San Francisco 49ers didn’t replace rookie defensive tackle Gracen Halton. That tells you everything. Gracen Halton broke his ankle with four minutes left in a 21-point game in Week 9. Two days later, the trade deadline came and went, and John Lynch didn’t bring in a single defensive tackle. Now, that doesn’t mean they didn’t make calls. But when you lose a starter and you don’t replace him, that’s a decision. The 49ers are telling us something, Faithful. They trust what’s already in the building. So let’s talk about who’s in that defensive tackle room. First, understand what the 49ers lost. Halton came in as a 4th-round pick out of Oklahoma to be a penetrating 3-technique. Get up the field, make the quarterback uncomfortable. But what he really showed us how good he was against the run. Fifteen tackles, five tackles for loss, and two sacks in eight games, six of them starts. Sports Info Solutions had him leading every defensive tackle on the team in Points Saved. The rookie was living behind the line of scrimmage. That’s the hole. Not a pass rusher. A run stopper. And this defense has always been built on stopping the run first. Right now the 49ers are giving up 3.3 yards a carry, the best mark in the league. The Raiders ran for 24 yards on Sunday. That standard doesn’t drop because one guy went down. Enter C.J. West. I’ll be honest, we went hard on West. He showed up to camp out of shape, got hurt, then tried to play his way into shape on a bad knee, and the performance wasn’t there early. Then came the surgery and the injured reserve. But he’s had time to rest; he’s set to return to practice this week, and he was the starting nose tackle for a reason. If he’s right, he’s the run stopper this defense needs. Then there’s the youth. James Thompson Jr., the 6-foot-6 undrafted rookie out of Illinois. Sebastian Valdez, another undrafted guy who already has a sack. These guys have to lift. This has to be a youth movement. And that’s exactly why DeForest Buckner matters beyond the stat sheet. Yes, he’s another veteran who can penetrate, and he had four sacks in Indy before he got here. But those young guys now get to watch a guy with 75.5 career sacks show them what it looks like to be a pro every single day. Losing Halton hurts. But this room can rally around it. It’s West, Thompson and Valdez.. And the 49ers are riding with it. Who steps up first, Faithful?
author: The Coach

title: 49ers bring back recently released cornerback to the practice squad
summary: The San Francisco 49ers officially announced the trade with the Indianapolis Colts for Keenan Allen, sending a 2027 sixth-round pick in return. The team also signed cornerback Jack Jones to the practice squad. Jones appeared in seven games with the 49ers before they released him on October 28. Jones came in when the 49ers were […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers officially announced the trade with the Indianapolis Colts for Keenan Allen, sending a 2027 sixth-round pick in return. The team also signed cornerback Jack Jones to the practice squad. Jones appeared in seven games with the 49ers before they released him on October 28. Jones came in when the 49ers were in dime personnel. After a strong start to the season, his play cooled. Big plays and penalties led to the 49ers releasing Jones. In his last game against the Falcons, Jones allowed over five yards per separation on his targets. Starting cornerbacks Renardo Green (back) and Deommodore Lenoir (foot) are day-to-day. Rookie Ephesians Prysock would likely get the first crack in the rotation if a starter went down, especially given how things ended with Jones. But in an emergency situation, you could see why the 49ers brought back a familiar face. Jones joins Brandon Codrington on the practice squad.

title: What would you have done differently as the 49ers GM ahead of the trade deadline?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers targeted two Indianapolis Colts players ahead of the trade deadline to solidify their roster. Defensive tackle DeForest Buckner fills a void in the middle of the defensive line. A productive pass rusher who can hold his ground against the run and allow the rest of the interior linemen to play fewer […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers targeted two Indianapolis Colts players ahead of the trade deadline to solidify their roster. Defensive tackle DeForest Buckner fills a void in the middle of the defensive line. A productive pass rusher who can hold his ground against the run and allow the rest of the interior linemen to play fewer snaps makes a fourth-round pick look like a steal, especially given Buckner’s production this season. Wide receiver Keenan Allen gives Brock Purdy a trustworthy veteran target, taking pressure off players like Jordan Watkins and Jacob Cowing in a playoff setting. Allen isn’t exactly the TE2 the 49ers had on their radar , but he’s close in usage and effectiveness as a blocker. The 49ers could have done more, but the question is whether they should have. The team with the best record in the NFL, the highest point differential, and an offense that leads the NFL in passing and rushing success rate probably felt pretty good about where they are at this point in the season. What would you have done differently as the 49ers GM ahead of the trade deadline? My answer: I would’ve targeted a cornerback. To me, that’s the one area where the 49ers can be susceptible. But you’d have to pry a cornerback from a bad team. A contender, or a team that thinks they’re a contender, isn’t parting ways with a premium position. Martin Emerson Jr. from the Saints is near the top of the league in completion percentage allowed. He’s 6’2″, has a couple of interceptions, and, up until last week, hadn’t allowed more than 47 receiving yards in a game. But you’d be giving up on Upton Stout and would need to move Deommodore Lenoir inside. Cornerback isn’t realistic, even if the current ones have their faults. But this is what I would do. Outside of a blockbuster trade that would’ve landed a player any team could use, it’s hard to poke holes in the roster from a team-building perspective. You can never go wrong adding more pass rushers. But you’d take away snaps from Mykel Williams and Romello Height by doing that. That’s a deep room as it is. Mike Evans is your WR1. George Kittle is your WR1b. You don’t need another household name when those are your top two options. Jordan Watkins and Demarcus Robinson make for ideal backups with different skill sets. Ideally, De’Zhaun Stribling contributes this season. That name will get lost in the discussion of wanting more. Allen gives them much-needed experience, which is likely the one drawback of having so many youngsters at the position. What would you have done differently? Let us know in the comments below.
author: Kyle Posey

title: The 49ers looked around for tight end help before the trade deadline
summary: The San Francisco 49ers made one move on Tuesday by adding veteran wide receiver Keenan Allen. According to ESPN, the Niners were snooping around for tight end help before the trade deadline: The 49ers looked around for tight end help, and the Broncos’ Evan Engram was on their radar. But they landed on Keenan Allen, […]
full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers made one move on Tuesday by adding veteran wide receiver Keenan Allen. According to ESPN , the Niners were snooping around for tight end help before the trade deadline: The 49ers looked around for tight end help, and the Broncos’ Evan Engram was on their radar. But they landed on Keenan Allen, who’s a bigger receiver and perhaps serves some of the same functions in the offense. Ingram lines up as an inline tight end 44% of the time for the Denver Broncos this year, compared to 40.9% in the slot and 14.5% outside. He’s listed at 6’3″, 240 pounds. The 32-year-old has an average depth of target under five yards this season. If you remove the tight end tag, Engram is essentially interchangeable with Allen. They’d move around the formation and run underneath routes. In the same article, Dan Graziano said, “The 49ers have been scrambling to fill those spots all season,” with “those” being wide receivers. Allen can line up in multiple spots and can help weather the storm until the Niners get fully healthy. Regardless, he’ll serve as the ultimate role player and security blanket for Brock Purdy. Graziano also mentioned that the Jaguars were in on DeForest Buckner before he landed with the 49ers. I wonder where the Niners would have pivoted if Jacksonville had gotten Buckner.

full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 1: Wide receiver Keenan Allen #10 of the Indianapolis Colts catches the ball for a first down while being defended by cornerback Travis Hunter #12 of the Jacksonville Jaguars in the first quarter at EverBank Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 49ers got Keenan Allen. Was it enough? (Paywall) “He’s not Jauan Jennings, but he can occupy a similar role. He’s been employed mainly as a possession receiver, and has excelled on short targets. Crucially, he’s been most effective on third downs. He’s got a +0.33 EPA when targeted on third downs, and has moved the chains seven times. More than 41 percent of his third-down targets turned into first downs. That’s what Jennings did for the 49ers. Now, he won’t be the blocker Jennings was. But, he’s also a much more natural talent than Jennings. He can play anywhere, and I do mean anywhere. He’s a plug-and-play option at any spot. And while he’s not what he used to be, he’s still got some wiggle.” Agent: Brandon Aiyuk plans to play this season, likely with ‘somebody that knows him’ (paywall) “He had an MRI, he had X-rays, he had a physical exam,” Rosenhaus said of Aiyuk, who had a multiligament knee injury in October 2024 and has not played since. “He’s working out on his own, he’s running routes, he’s catching footballs. He says he’s 100 percent ready to play. We’d be glad to go work out for interested teams if he is released by the 49ers….. I think he’s in a really good place. He met with the 49ers. He did a good job in the meeting with them. He said hello to John Lynch. He met with the team. I just feel like he’s in a good place. And getting to know him over the last week, I’m confident in his future moving forward.” How veteran WR Keenan Allen boosts depleted 49ers’ biggest position of need “Allen signed a one-year, $3.32 million contract with the Colts before this season. The 49ers will owe him approximately half of his $1.3 million base salary for the remainder of the season.” 49ers overreactions: Do Super Bowl chances depend on the health of Mike Evans? “Evans missed his second game in a row due to Achilles tendinitis. He might be out even longer, as the 49ers likely agree: They need him healthy for the games that matter the most. He is a unique talent who makes the offense so much better. Evans has the rare ability to be the difference maker.” 49ers practice and media schedule ahead of Week 10 matchup vs. Cowboys “ Wednesday, November 11 12:35 p.m. – Kyle Shanahan press conference 1:30 p.m. – Practice Thursday, November 12 12:30 p.m. – Practice After practice (approx. 2:10 p.m.) – Raheem Morris press conference Following Morris – Klay Kubiak press conference Following Kubiak – Brock Purdy press conference Friday, November 13 12:35 p.m. – Practice After practice (approx. 1:35 p.m.) – Kyle Shanahan press conference.” 49ers trade for Colts’ Keenan Allen to bolster injury-plagued WR room “Coincidentally, if Allen is able to play Sunday, it will mean playing against the Cowboys two weeks in a row. He had four catches for 26 yards against Dallas in Week 9.” Keenan Allen is the newest member of the 49ers “Allen’s air yards per target is the lowest it’s been since 2017. On targets under 10 air yards, Allen has caught 31 of his 38 targets for 230 yards and a touchdown. That’s the seventh-most yards among all wide receivers under 10 yards. The 49ers average 5.29 yards to go on third down. That’s first in the NFL. To me, this is the Niners giving themselves a reliable veteran option underneath on third down. Allen has a couple of drops this season, but 50% of his targets result in a first down, despite a low depth of target. Brock Purdy’s on-target percentage is over 3% higher than Daniel Jones. Same with his catchable passes. Allen has had targets within the last couple of games that were uncatchable, or he had to obnoxiously adjust to. Allen provides a big body who can block from a condensed split. He’s a competitive blocker, which makes it easier to play him on every down.”

title: Titans’ 3 biggest 2027 cap hits after 2026 trade deadline
summary: If Tennessee Titans fans expected a flurry of activity on trade deadline day, they were left disappointed. General manager Mike Borgonzi made one trade, sending Amani Hooker to the Buffalo Bills for a second-round pick. The Titans did not make any additional trades. Borgonzi obviously feels he has enough draft capital after trading Jeffery Simmons […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 20: Calvin Ridley #0 of the Tennessee Titans warms up prior to the game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Nissan Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images If Tennessee Titans fans expected a flurry of activity on trade deadline day , they were left disappointed. General manager Mike Borgonzi made one trade, sending Amani Hooker to the Buffalo Bills for a second-round pick. The Titans did not make any additional trades. Borgonzi obviously feels he has enough draft capital after trading Jeffery Simmons for three picks, including two first-round selections in 2027 and 2028, and he got another premium pick for Hooker. With the Titans’ 2026 roster mostly intact, we’re looking ahead to the team’s three biggest-scheduled cap hits in 2027. Let’s analyze each situation. WR Calvin Ridley ($29.7 million) The Titans increased Calvin Ridley’s 2027 cap charge when they restructured his contract this past offseason. Borgonzi did that by design. There’s essentially no scenario whatsoever where Ridley is on the team next season. The veteran wideout has been an afterthought on offense this campaign. Ridley is struggling with drops and could fall behind Chimere Dike and Elic Ayomanor on the depth chart after Week 8. Releasing Ridley this offseason will clear $22.2 million in cap space, leaving a manageable dead-cap charge of $7.5 million. CB Alontae Taylor ($25 million) The Titans signed Alontae Taylor to a three-year, $58 million contract in the offseason. His cap number is scheduled to jump sizably, from $14 million this season to $25m next season. That’s unfortunate, considering how the Titans misjudged his role in Robert Saleh’s defense. The Titans signed Taylor to play boundary cornerback, but they abandoned that mission after seeing him routinely struggle there. They’re now making Taylor an overpaid nickelback. That’s the position he most commonly played with the New Orleans Saints. The Titans probably just have to swallow this mistake. DL John Franklin-Myers ($23 million) Speaking of Taylor, John Franklin-Myers is another high-priced offseason addition who isn’t meeting expectations. The Titans have said he’s playing through a painful and limiting back injury. Franklin-Myers’ cap charge increases from $14.9 million to $23m next season. Franklin-Myers was brought to Tennessee to pair with Simmons, but that was short-lived. JFM has produced just 16 tackles, 1.5 sacks, and 14 pressures in eight appearances. The Titans need way more production from Franklin-Myers to justify this $63 million contract next season. honorable mentions: LT Dan Moore ($22.1 million); LG Peter Skoronski ($22.4 million); WR Wan’Dale Robinson ($20.7 million)

title: Washington Commanders vs New York Giants Week 10: Five Questions with Big Blue View
summary: It’s week 10 of the NFL season, and the 2-5-1 Washington Commanders will be facing the 5-2-1 New York Giants on the road at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey this Thursday (today) at 8:15 p.m. ET. The Giants’ wins have been against the Cowboys, Titans, Cardinals, Texans, and Eagles, while their losses have […]
full_text: It’s week 10 of the NFL season, and the 2-5-1 Washington Commanders will be facing the 5-2-1 New York Giants on the road at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey this Thursday (today) at 8:15 p.m. ET. The Giants’ wins have been against the Cowboys, Titans, Cardinals, Texans, and Eagles, while their losses have been to the Rams and Saints. I covered the overview of the Giants in the week 5 matchup article , so I won’t rehash the same points here except for the basics. Instead, I’ll focus on what has changed. On offense, the Giants have moved from Jameis Winston to J.J. McCarthy as their starting QB. McCarthy is a highly mobile QB who has shown considerably more zip on deep throws and is 2-0 in his starts so far this year. McCarthy is 5th in the NFL in third-down completion percentage at 71.4% since Week 7. He suffered what looked like a very painful hip pointer injury last week against the Eagles, but managed to return to the game and doesn’t carry an injury designation for this matchup, though it’s worth monitoring if it impacts his mobility. RB Cam Skattebo missed the last two weeks with a hamstring injury, but is expected to lead the backfield again in this matchup. WR Malik Nabers has had a breakout season and was named NFC Offensive Player of the Month for his play in October. TE Isaiah Likely seems to have developed a rapport with McCarthy as well, and fans may remember Likely going berserk against Washington with 11 catches for 94 yards and 2 TDs in their week 5 matchup. The Giants offense is ranked 14th with 333.1 yards per game over the season. On defense, the Giants have managed to stay mostly healthy outside of losing one of their best players, EDGE Brian Burns, to a torn ACL in week 3. Prior to the Burns injury, the Giants had one of the lower blitz rates in the league, but since week 4 have gone up to a 46.5% blitz rate , one of the highest in the league. However, the Giants ran a Flores-worthy 62.2% blitz rate in their week 5 matchup against Washington, so David Blough better have answers ready to deal with the blitz. Overall, the Giants’ defense has given up the 5th-fewest yards per game in the NFL this season. though they have been better against the pass (3rd) than run (19th). I asked Ed Valentine of Big Blue View five questions to better understand the state of the Giants and what to look for in this game. 1) What has changed for the Giants since the last time these teams faced off? Well, the biggest personnel change is that J.J. McCarthy is now the starting quarterback instead of Jameis Winston. That changes the Giants’ offense because it opens up more of the playbook. 2) What have you seen out of JJ McCarthy since he joined the Giants? What do you think his future is with the team and could he supplant Jaxson Dart next year? McCarthy has been good. He was fantastic in his first start against the Texans. He wasn’t nearly as good against the Eagles, but he was OK. I keep saying this — I just don’t think the Giants want to go into next year with any hint of a quarterback controversy. I think McCarthy has to do a LOT to make them even think about doing anything other than handing the reigns back to Dart next year. The Giants got McCarthy for a fifth-round pick. I think the ideal scenario is for him to play well enough for the Giants to be able to trade him to a QB-needy team in the offseason for much more than they spent to acquire him. 3) Where have the Giants performed the best this year and where do you think they still have the most room for improvement? The defense continues to impress. Arvell Reese is a star, and the secondary has been better than expected. They need to run the ball more consistently. The blocking hasn’t always been up to par. 4) What is your realistic best-case scenario for the rest of the Giants’ season and in the offseason? I don’t know about the offseason, though I think using McCarthy to get a haul in the draft would be great. The best-case scenario? Win the NFC East, which would give them a home playoff game for the first time since MetLife Stadium opened in 2010, get a favorable matchup, and win one playoff game. 5) What’s your prediction for this game’s outcome? What do you think will be the critical factors determining that outcome? I think the Giants win this game. They have some momentum, they know what kind of opportunity they have. I think they need to keep Jayden Daniels from hurting them with his legs like they did in Week 5, and they need to limit mistakes. They will win if they do those things. A companion article to this with my answers to Ed’s questions is linked here . Thanks again to Ed Valentine for taking time out of his day to answer our questions about the Giants.

title: Washington’s offensive problems run deeper than you think | Commanders Film Session With Scott Turner
summary: Former Washington Commanders offensive coordinator Scott Turner joined the Trap or Dive Podcast this week for an in-depth film review of Washington’s offensive performance against the Los Angeles Rams. With a short turnaround ahead of Thursday night’s matchup against the New York Giants, the Commanders face another difficult defensive test — and one that could […]
full_text: Former Washington Commanders offensive coordinator Scott Turner joined the Trap or Dive Podcast this week for an in-depth film review of Washington’s offensive performance against the Los Angeles Rams. With a short turnaround ahead of Thursday night’s matchup against the New York Giants, the Commanders face another difficult defensive test — and one that could further expose the issues plaguing David Blough’s offense. According to SumerSports , both the Rams and Giants rank among the NFL’s top eight defenses in total EPA over the last four weeks, with New York sitting eighth. More importantly, the Giants present another significant challenge for Washington’s struggling offensive line. New York ranks fifth in pressure percentage and 10th in sack percentage, two categories that should concern anyone who watched the Commanders attempt to protect Jayden Daniels against the Los Angeles Rams. The Giants may not boast the same caliber of defensive talent Washington faced against the Rams, but the underlying concerns remain. If the Commanders fail to correct the protection breakdowns, inconsistent execution and schematic shortcomings that defined Sunday’s loss, Thursday night could become another indictment of Dan Quinn and his coaching staff. If Washington loses to New York, the loud, dominating conversation will be how much longer owner Josh Harris is willing to tolerate the same recurring mistakes. So, what exactly went wrong against the Los Angeles Rams? Despite an encouraging start that saw Washington establish an early rhythm offensively, its efficiency deteriorated significantly as the game progressed. What initially appeared to be a promising offensive performance quickly unraveled into another frustrating display of missed assignments, poor technique and an inability to sustain drives. Pass protection was problematic from the opening possession. Beyond the challenges of accounting for Aaron Donald and Myles Garrett, Washington’s offensive line struggled with its individual responsibilities. With Sam Cosmi as a notable exception, the unit repeatedly abandoned its technique, allowing defenders to win matchups that weren’t always the result of superior talent. While the protection plan deserves scrutiny, the film also revealed instances in which Washington’s linemen simply failed to execute their assignments. The running game presented a different set of problems, but the underlying theme was familiar: small details creating significant consequences. One particular third-and-1 sequence illustrated how alignment, timing and blocking angles can determine the success or failure of an otherwise well-designed play. Washington aligned rookie receiver Antonio Williams in the slot before running a toss-crack concept toward the boundary. The design itself raised an interesting personnel question: Should Washington have used a bigger body to execute the crack block, even at the risk of tipping its intentions to the defense? There is a reasonable argument for doing so. However, the coaching staff clearly trusts Williams to handle these responsibilities, and his assignment was not inherently unreasonable. Williams also could have helped himself with a slightly tighter alignment, potentially creating a more favorable angle to seal the edge defender. Of course, that adjustment comes with a tradeoff. A tighter split could prompt the defender to widen his alignment, changing the leverage Williams would need to account for. Ultimately, the play came down to execution. Williams was late off the snap and, more importantly, took a poor angle to his assignment. That allowed the defender to beat him upfield and disrupt what should have been a manageable third-and-1 conversion. It’s a perfect example of how an offense can put itself in a favorable situation schematically and still fail because of individual execution. Those details matter, particularly for a Washington offense that has consistently struggled to capitalize on manageable down-and-distance situations. But the film session went beyond offensive line technique and missed blocks. Turner also provided valuable insight into Washington’s passing concepts and the responsibilities shared between offensive coordinator David Blough and quarterback Jayden Daniels. One central question we explored was whether Blough’s passing scheme consistently provides Daniels with the answers he needs against opposing defenses. Are the route combinations creating favorable opportunities? Is the offense giving Daniels viable solutions when defenses take away his initial reads? And when protection breaks down, does the scheme give Daniels enough flexibility to keep the offense on schedule? Those questions matter, but so does the other side of the conversation. Daniels is already a talented quarterback capable of elevating Washington’s offense. However, there are still areas of his game that require development, particularly his post-snap processing and ability to identify and exploit defensive adjustments. Understanding where the coaching staff can better support Daniels is just as important as identifying the opportunities he must capitalize on himself. Ultimately, Washington’s offensive struggles cannot be reduced to one player, one position group, or one coordinator. The film revealed a combination of schematic questions, technical breakdowns, and missed opportunities that continue to prevent the Commanders from playing consistent football. With another formidable defensive front awaiting Washington on Thursday night, the margin for error is shrinking. The question now is whether Blough and his offense can make the necessary adjustments—or whether the same problems will continue to define a season that is quickly slipping away. Watch the full Trap or Dive film session below as former Commanders offensive coordinator Scott Turner joins us to break down Washington’s offensive struggles, the passing scheme, and what Jayden Daniels needs to take the next step. Comment and let us know where you stand on the Commanders Offense. Don’t forget to also subscribe to the Trap or Dive Podcast.

Commanders links Honoring all who serve or have served this #VeteransDay 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/XVQ2p9YDfN — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) November 11, 2026 Articles Washington Post (paywall) Commanders’ season is on the line vs. the Giants; here are the X factors to watch This game means everything. Washington will face the New York Giants on Thursday night in East Rutherford, New Jersey. Given the state of the NFC East race, it’s easily the Commanders’ most important game of the season. Whether they come out on top will probably dictate their fate. While a win won’t ensure anything, it would at least give Washington a chance moving forward. A loss, however, would make the team’s road to the playoffs [effectively impossible]. After the Giants lost star outside linebacker Brian Burns to a torn ACL in Week 3, defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson…turned up the heat. Since Week 4, New York’s defense has blitzed opponents on 46.5 percent of their dropbacks (second-highest rate in the NFL). That has helped the unit generate a pressure rate of 36.4 percent (13th) and a sack rate of 9 percent (sixth). Wilson hasn’t blitzed anyone more than he did the Commanders in Week 5. They blitzed on 62.2 percent of Washington’s dropbacks and sacked quarterback Jayden Daniels five times. The Giants had a season-high seven sacks in their win over the Eagles. Although they have a talented defensive line, their most effective pass rusher has been inside linebacker Arvell Reese, who had three sacks against Philadelphia. As the Commanders attempt to curb New York’s aggression, they will have to do so with a backup at center. Starting center Lucas Patrick suffered a concussion against the Rams and won’t be able to clear concussion protocol by Thursday. Veteran Nick Allegretti will start in his place against the Giants. The Commanders are optimistic Burks (foot) will play Thursday after he sat out last week. They also believe cornerback Amik Robertson, who suffered an ankle injury late against the Rams, will be good to go. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE The Athletic (paywall) Why the Commanders decided to stand pat at the trade deadline With their season hanging in the balance in the form of a Thursday night game at the division-leading New York Giants, the Washington Commanders stood pat at the trade deadline Tuesday — a tacit acknowledgment that they’re trying to salvage the tenure of coach Dan Quinn but aren’t willing to part with draft picks to add to an injury-riddled group that has produced just two wins in the first half of the season. The Commanders — at 2-5-1 — are within a victory at New York of pulling within two games of the 5-2-1 Giants. Given their tie against New York last month — a game the Commanders should have won if not for an egregious late-game management situation — it’s not unreasonable that Washington [are] holding out hope to get back into a divisional race that has no surefire winner. Now, the Commanders head into the final nine games of the season — a stretch that will determine whether Quinn gets a fourth year or not — with a roster that is thinned by injury and hasn’t efficiently closed out games. The Thursday night game against the Giants provides the first test as to whether that was the right path forward. Unfortunately, Patrick left Sunday’s game against the Los Angeles Rams with an apparent concussion. He has been ruled out for Thursday’s game against the New York Giants, and Allegretti will replace him. Rookie center Matt Gulbin replaced Patrick against the Rams on Sunday and struggled to fill the role effectively. So, it makes sense that veteran Allegretti is getting the nod. However, the issue here is why didn’t the Commanders turn to Allegretti on Sunday? Quinn said after the game it was because Allegretti had been practicing at guard. Terry McLaurin, Dyami Brown, Daron Payne, Jacory “Bill” Croskey-Merritt, and Javon Kinlaw played; all five are now on IR. A month later, Washington has managed only one win since, and will enter the game at 2-5-1 after losing 20-13 to the Rams in Week 9. Van Jefferson has a much bigger part in this offense now, too. He played just three offensive snaps against the Giants, compared with 36 against Los Angeles, where he caught five passes for 58 yards and a touchdown. Antonio Williams’ workload has grown from 42 snaps in the tie to 52 against the Rams. Jefferson should stay involved even if Treylon Burks returns from the foot injury that kept him out Sunday. Rachaad White and Austin Ekeler handled the running-back snaps against the Rams. Daronte Jones has two substantial workloads to replace up front. Payne played 63 of Washington’s 89 defensive snaps in the tie, while Kinlaw played 56. Payne also recorded a sack and a forced fumble. With both players now on IR , Washington will ask a different group to handle the interior work and create some disruption of their own. title: Washington Commanders vs. NY Giants on TNF Week 10: Inside the Matchup
summary: Back in June and early July, HH veteran writer Bill-in-Bangkok, offered a week-by-week preview via the 5 O’Clock Club of the Washington Commanders regular season schedule for 2026. As we roll into the actual games during the regular season, Hogs Haven will revisit each of these previews with John Portis adding additional thoughts and updates […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - OCTOBER 11: Jeremy Reaves #39 of the Washington Commanders loses his helmet on his tackle against Cam Skattebo #44 of the New York Giants during overtime in the NFL game at Northwest Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images Back in June and early July, HH veteran writer Bill-in-Bangkok, offered a week-by-week preview via the 5 O’Clock Club of the Washington Commanders regular season schedule for 2026. As we roll into the actual games during the regular season, Hogs Haven will revisit each of these previews with John Portis adding additional thoughts and updates as we go inside the matchup to get you ready for every opponent the Commanders face in 2026. Date/Time : Thursday, November 12th, 2026 | 8:15 p.m. ET Location : MetLife Stadium (East Rutherford, New Jersey) The 2-5-1 Washington Commanders have a short week before taking on the NFC East-leading New York Giants (5-2-1 ), on Thursday Night Football. While Sunday’s loss to the Rams dissolved any positive feelings surrounding Washington’s win over Philadelphia, the good news is the Giants barely scraped by that same team on Sunday with an ugly score of 19-11 . A win on Thursday night would hand the Commanders the tie-breaker against the G-Men and narrow their division lead to only two games with 8 games left in the season. Things have changed significantly since the two teams met in Week 5, and J.J. McCarthy is now the Giants starting quarterback. The 10th overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft, J.J. is 2-0 as a starter and proven to be clutch when called upon for Big Blue. McCarthy is 5th in the NFL in third-down completion percentage at 71.4% since Week 7. On the opposite side of the matchup, Jayden Daniels and the Washington Commanders have a bottom of the league third down conversion rate of 31%. J.J. McCarthy on 3rd down against the Eagles: 6/7 88 passing yards 20 rushing yards 2x sacked 5 first downs Today wasn't an offensive clinic, but he did enough when it counted and was efficient on the money down that lead to some points in a defensive battle. #BigBlue pic.twitter.com/6I5hn8pkmF — WBG84 (@WBG84) November 8, 2026 Running back Cam Skattebo was briefly on the outside looking in, but returned to John Harbaugh’s good graces with a 124 yards on 17 carries performance in Week 7 against the Houston Texans. He leads the Giants with 418 rushing yards on 98 carries(4.3 ypa), and is projected to be available for Thursday’s game after missing the last two weeks with a hamstring injury. Malik Nabers has continued his standout performance since his breakout game versus the Cardinals earlier in the season. Nabers had 36 receptions for 509 receiving yards and two touchdowns last month and was named the NFC Offensive Player of the Month for October. After struggling briefly, tight end Isaiah Likely has developed a strong on-field connection with McCarthy, and the duo connected for 5 receptions for 53 yards and a touchdown versus the Eagles. The Giants currently rank 14th in total offense. The Commanders are reshuffling things yet again after center Lucas Patrick suffered a concussion on Sunday, and the team is returning to Nick Allegretti at the pivot Thursday night. While that in and of itself should be concerning for Commanders fans, defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson just deployed a variety of pressure looks aimed at the center and guard positions against the Philadelphia Eagles last week. Dennard Wilson has done an elite job scheming to the strengths of rookie LB Arvell Reese. Stack LBs w/ 5 man pressure…send Harris (1T) wide & Pinnock through the B to expand the OGs and isolate Reese vs. RB in protection. Reese is a weapon Wilson knows how to use best. pic.twitter.com/VG1fJjOryB — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) November 9, 2026 Arvell Reese has been on a tear recently, and the first-round rookie is the only NFL player with 65+ tackles, 8+ TFL, and 1+INT on the season thus far to go along with 4.5 sacks. The Giants lost linebacker Tremaine Edmunds in Week 6, but replacement Micah McFadden has stepped up and also played well with 9 tackles, 1 sack, 2 TFLs, and a fumble recovery versus the Eagles. Once considered a liability, the Giants’ secondary has been one of the team’s strengths in 2026. New York ranks among the league’s best in total takeaways (9) and interceptions (6), five of which came from Giants defensive backs. Safety Jevon Holland has been playing at a high level and leads the team with three interceptions on the season. The Giants are ranked 5th in total defense. The interior of the Giants’ offensive line is questionable and could be where the Commanders’ defense can attack New York’s offense, even without starting DTs Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw. The Giants allowed 4 sacks and 11 pressures to the Eagles defensive line in Sunday’s matchup and are tied for 27th in sacks allowed with 27 total on the season. Nick Cross and Trey Amos were out with injury during their first meeting this season. Their return to Washington’s secondary for the team’s second meeting should go a long way in preventing repeat performances from Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely. The development of defensive coordinator Daronte Jones should help prevent another late game collapse. The addition of Steve Wilks to the defensive coaching staff is another positive development towards that goal. The true question marks for Thursday night surround David Blough and the team’s offensive line in a game that quarterback Jayden Daniels has declared is a must-win in order to keep the Washington Commanders season alive. Betting Lines Point spread : Commanders +1.5 Point total : 43.5 Opening odds for the Commanders have them as 1.5-point road underdogs against the New York Giants. The Over/Under opens at 43.5 in a game expected to be low scoring with the home team barely favored.
