title: Kirk Cousins makes first comments on Minnesota trade at Great Clips
summary: Kirk Cousins offered some thoughts on his trade to Minnesota after the news broke in the most on-brand location imaginable.
full_text:
Before Kirk Cousins could head to the Land of 10,000 Lakes after being traded to the Minnesota Vikings , he had to make an on-brand stop: at Great Clips.

 Cousins is a longtime aficionado of the budget-friendly salon chain, having been awarded its first-ever VIP card back in 2025 -- the "Hall of Fade" card affords free hair cuts to both Cousins and everyone who's at the location with him when it's used.

 

 But it wasn't just a haircut for Cousins on Tuesday. When the veteran quarterback dropped by Great Clips following the trade, they took the time to get his thoughts on the news.

 Reflecting on the trade, Cousins acknowledged that there was something in particular about the destination -- he quarterbacked the Vikings from 2018 to 2023 -- that made the transaction particularly special.

 "There's so many memories, so many great people," Cousins said. "I understand the challenge on the football field, there's a lot of work to go get done, but it would be really special. If you're going to go win somewhere and have success, I want it to be in Minnesota."

 He also had a message to Raiders supporters, complimenting the fanbase and organization for their hospitality in his short stay in Las Vegas.

 "To the fans in Vegas, I just feel so grateful for how they welcomed me with open arms for the several months I was here -- that includes teammates, the organization," he said. "I really couldn't speak more highly of my time here in Vegas."

 

 Cousins also addressed fans in Minnesota, saying he was excited to reunite with his former team -- though the roster wouldn't quite be the same as the one he left.

 "To the fans in Minnesota, I'm thrilled to have the chance to come back," he said. "And to hopefully write the ending to a story for me that started eight, nine years ago when I first arrived. Ready to take on this new challenge with this, really, new team in Minnesota and see where we can go."

 Asked for his parting thoughts before he left the hot seat (barber chair?), Cousins reflected on the balance between saying goodbye to his former team and also getting to reunite with a place he already had to depart.

 "I've got a lot of emotions right now that are mixed. Always difficult to say goodbye, especially to people that mean a great deal to me, and there are so many of them here in Vegas," he said. "There's also a lot of people waiting for me in Minnesota that mean a great deal to me, that it was difficult to say goodbye to three years ago."

title: Inside the physical and mental toll of Malik Nabers' knee injury
summary: Giants star wide receiver Malik Nabers opens up about his rehab experience for the first time.
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers had a conversation with his uncle before training camp in 2025. His uncle was asking about his nephew's journey to NFL stardom, when he became a Pro Bowl player while setting a Giants record with 109 receptions during his rookie season.

 Nabers, the sixth overall pick out of LSU in 2024, told him how he didn't view his journey as all that hard. In fact, it came relatively easy for the wide receiver while compiling 1,204 yards and seven touchdowns despite playing with four quarterbacks in 2024. Nabers noted there were a lot of other players who had gone through "way harder things."

 Little did he know what was coming.

 Fast forward to three months later in Week 4 of the 2025 season against the Los Angeles Chargers , with Nabers lying on the MetLife Stadium turf reaching for his right knee. He had jumped to make a catch deep down the right sideline and knew immediately, in midair, that something was wrong.

 The Giants' young playmaker tore the ACL and meniscus in his right knee. 

 This was the test he subconsciously knew was coming even if it was one he hadn't asked for.

 On Nov. 1, 2026, Nabers is standing in the middle of the Giants' locker room seemingly fully back after four straight 100-yard receiving games, answering questions about the emotional challenge that came with the serious knee injury that cost him most of last season.

 Nabers revealed to ESPN prior to the first-place Giants' matchup Thursday night with the Washington Commanders (8:15 p.m. ET, Prime) details about that private conversation with his uncle that left the wide receiver once upon a time thinking his journey wouldn't be that formidable.   

 "Kind of ... kind of just ... and then this happened," Nabers reminisced last week. "And I was like, OK, well, this is the challenge that I said I never had. It's an opportunity to get back from a challenge and see how I can come back off of it."

 Nabers found out the physical and mental toll recovering from such a significant injury would entail ups and downs in the process, everything from lack of flexion in his knee to a second "cleanup" procedure to eliminate stiffness.

 

 The original thought from the Giants was that he would be back in the spring. Then even the summer and training camp was in doubt.

 "He had a slow comeback process just due to the severity of his injury," said Dr. Sharif "Reef" Tabbah, a physical therapist who worked with Nabers in Miami earlier this year.  

 Nabers tried hard to keep his faith, believing and telling himself everything was going to be fine when, in reality, he had no idea. The thoughts were bouncing like a ping pong ball off a wall, volleyed away but returning with a vengeance.

 "He was definitely struggling. You could tell he was struggling with the process," said Giants coach John Harbaugh, who was hired in January. "He even told me he was never hurt before, how hard it was. I think every little up and down in the process would really affect him emotionally, mentally, whatever."

 Nabers was going through an internal battle during a long and hard rehab. Through it all, he was trying to find himself. There were days when he was searching for answers but couldn't find them. He would have to figure out where and when they would come from. It wasn't going to be easy.   

 "I kind of lost myself in the process," Nabers said while opening up about his rehab for the first time. 

 

 

 NABERS' INJURY HISTORY prior to the Giants was not extensive. There was a shoulder injury that forced him to miss a couple of games at LSU his freshman season. He had some problems with his toe in New York, but nothing major. No long-term injuries or extended periods out of football.

 This knee injury was a new experience that drew Nabers into a scary, unexpected place.   

 "Just my attitude," Nabers said of why he lost himself. "Everybody didn't know what my mindset was. Just at a loss for words. Didn't really have a lot of words to say. Didn't really have, I don't know, I kind of was empty. Just didn't know what the future holds, how I was going to respond, just with everything that was going on. Everybody just didn't know."

 There were days when his knee swelled, when it was stiff and didn't bend. His progress, if it was outlined in a graph, might resemble the stock market during its most volatile month.  

 This sent Nabers into a tailspin. He was fighting himself. 

 "My mind was just all over the place. I didn't really understand and didn't really want to communicate well," he said. "Just didn't know how to communicate how I was feeling and how things were going because every day it was something new. ... So I just didn't know, I just didn't really see a process. I didn't really see progress from week to week."

 Nabers said he didn't lean on anyone in particular, not even Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels , one of his closest friends -- who also spent this past offseason combating an injury-plagued season . He was around Giants running back Cam Skattebo a bunch as they both rehabbed injuries -- Skattebo suffered an open fracture to his right leg in October of last year and still ultimately returned for the start of mandatory minicamp before Nabers. But Nabers kept to himself. He didn't feel like sharing.

 "When he was in that deep place, I was in that deep place, too. We were both together," Skattebo said. "We were both in that same spot as not being able to say anything, not being able to express ourselves. ... He wasn't seeing the progress that he wanted but as he kept going and up until now, he's starting to feel that progress that's being made."

 In a way, it was an extension of Nabers' nature. He is generally a quiet guy.

 "When you go through an internal battle with yourself you start to figure out what you need better than other people telling you what you need when they don't know you," Nabers said. "... You start finding more about yourself that you didn't know yet. ... So I just went through it myself."

 

 

 RECOVERY FROM A torn ACL can be a beast. Adding a full meniscus repair only adds to the difficulty.

 It's why Nabers was still walking with crutches and wearing a brace in January, some two-plus months after the surgery was performed by Dallas Cowboys head team physician Daniel E. Cooper -- a renowned doctor known for recently operating on other NFL players such as Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes and Las Vegas Raiders tight end Brock Bowers . Typically, full meniscus repair adds to the recovery timeline. It turned out to be the case for Nabers, who almost didn't play Week 1 roughly a year after his injury.

 "His rehab protocol was a little bit slow," Tabbah said. "He had a lot of limitations still with mobility and strength and tolerance of functional exercises and things like that. So we were in that phase of ... tolerating different functional movement patterns and trying to get him ready to progress to that later stage."

 Dr. Reef, as he is known, is a doctor of physical therapy and certified strength and conditioning specialist who founded Alkeme Sports RX in South Florida. He has worked with a long list of professional athletes, including Commanders wide receiver Stephon Diggs last year as he rehabbed from a torn ACL.

 Dr. Reef worked with Nabers in Florida for most of February through May. He admitted it was a "challenging rehab case." But, along with new Giants trainer Adam Bennett, they together a plan that would be best for Nabers' healing. Together, they monitored the wide receiver's rehab, and early on in the process, Nabers needed the mental boost.

 

 "I just try to give them reassurance and just let them know, 'Hey, this will pass. I know this is tough right now, but this is where you are today. It's not where you're going to be in months to come,'" Dr. Reef said. "I know this is your first rodeo when it comes to dealing with something like this, but it's not mine."

title: Why 2-7 Jets preferred to keep roster intact at trade deadline
summary: A year after making two blockbuster trades, New York stayed quiet at the NFL trade deadline.
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. -- One year after rocking the NFL with the Sauce Gardner and Quinnen Williams blockbusters at the trade deadline, the New York Jets made no splashy deals despite obvious roster needs and a handful of players that would've fetched nice returns.

 Ahead of Tuesday's deadline, general manager Darren Mougey was quiet -- well, except for a minor trade involving backup safety Andre Cisco , who was sent to the Detroit Lions for a 2029 sixth-round pick.

 The Jets were only interested in trading players on expiring contracts (like Cisco), preferring to keep their 2027 roster intact. While some might argue that a team with 21 losses in its last 26 games should've reached for the sun and moon to improve its future, the Jets sent three messages by standing (almost) pat:

 
 They like their foundation. 
 They already have enough draft capital (three first-round picks in 2027). 
 They want to give embattled coach Aaron Glenn a chance to develop the current roster. 
 
 

 Plus, let's be honest, there also was a subliminal message: With Glenn on the hot seat, they wanted to wait until the coaching dust settles in the offseason before selling off players that might intrigue a new coaching staff.

 Explaining their approach to the deadline, Glenn said Wednesday, "[Our] philosophy hasn't changed from last year."

 He said they will always listen to inquiries, but "we won't force any issues, and we'll make sure we do what's best for the organization."

 Glenn likes the current roster, claiming, "We're right on the cusp of trying to break through."

 He noted that the Jets have lost five one-score games against a tough schedule. In fact, they're 1-5 in one-score games, 4-10 in two seasons under Glenn. Based on their opponents' records, the Jets' strength of schedule ranks 23rd, per ESPN Analytics.

 Some might argue, "So close, yet so far."

 

 A look at why the Jets retained certain players and what it means for their future:

 Quarterback Geno Smith : Smith fit the expiring-contract criterion, but they never entertained the idea of moving him despite pre-deadline buzz with the Minnesota Vikings . The Jets don't have an experienced backup, so trading Smith would've been tantamount to surrendering the season and ending Glenn. The No. 2 is rookie Cade Klubnik , a fourth-round pick who has yet to take a snap.

 At 2-7, the season is basically lost, but a downgrade at quarterback would've hampered their ability to develop young players such as wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr . and tight ends Mason Taylor and Kenyon Sadiq . At this point, player development is paramount. Smith, ranked 19th in QBR, can keep the offense operating at a functional level.

 Smith, who said he paid no attention to the speculation, also could fit into their 2027 plan as a stopgap starter/mentor for a highly-drafted rookie.

 Wide receiver Garrett Wilson : A trade never was a realistic possibility even though the Kansas City Chiefs and San Francisco 49ers were interested. Wilson didn't want to leave, and the Jets didn't want to deal arguably their best player. Under contract through 2030, he's viewed as a foundational piece.

 This storyline could be re-visited in the offseason, depending on how Wilson feels about the direction of the team. As he said recently, "I want to win games and that's the one thing we've been missing here. I love it here. Do I love it more than I love winning? Nah, to be completely honest, but I'm hopeful."

 

 Running back Breece Hall :   Braelon Allen 's emergence fueled trade speculation, but the Jets made it clear they didn't want to part with Hall, who's under contract through 2028 after signing a three-year, $43.5 million extension in May. Allen still is on his rookie deal, allowing the Jets to keep the Hall-Allen tandem together for at least one more season.

 Edge rusher Will McDonald IV : Their decision to retain McDonald, who requested a trade, raised a few eyebrows around the league.

 The Jets received a "significant" offer recently from the Jacksonville Jaguars , Sports Illustrated reported. One AFC personnel director told ESPN that McDonald would've been worth a second-round pick, speculating the Jets probably wanted a first-round pick.

 He's only a part-time player, averaging only 27 snaps per game over the last five, which makes the non-trade a bit curious. Glenn, who had a one-hour conversation with McDonald last Saturday, said the former first-rounder pick is a "huge part of what we're doing" and has earned more playing time.

 "His pass rush, I think we all know, is second to none," Glenn said.

 McDonald said he has "no hard feelings" toward the coaching staff, that he simply wants to be on the field. His cap charge next year is $14.4 million. Will that prompt them to re-think their position and trade him in the offseason? Stay tuned.

 Cornerback Nahshon Wright : It's a surprise that he's still around. With no role on defense, Wright told ESPN recently that he was open to a trade, a sentiment he shared with team officials. He didn't get his wish, so now he will play out (or ride the bench) the final eight games of his contract before becoming a free agent again.

 It seems odd that the Jets, who have intercepted only one pass in the last 26 games, can't find a niche for a player who made five interceptions last season.

 Nickel back Jarvis Brownlee Jr .: He appears to have lost his job to rookie  D'Angelo Ponds , the starting nickel back last week in Kansas City. That made Brownlee expendable, so why is he still a Jet? He's signed through 2027 for a minimum salary ($1.2 million). Mougey has a personal investment in Brownlee, having traded for him last year.

title: The Philadelphia Eagles' 2026 trade haul is likely to age well over time
summary: Whether Philadelphia wants to go after its QB of the future or build up around Jalen Hurts, it has options.
full_text:
The bright side for the Philadelphia Eagles  (2-7) is that once this no-good, snake-bitten, avert-your-eyes season is over with, they'll exit the dust storm with a sack full of valuable NFL draft capital that will make them power players over the next several offseasons.

 Eagles general manager Howie Roseman made sure of that.

 He pulled off a pair of trades -- one back in October and one before the trade deadline -- that surpassed expectation and promise to age well over time.

 The first was sending center Cam Jurgens and a 2027 seventh-round draft pick to the  Baltimore Ravens  for a 2028 second-round draft pick and a 2027 fifth-round pick.

 Then on Monday , the Eagles traded defensive tackle Jordan Davis to the Jacksonville Jaguars for a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-rounder.

 Add in the A.J. Brown deal this offseason that netted New England's first-round pick in 2028 and a fifth-round pick in 2027, and you're talking about a haul that will provide Philadelphia with a wealth of optionality.

 

 They have two first-round picks in both the '27 and '28 drafts, a pair of second-round selections in '28 and '29, and a total of 12 Day 1 or Day 2 selections spanning the next three years with the possibility of adding more via compensatory picks. It's a good time to be loaded up, as the next couple drafts are projected to be full of talent as some players who have stayed in college longer due to NIL money run out of eligibility.

 If the 2026 season ended today, Philadelphia would hold the No. 5 and No. 25 overall selections come April. Whether they want to go after their quarterback of the future or build up the offense around Jalen Hurts , they have the maneuverability they need.

 And they need a lot.

 The offensive line has really fallen off and the trenches on both sides of the ball need to be fortified -- an issue that only got more urgent with the decisions to trade both Davis and Jurgens. They badly need safety help and could use reinforcements at tight end, corner and running back, to name a few.

 This is not exactly screaming quick fix. And with the futures of both offensive coordinator Sean Mannion and defensive coordinator Vic Fangio up in the air -- not to mention the fate of coach Nick Sirianni -- there's a good chance some players on the current roster won't be scheme fits for what comes next. (To that end, the decision to part with Davis now for such a strong return may look prescient should the Eagles shift to a defensive system that doesn't value a run-stuffing nose tackle as highly.)

 With just two wins, the Eagles are in the throes of a season that feels similar to 2012 and 2020 when the bottom fell out and change and repair were needed.

 The outlook has been poor enough this season that the front office felt comfortable trading away of pair of starters in-season in Jurgens and Davis, the latter of which was a team captain.

 These are not waters the Eagles have found themselves swimming in much over the past couple of decades. But in the mess lay opportunity, and Roseman has found a way to capitalize on it.

title: How Kobe, LeBron, Steph and Brady are helping Jayden Daniels chase greatness
summary: The Commanders QB has tapped into some of sports' all-time greats like Brady and LeBron in search of an edge.
full_text:
ASHBURN, Va. -- Shortly after midnight in the wake of Washington's Week 8 win over the Philadelphia Eagles , quarterback Jayden Daniels exited his news conference and channeled one of his idols. Instead of driving home, Daniels took an hours detour to the Commanders' practice facility.

 He had more work to do.

 For approximately two and a half hours, Daniels worked in near silence. He lifted weights under the guidance of strength and conditioning coach Chad Englehart. The only sounds in the building came from the two men: their conversation and the clanking of weights.

 

 Daniels, who grew up as a massive Kobe Bryant fan, is well aware the  Los Angeles Lakers  legend used to work out at 4 a.m., hours before anyone else arrived. It was part of the "Mamba Mentality," a phrase based on Bryant's Black Mamba nickname. And now, Daniels has adopted similar habits in his quest to tap into his potential.

 "It's just the work ethic and the obsession to want to be better and obviously wanting to win," Daniels said. "As I got to learn more about the Mamba Mentality ... Kobe is a huge inspiration for me. You do whatever it takes to win."

 That includes talking to as many people as possible about how they succeeded, picking up tips along the way. Daniels has done so since entering the NFL as the No. 2 pick in 2024. He says it is not about trying to insert himself into the circles of famous people. It's about learning what made them great, or how they overcame injuries, scrutiny and adversity early in their careers -- situations with which Daniels has experience.

 In Washington, he leaned on Super Bowl winner and future Hall of Fame linebacker Bobby Wagner in their two seasons together. He has tapped into Hall of Fame quarterbacks Tom Brady, Drew Brees, Peyton Manning and reigning MVP Matthew Stafford . He has taken advantage of his wider profile in the sports world, establishing relationships with players such as  LeBron James , Steph Curry and Draymond Green among others. He has also picked the brain of Lakers executive Rob Pelinka, Bryant's former agent, and he routinely talks to Commanders advisor Bob Myers, the architect behind the  Golden State Warriors ' basketball dynasty.

 "All the great ones have overcome adversity at some point," Daniels said. "Everybody has to deal with it. It's good to just hear a perspective of how other people dealt with it."

 Daniels' adversity included dealing with multiple injuries, questionable in-game decisions that proved costly and even a flap about not wanting LSU to reassign his No. 5, which Daniels thought had been retired.

 What he learned from them all: Bury yourself in the work.

 That's why, after the Week 8 weight-lifting session that lasted into the wee hours, Daniels stuck around to watch film of the 27-10 win over the Eagles while it was still fresh in his mind before finally heading home around 3:30 a.m.

 "It's just all about the process and trying to get better," Daniels said. "And you just build up those callouses, that mental stuff over time and hopefully you look up and you're better than what you were at the beginning of the season."

 Here is what Daniels learned along the way.

 

 

 Manning, Brees and Brady: Daniels' Hall of Fame helpers 

 Long before Daniels picked the brains of those in places he wanted to reach, his father, Jay, had him watch interviews of Manning and Brees when he was growing up.

 The reasoning: Jay wanted to make sure young Jayden heard what time they arrived at the facility (around 5 a.m.). He wanted to show Daniels the work ethic required to achieve at the highest levels of sport.

 Now leading a franchise, Jayden no longer needs to watch videos of the quarterbacks, he can reach out to them on his own. He doesn't proclaim they're close friends; he has developed a relationship and knows they're available to him.

 

 "For him it's a genuine relationship," Jay said. "I always told him these are people who have been where you've been [or want to reach] so be a sponge around them and how they handle different situations you may face. He's really good at listening."

 Daniels has developed relationships with others, including Brady. The seven-time Super Bowl champ has broadcast multiple games featuring Daniels, and the two communicate on other occasions.

 Brady has joked with him needing to always protect himself when he runs "so he can call more of my games," Daniels said. "But it's anything I need like how did he deal with the pressure every year? He was at the top of his game for so long, how did he deal with all that?"

 Their personalities are different, Daniels said, so it's not as if he can just mimic Brady or any of these athletes, but he can adapt habits.

 "It's just a race that not many of us have really run," Myers said. "Identifying with a high-level professional athlete, it's a small group of people.

 "And then look, an NFL quarterback is probably the equivalent of an NBA star as far as tension and pressure."

 

 

 Kobe Bryant: Adopting the Mamba Mentality 
 Daniels grew up in San Bernardino, California, rooting for the Lakers and idolizing Bryant. Friends say he often wore a Bryant Lakers jersey. Even now, he often works out in a Bryant T-shirt.

 "He's always been a Kobe guy," Daniels' longtime friend Rome Weber said. "Kobe's his GOAT."

 Weber recalled a Pop Warner game when Daniels was drilled, causing him to cry. Rather than leave the game, the 8-year-old Daniels led a drive that ended with him throwing a touchdown.

 "It kind of felt like a movie," Weber said. "It brought out that Mamba Mentality."

 Daniels never formally met Bryant, who died in 2020, aside from a chance encounter at a 2008 Lakers game. Then, the 7½-year-old Daniels, who was spotted in his Kobe jersey by a Lakers staffer before the game, was selected to be one of the kids who high-fived the team as they entered the court.

 As he got older, Daniels began trying to mimic how Bryant worked, how he overcame injuries or played through pain. To learn more, he would talk to Pelinka, the Lakers president of basketball operations. Daniels initially met Pelinka at a Lakers game in the offseason after his rookie year, and he would pepper him with questions about Bryant each time they spoke.

 "Jayden really dug into Kobe, and all he stood for," Pelinka told ESPN via email. "Jayden knew that one of Kobe's most incredible attributes was his infinite curiosity. Kobe would study art or animals or geniuses -- to find ways to improve his game.

 "He always wanted to learn and grow. In getting to know Jayden, two things stood out -- Jayden was incredibly humble, but he was also incredibly curious to be great."

 Part of Bryant's greatness, Daniels believed, was his ability to overcome serious injuries -- an aspect of his career that generated particular interest to Daniels, who has missed 12 of a possible 25 games the past two seasons due to elbow, knee and hamstring injuries. And it's why Daniels wanted to return as soon as possible after his latest injury -- a dislocated left elbow suffered in Week 2. He was sidelined by the same injury last season, and a second such injury can often result in surgery. Instead, Daniels missed only two games and wears a brace to prevent his arm from extending fully.

 "When an injury occurred in Kobe's career, he completely avoided discouragement or self-pity," Pelinka said. "Instead, he embraced it as a new challenge, another 'dragon to conquer,' Kobe used to say.

 "It will be hard, but you have to actually relish that process -- and come to find a twisted joy in it. Ultimately, when you get to the top of the mountain -- and summit -- you will actually be stronger and better for the climb. Jayden really appreciated and took in that perspective."
